News.title: Volodymyr Zelensky's message to King Charles days after Donald Trump takes swipe at Ukraine leader
News.content:
Volodymyr Zelensky's message to King Charles days after Donald Trump takes swipe at Ukraine leader

The Ukrainian president and King Charles were snapped smiling and shaking hands inside Buckingham Palace before Volodymyr Zelensky thanked the monarch for his support

View 6 Images Zelensky and King Charles shake hands at Buckingham Palace (Image: Aaron Chown/PA Pool via AP)

Volodymyr Zelensky personally thanked King Charles for his "unwavering support" for Ukraine as the president met the monarch as he visited London days after a vicious attack by Donald Trump.

‌



‌



The Ukrainian leader was given a warm welcome by King Charles at Buckingham Palace before meeting Prime Minister Andy Burnham for talks. The monarch greeted the president in the Chinese Dining Room of the royal residence on Wednesday afternoon. The King and Mr Zelensky were pictured smiling as they shook hands.

‌



Charles and Mr Zelensky then moved to the King's private audience room for discussions which lasted around 25 minutes. The Ukrainian leader later shared a message on social media thanking the King for the meeting and his support.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 6 Images The president and King had a private meeting that lasted 25 minutes (Image: Getty Images)

NATO fighter jets scrambled as Russia launches massive drone attack on Ukraine READ MORE :

Mr Zelensky, on X, wrote: "I thank His Majesty King Charles III for the audience. It is important for me to have the opportunity to personally thank him for his unwavering support for Ukraine. We appreciate all the assistance provided by the United Kingdom."

‌



The Ukrainian president also was given an unprecedented honour guard, made up of troops from the Irish Guards, and arrived to loud cheers outside No10 to meet the Prime Minister.

View 6 Images Mr Zelensky met the Prime Minister for talks at No 10 (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

The Prime Minister told him: "You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain. We are behind you and that will not change."

‌



Mr Zelensky has been at the heart of a diplomatic crisis after the US President cut a deal with warmonger Vladimir Putin to buy diesel. Following his criticism at the weekend, Trump claimed it was "time for Ukraine to get a new President".

Speaking on Wednesday, Mr Zelensky said he was "thankful" for the support, saying the British people had proved "one of the strongest partners in our history".

View 6 Images The Ukrainian leader was given a honour guard made up of troops from the Irish Guards (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

‌



Following the meeting on Wednesday, a Downing Street spokeswoman said the leaders discussed "Russia's blatant indiscriminate attacks on civilians and energy infrastructure since President Trump called for an energy ceasefire".

The spokeswoman said: "It was clear that Russia had no interest in peace, the leaders underlined. Turning to how Ukraine's allies could step up support, particularly in response to Russia's barrage of jet-powered drones, the Prime Minister set out the UK's latest package of Lightweight Multirole Missiles.

View 6 Images Mr Burnham said the UK would step up support for Ukraine in the face of a barrage of Russian drone attacks (Image: BETTY LAURA ZAPATA/POOL/EPA/Shutterstock)

‌



"The UK would continue to develop innovative military solutions for use on the battlefield in Ukraine, including retrofitting British capability onto equipment gifted from other partners, the Prime Minister added.

"On long range missiles, the leaders discussed how the UK could accelerate defensive support to Ukraine ahead of the winter. The UK would also continue its diplomatic efforts to support international supplies of defensive equipment too."

The meeting comes during a period of strained relations between Ukraine and the United States after Donald Trump eased sanctions on Russian diesel last week as high fuel prices in the US threatened to overshadow November's mid-term elections. The UK responded to news of the deal by pledging to "maintain pressure on Russia".

Article continues below

View 6 Images Before meeting Mr Zelensky, the PM told the Commons that the president 'won't be going away today empty-handed' (Image: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Recent days have also seen the US president suggesting Ukraine needs a new leader and claiming Russian leader Vladimir Putin wants a peace deal more than the government in Kyiv. Concerns have also been raised about intelligence sharing from the US, with Mr Zelensky saying Kyiv had received no warning about Russian missile strikes on Monday and Tuesday.

Speaking in the Commons ahead of his meeting with Mr Zelensky, the Prime Minister said he would seek to restore Donald Trump's support for Ukraine. During Prime Minister's Questions, Mr Burnham said he was being "careful" in his language after Mr Trump's diesel deal with Russia, as he said he was "laying the ground" for a reconciliation. He added: "I will listen to President Zelensky carefully, but he won't be going away from Britain today empty-handed."

New Met Office weather maps suggest 50 locations in England could reach temperatures of 20C or more tomorrow, including London, Nottingham and Cambridge

‌

‌

‌

News.title: Most royals 'do no real work' fumes peer as he slams £100million grant to King Charles
News.content:
Most royals 'do no real work' fumes peer as he slams £100million grant to King Charles

In an explosive speech criticising the royals, former Cabinet member and Labour peer Lord George Foulkes said King Charles and co do no "real work" as he blasted the Sovereign Grant settlement

View 3 Images A Labour peer blasted the £100million grant being given to the royals - saying most of them do no 'real work' (Image: LUDOVIC MARIN, AFP via Getty Images)

A Labour peer has lashed out at a £100million grant handed over to the Royals - saying they do "no real work".

‌



‌



Former Cabinet minister Lord George Foulkes told peers The Firm offer poor value for money as he criticised the vast sum set to be handed over next year.

‌



King Charles will be given £99.9m in the Sovereign Grant by the Treasury in 2027-28. This funds the monarch's official duties, staff and upkeep of royal palaces - and the government says it offers good value for money.

‌



But former Scotland Secretary Lord Foulkes said: "While European neighbours have streamlined their monarchies, we continue to fund a sprawling network of so-called working royals.

"Working royals - this ribbon-cutting duties of pulling open a slate, a tableau . That is not real work, not like a teacher who works five days a week, or a nurse in a geriatric hospital might be working a 12-hour shift. It's not real work that they do."

Andy Burnham to welcome Zelensky to No10 after Donald Trump's latest attack READ MORE :

View 3 Images Lord George Foulkes blasted the amount of cash handed over to the Royal Family

‌



Lord Faulkes praises 'notable exception'

He went on to exclude Princess Anne as a "notable exception", stating: "Perhaps that's an example that other members of the royal family might think about."

The £99.9m settlement is down from £137.9m because a decade-long, £369m refurbishment of Buckingham Palace is finished. But the sum is three times the £31m awarded when the Sovereign Grant was created by Tory austerity Chancellor George Osborne in 2012/13.

Lashing out at the government, Lord Foulkes said: "At a time where sadly we know many of the people in this country face severe pressure on their household budgets, we here have a duty to ask two fundamental questions . First of all, are we getting value for money? And secondly, do the actions of the institution match the values that it preaches?

‌



"I would argue that in both cases, the answer is no. We hear glorious announcements on climate change, yet official reports reveal hundreds of private jet and helicopter flights for short domestic trips - one recently to the races, where the royal concerned could have easily gone by car.

"And the taxpayer has funded two new helicopters for the royal family, whereas mountain rescue for their helicopters have to raise money through charitable efforts . Now, is that right in the 21st century?"

View 3 Images Lord Foulkes singled out Princess Anne as an exception (Image: Getty Images)

‌



'A mega-rich family receive a large chunk of money'

In the year to March 31, the royal annual financial report showed £5.1m was spent on travel, £33.7m on payroll and £3.5m on housekeeping and hospitality. Property maintenance totalled £67.5m.

Nearly £127,000 was spent on travel for the King and Queen to make an official visit to Rome last April. Documents show £733,000 was spent on 177 helicopter flights over 12 months. And 60 charter flights cost £837,000 in that time.

‌



Fellow Labour peer Lord Prem Sikka said: "Under this bill, the core funding of the Royal Household — that is, after ignoring the money allocated for refurbishment of Buckingham Palace — rises from £51.8 m for 2024–25 to £99.9m for 2027–28.

"That is an increase of 97%. I'm not aware of any ordinary household that has secured an increase of this magnitude in its income to discharge its essential duties.

"The average real wage of workers has barely changed since 2008. Some 25.3 million people live below the minimum income standard. Around 300,000 people a year are dying while waiting for NHS hospital appointments.

‌



"But here we are giving away a large chunk of money. This massive increase is being given to a family which, according to Forbes magazine, could be worth £21billion."

And he continued: "Under this bill, a mega-rich family would continue to receive public money. Many people would not be happy with that arrangement at all, and clearly the government must notice that issue."

Treasury minister Lord David Pitt-Watson told the House that the settlement is justified. He said: "The Sovereign Grant supports the monarch's official duties, so it funds the staff, the official travel, the property maintenance, the essential services required for the sovereign to fulfil their unique constitutional role .

Article continues below

"That role, it extends beyond ceremonial functions; it includes hosting heads of state, supporting diplomatic engagement, representing the United Kingdom overseas, and strengthening our relationships across the Commonwealth and the world .

"These activities support UK interests, including trade, investment, security, and diplomacy . At home, the grant supports the sovereign's significant role, from recognizing charitable and voluntary service to bringing communities together across the United Kingdom . I would also note that with a new and younger monarch, there have been more activities than in the immediate past."

And he added: "The grant level provided for by this bill therefore ensures value for money for taxpayers and that the Royal Household can continue to discharge its functions effectively . In conclusion, then, I think this bill delivers a fair and proportionate funding settlement."

News.title: World's oldest shipwreck - thought to be 4,700 years old - found off coast of Turkey
News.content:
World's oldest shipwreck - thought to be 4,700 years old - found off coast of Turkey

The shipwreck dates back to the Early Bronze Age and is believed to have been built around the same time as the Great Pyramid of Giza

View 4 Images Archaeologists with artefacts from the shipwreck (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

The world's oldest-known shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, which archaeologists have dated back 4,400 to 4,700 years ago.

‌



‌



The ship was dated back to the Early Bronze Age and is believed to have been built around the same time as the construction of the Great Pyramid. Researchers said they believe the wreck could have been a trade vessel that was carrying goods across the Mediterranean Sea. The wooden structure of the ship had not survived but ceramic pots carried on the ship were remarkably discovered on the sea floor.

‌



Some of these pots incredibly even included traces of what they held inside thousands of years ago.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 4 Images The pots were recovered by divers (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Prehistoric village unearthed at Devon reservoir after water levels drop to lowest in decades READ MORE :

The wreck was discovered off the coast of Kekova Island, in Antalya, southern Turkey. The ship was around 10m long, according to the researchers from Mediterranean Archaeology Association who made the discovery.

‌



Archaeologists said they fond artefacts on an underwater slope, 30m deep into the sea. Some of the items retrieved included 30 ceramic pots and three large stone anchors.

View 4 Images The discovery was made near the coast of Kekova Island, by Antalya (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Despite the wooden structure of the ship not surviving, archaeologists were able to date the discovery to 2600-2400 BC, making it the oldest discovered shipwreck in the world.

‌



A study of the discovery, in the Journal of Maritime Archaeology, said: "Current information suggests that the shipwreck is from a small vessel that sank while sailing east to west during the Early Bronze Age."

Researchers dated wreck by analysing the shape of the ceramic pots, called amphorae, as different styles link to different periods of time. These pots had two handles on either side, a flat base and ridge in the middle.

View 4 Images A shipwreck believed to be up to 4,700 years old was discovered (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

‌



The expedition was led by Prof Hakan Öniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, and he said that matched the pottery styles from the Early Bronze Age popular in the Levant - modern-day Syria, Lebanon Palestine and Israel.

Prof Öniz said: "Comparing the decoration techniques… we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%" He added: "The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea."

The pots were brought out of the water by divers and the artefacts are now being conserved by experts. Archaeologist Dr Karin Sowada, from Macquarie University, Australia, looked the amphorae after they were recovered.

Article continues below

Dr Sowada said she was shocked to see the pots still contained a viscous, glossy residue, according to the BBC. She said: "I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots…. a lot of this material was still remaining."

Experts are now examining what the pots could have been used for as Dr Sowada suggested they could have carried wine, olive oil or tree resins.

She added: "It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge - they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years."

News.title: UK weather maps show parts of Britain braced for -4C cold snap as temperatures plunge
News.content:
UK weather maps show parts of Britain braced for -4C cold snap as temperatures plunge

Temperatures are poised to plunge as low as -4C this weekend, which is a stark contrast to the 21.8C recorded in Teddington, southwest London, on Tuesday afternoon

View 3 Images A weather map shows temperatures staying below freezing for some at midday on Sunday (Image: WX Charts)

Brits are to brace for a dramatic cold snap within days — with temperatures set to plummet as low as -4C.

‌



‌



Maps produced on Wednesday by WXCharts reveal the coldest areas will be concentrated in the north of the country, though single-figure temperatures are forecast nationwide.

‌



Higher ground in the west of Scotland could experience -1C to -4C at midday on Sunday, with 0C to 1C across the wider region. Elsewhere, the thermometer in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will range from 1C in south Wales to 6C in Southampton, 9C in Norwich, 5C in Manchester and 8C in Newcastle.

‌



This is a huge difference to the 21.8C recorded in Teddington in southwest London, and the 20.3C recorded in Pershore, Worcestershire on Tuesday afternoon. It was a balmy 19.6C as far north as Bridlington, East Yorkshire.

Body pulled from water and two missing after fishing boat vanishes off Isle of Lewis READ MORE :

I found Christmas gifts for men from £12 at clothes brand loved by David Beckham READ MORE :

View 3 Images A weather map shows temperatures as low as -4C at 6am on Sunday (Image: WX Charts)

But the areas most likely to face freezing conditions this weekend include: the Highlands, Na h-Eileanan-Siar, Argyll and Bute, Stirling, Perth and Kinross, Inverclyde, Lanarkshire, Renfrewshire, Ayrshire and Dumfries and Galloway, according to WX Charts. The coldest spot on Sunday at midday is expected to be around Argyll and Bute and the Highlands.

‌



Snow, though, is unlikely, as the Mirror previously confirmed in a weather report. The heaviest of any rain, forecast for Sunday will be across the East of England and parts of the Southeast of England.

Met Office meteorologist Honor Criswick explained that high pressure will bring dry, settled conditions over the weekend, with isolated patches of rain and showers pushing in from the north. She warned it will feel considerably chillier than the recent mild spell the country has been enjoying this week.

The forecaster's five-day outlook confirms it will be "much cooler" than of late come the weekend, with a handful of showers possible across the far north and south. BBC Weather's Darren Bett said a belt of rain and cloud will shift eastwards overnight into Friday, with colder air from the north moving southwards, reports the Express.

‌



Mr Bett added it would be considerably cooler across the entire UK this weekend, with temperatures notably lower than those experienced recently.

The forecaster anticipates dry and settled conditions on Saturday thanks to high pressure. Showers could drift into the south-east on Sunday while cloud and light rain push into the north-west, according to BBC Weather.

View 3 Images The trees around Clifton Downs in Bristol are filled with autumnal colours - today at least (Image: Tom Wren / SWNS)

‌



Met Office UK five day weather forecast

Wednesday, October 14 - Sunday, October 18

Today will be blustery across the north and particularly in north-west Scotland which will experience severe gales. Most areas will be dry and bright, with the finest sunshine in the south.

Cloud will build in the north-west, bringing patchy rain across Scotland. It will be rather warm.

Article continues below

Tonight will bring heavy rain and brisk winds spreading south-eastwards across Scotland and Northern Ireland, followed by clear spells and showers. Much of England and Wales will remain dry, with variable cloud.

News.title: 'Racist' British Army soldier with 'cannon' had horrific plans for UK, court hears
News.content:
'Racist' British Army soldier with 'cannon' had horrific plans for UK, court hears

British Army chef Mark Broadhurst, 28, had a terrifying array of weaponry including explosives and a court has heard he had been communicating with now convicted terrorists for nearly two years

View 2 Images Mark Broadhurst has been sentenced for terror-linked offences (Image: Counter Terroism Police)

A serving British Army soldier has been jailed for almost four years after he made explosives and a "homemade cannon" while promoting extreme right-wing views and talking of raising a militia.

‌



‌



British Army chef Mark Broadhurst, 28, was arrested at Catterick Garrison, North Yorkshire, in September 2024 and a range of weaponry and explosive substances was then found at his home in Chesterfield, Derbyshire, Sheffield Crown Court was told.

‌



When police raided his quarters at the barracks and his home address, they found gun powder and a home-made cannon, described by an expert as "crude" and similar to a 14th century gun. He was also found to have crossbows and bolts, six large knives and a baseball bat.

‌



He wanted to be "in history books and criminal records" for terrorism and killing police officers, the court heard.

View 2 Images British Army chef Mark Broadhurst was arrested at Catterick Garrison (Image: PA)

Teenager accidentally shot dead by pal with air rifle at drunken house party READ MORE :

Mr Justice Hilliard jailed him for 46 months after the soldier admitted possessing explosives and a firearms offence. At a previous hearing, Broadhurst denied the offences were terror-related, but the judge found that he was trying to impress other members of extreme right-wing groups and encourage them in their violent, racist and anti-authority ideology.

‌



Matthew Donkin KC, prosecuting, said most of the activity surrounding the offending happened before he joined the army. Counter terror police became aware of Broadhurst while carrying out investigations on other members of extreme right-wing groups and saw his messages on two online forums.

Mr Donkin said: "The things he was posting were hateful, racist, aggressive and they demonstrated clear, extreme right-wing beliefs and views."

The messages demonstrated a hatred of “black, Asian, Muslim and Jewish people”, the prosecution said. He made references to anarchy, the end of society and his preparedness to bring this about, the Crown said. Broadhurst had shared the online order he made for the ingredients to make gunpowder.

‌



The court heard evidence that Broadhurst had been communicating with now convicted terrorists Christopher Ringrose, Brogan Stewart and Marco Pitzettu for nearly two years on Facebook and Telegram.

Jim Littlehales, defending, read a reference from a superior officer which described the chef as “excellent at mentoring junior members of the catering team” and said he worked to the highest standards. Mr Littlehales said the firearm he made was not used to threaten anyone.

The judge sentenced Broadhurst on the basis that he made the weapon and gunpowder so he would be taken seriously by other members of the extreme right-wing groups.

‌



After the sentencing, Detective Chief Superintendent James Dunkerley, head of Counter Terrorism Policing North East, said: “Whilst Broadhurst pleaded guilty to these offences, he did not accept that his intent had a terrorist motivation.

“A thorough investigation was conducted which uncovered an extreme right-wing mindset and he was engaging in extensive conversations online with other individuals who hold similar views. He was proactively ordering components to make explosives, plus he amassed multiple weapons including firearms.

“After hearing the extensive evidence compiled throughout our investigation, the judge was satisfied his offending had a terrorist connection. I welcome the sentence handed down to Broadhurst which reflects his mindset and the danger he posed to the public.”

‌



Frank Ferguson, Head of the Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said: “Mark Broadhurst was clearly interested in violence and developing weapons that had the ability to cause untold harm to innocent people.

“He was immersed in extremist material and maintained close contact with three now-convicted terrorists inspired by SS tactics and supremacist ideology over a prolonged period.

“The prosecution was able to use evidence from Broadhurst’s own devices and online communications, which meant he had little choice but to admit his guilt. There was simply no legitimate or lawful explanation for Broadhurst having these illegal weapons and explosives inside his bedroom.

Article continues below

“Where individuals acquire weapons or explosives to further their extremist beliefs, we will always work closely with Counter Terrorism Policing to make sure they are brought before the courts and any terrorist activity is disrupted at an early stage.”

News.title: 'I caught the new American Covid XFG - new symptom left me calling my mum for help'
News.content:
'I caught the new American Covid XFG - new symptom left me calling my mum for help'

EXCLUSIVE: As Coronavirus cases soar across the UK, two women explain what it's really like to catch the new XFG strain, otherwise known as American Covid or Stratus

View 5 Images A new Covid strain is doing the rounds as flu numbers rise, with Georgia Bondy suffering new symptoms

A new Covid strain is sweeping across the country with cases doubling and hospital admissions up five-fold this month.

‌



‌



But it's also cold and flu season, leaving Brits at risk of an array of different illnesses just before Christmas.

‌



Latest figures from the UK Health and Security Agency (UKHSA) show that positive Covid cases recorded in hospital settings had climbed from 5.9 per cent to 7 per cent in just a matter of weeks.

‌



Two women unfortunate enough to have caught the latest XFG strain - also known as American Covid - have now revealed how it compares to previous mutations and the surprising warning signs to look out for...

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

'The worst came after my negative test'

For Georgia Bondy, 32, from Walthamstow, the most alarming part was how unwell she felt after she had started testing negative.

‌



The woman, who has multiple sclerosis (MS), first noticed a scratchy throat on September 6 before testing positive for Covid the following day.

During the week she was testing positive, she experienced shortness of breath but said she was not particularly tired and was still able to work. However, after she began testing negative, her condition strangely deteriorated.

XFG variant symptoms as American Covid cases soar in the UK READ MORE :

View 5 Images Georgia has been diagnosed with MS and needs to take extra precautions around viruses

‌



"I was exhausted," she tells The Mirror. "I couldn't stand up for long, it felt like I couldn't breathe properly." She also described struggling to move around normally and said it took a while for her to recover.

For Georgia, who first caught Covid in 2021, the experience was particularly difficult because the worst of her symptoms appeared to come after the initial infection. "It was strange how it felt horrible after I tested negative and the Covid left me feeling tired," she explains.

She says that her disability affects her body's ability to regulate its temperature, meaning she cannot rely on a fever as a warning sign when she becomes ill.

‌



Georgia lives with her partner and isolated during the infection. She also believes that much like the NHS data shows, the number of people becoming ill has increased since the beginning of September. "I know who I got it from, they showed up to a meeting and were coughing their guts up," she says.

The experience has left her concerned about how easily illnesses can spread when people continue attending work and social events while symptomatic. "People should stay home," she argues. "We need to get better at saying if you're feeling unwell, it's great if you still want to work, but stay home so other people are safe."

Georgia runs an organisation supporting disabled people and says the impact of Covid has not disappeared for those living with underlying health conditions.

‌



Although she works from home, she regularly attends in-person meetings and said other people may not realise she is vulnerable.

"I don't look disabled, I look fairly young, so when you're on the train, no one looks at me and thinks that person might be at risk, or in a meeting people always see me as healthy," she says.

Through her work with Disability Rights UK, Georgia repeatedly hears from disabled people who remain concerned about Covid and the consequences of infection.

‌



"For them, the pandemic is not done, it's not done, we're still dying from Covid, we're still getting long Covid on top of our pre-existing health conditions," she warns.

She acknowledged that death rates are lower than during 2020 but warned against overlooking the impact of long Covid, which can leave people with debilitating symptoms long after their initial infection.

'The rash suddenly spread'

Another 34-year-old woman who previously caught Covid in 2020 tells us that her latest infection brought back familiar symptoms of a cough, sore throat and crushing fatigue. But there was one unexpected difference - a furious, itchy rash that appeared across her body.

‌



"It really knocked me for six this time," the unnamed sufferer says. "I had a heavy head, [like] it was filled with concrete."

The woman, from Burgess Hill, said her symptoms seemed to improve before suddenly returning, leaving her feeling as though she was experiencing the illness in waves.

Her symptoms initially began with cold-like signs, alongside a small rash on her neck that appeared on a Friday before disappearing after a couple of hours.

‌



But by Sunday morning, the rash had spread to her face, leg and neck, leaving her skin looking angry and feeling intensely itchy. "I didn't go to the GP, but I had a mad rash all over my body," she explains.

View 5 Images UKHSA chart shows cases are higher than previous years (Image: UKHSA)

Worried she might have measles, she contacted her mum, who works in a hospital and suggested the rash could be connected to Covid. The woman subsequently took a Covid test, which came back positive.

‌



She tried taking an antihistamine, but said it did little to ease the rash, which continued to disappear and flare up again over the following days.

The woman says that the most difficult part of her latest Covid infection was also the exhaustion and the way her symptoms repeatedly returned. "I found it would come in waves, I'd start to feel better, then bam it would hit you again," she explains.

She also experienced a sore throat, cough and fluctuations in temperature, describing periods when she felt cold enough to need to get under a blanket.

‌



Despite the discomfort, she did not lose her sense of taste or smell, just as she had not during her first infection. Her husband subsequently caught Covid, experiencing fatigue, a cough and sore throat, although he did not develop the same rash.

View 5 Images A contagious Covid variant is on the rise (Image: Shutterstock/ozrimoz)

The woman said she spent much of her illness resting at home, even though she felt she could technically have gone out. "It's like feeling like you're in lockdown again," she says. "I know you can go out, but I felt a sense of responsibility to stay inside."

‌



More than a week after her infection began, her cough had improved considerably, although she was still experiencing what she described as a "wooly head".

She also noticed that Covid tests appeared to be in short supply when she went to collect some, and her mum had encountered the same problem when trying to buy one.

How can I tell if I have Covid or the flu?

Wendy Lee, deputy superintendent pharmacist at Well Pharmacy, says that Covid remains a respiratory infection, with symptoms that can overlap with those of colds and flu.

‌



"Similar to these other infections, Covid spreads from person-to-person through breathing, sneezing and coughing," she explains.

"The symptoms of any respiratory infection are similar with a high temperature, tiredness, a new continuous cough and a loss of taste or smell among the most common reported symptoms."

Wendy highlighted a hoarse throat as a possible early sign of the XFG Covid variant, which has also been referred to as Stratus. "It is the symptom that many patients have reported as an early sign."

‌



However, the XFG variant is not entirely new. The UKHSA said on October 8 that it had been circulating in the UK and other countries for around a year.

The rash experienced by the woman from Burgess Hill is also something that requires caution when interpreting symptoms.

View 5 Images Wendy Lee urges those eligible to get the flu jab

‌



Wendy said a rash is not commonly recognised as a symptom of Covid or flu, although skin changes can sometimes occur when the immune system is activated.

"It is important to speak to a medical professional especially if the rash does not fade when a glass is pressed against it or the rash or the patient is suffering from a high fever that does not respond to medication, stiff neck or confusion," she says.

Away from the new Covid strain, the term "super flu" has been flying around online amid concerns about flu circulating earlier than usual, but the symptoms described by pharmacists are consistent with typical influenza.

‌



Lee says people should look out for headaches, chills, a high fever, persistent dry cough, sore throat and a runny nose. Loss of appetite, sickness and diarrhoea can also occur.

She said Well Pharmacy is seeing increasing numbers of people seeking flu remedies and pain relief, alongside more requests for Covid tests.

"People may think Covid is long gone so may not be using hand sanitiser as often as they should," she says. "Self-isolating while unwell also seems to be a thing of the past."

‌



She added that colder, wetter weather and people spending more time indoors create favourable conditions for respiratory viruses to spread.

While many otherwise healthy adults will recover from Covid or flu at home, both illnesses can have more serious consequences for vulnerable people.

Wendy says: "For most healthy adults, a bout of covid or flu will mean a miserable few days at home in bed, but frail and vulnerable patients – particularly the immunosuppressed – should be especially concerned, because the virus could be fatal."

‌



She urged people who are eligible for vaccination to take up the offer when contacted. "The vaccine is designed primarily to reduce the risk of becoming seriously unwell with COVID-19, rather than guaranteeing that you won’t catch the virus."

In England, the free NHS flu vaccine is available to eligible groups, including people aged 65 and over, pregnant women, people with certain long-term health conditions, care home residents and some carers and household contacts of people with weakened immune systems.

People should check the current NHS eligibility criteria for both flu and Covid vaccinations, as the eligible groups and arrangements differ between programmes.

Article continues below

Wendy also advised people to maintain good personal hygiene and stay at home when unwell to reduce the risk of spreading infection.

"If you do become unwell, it is best to stay at home to prevent spreading the virus to others - especially those less able to fend off these nasty bugs," she says.

For people who develop symptoms, a pharmacist can offer advice on managing them, suitable treatments and whether further medical assessment is needed.

News.title: Musk says US government may be behind curbs on Ukraine's use of Starlink internet
News.content:
Elon Musk has suggested that the US government may be behind restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connected to his Starlink internet network.

Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said unexpected new speed limits were disrupting its battlefield missions.

An advisor to president Zelensky said he believed the restrictions were not a co-incidence and were related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington

Musk said that Starshield, the military-grade sister service to Starlink, is controlled by the US government, and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]".

Musk - writing on X - had been responding to pleas from Ukrainian officials to restore connectivity, including from President Volodymyr Zelensky who told UK media: "I hope that it's a mistake, maybe huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to... switch (it) on."

Starlink, which is owned by Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.

It had been partially restored by Wednesday evening, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said.

"Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," he wrote on X, thanking Elon Musk and asking for his "continued support".

About an hour later, Musk replied to that post, defending his company's involvement.

"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote.

Musk added that Starlink is for "civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company".

The US government has not commented.

While both companies are owned by Musk's SpaceX, Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas, while Starshield is designed for government and military use.

The restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine, that killed several people in Kyiv, officials said, and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.

At least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity, and residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit.

"It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation, Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning.

News.title: We are behind you and that will not change, PM tells Zelensky
News.content:
"We are behind you and that will not change," Andy Burnham has told Volodymyr Zelensky, as he hosted the Ukrainian leader in Downing Street.

Zelensky was in London as part of efforts to reinforce backing from allies after Donald Trump called for him to go and lifted sanctions on Russian diesel.

The prime minister said Ukraine was willing to discuss an energy ceasefire proposed by the US president but said Russia's response had been "further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine".

Zelensky said: "Our people, we survived and continue to do this because we have strong partners and I'm very proud that we have one of the strongest partners in our history and it's your people, Andy."

The Ukrainian president was greeted with a hug from Burnham, cheers from civil servants and a rare honour guard as he arrived in Downing Street.

Ahead of Zelensky's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones.

News.title: Russell Brand was a 'sexual predator', prosecution alleges as rape trial begins
News.content:
The fourth complainant says Brand pushed her up against a wall at Capital Radio in 2004 or 2005 and kissed her "sloppily and aggressively", and "grabbed her body, at her breasts, sides and buttocks, aggressively".

She was able to push him away and he "just sniggered, like it was a joke", the prosecutor said.

The jury then heard how the fifth complainant says she met Brand when he was performing at the Hammersmith Apollo in London in 2009.

The prosecution said their encounter began with consensual activity, but that he raped her anally on a later occasion.

The jury heard how the woman "spent months and years blaming herself", becoming anxious and unwell.

They were told Brand texted the woman after seeing her at an event the following summer, saying: "I wanna push you further."

She is said to have replied: "I think you pushed me far enough â you treated me like an animal." He allegedly replied: "I'm sorry."

The sixth complainant - who has accused Brand of sexual assault - says he demanded a massage when she was on a work assignment in 2009.

He "fell to his knees and placed his head directly into her groin area", the prosecution said.

After the accounts of the final two women were heard, the prosecutor said Brand told police in 2023 "he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity, and that any accounts had been reinvented or imagined after a defamatory documentary and subsequent press reporting".

On Wednesday afternoon, Brand's former flatmate Mark Pinheiro was the first witness to give evidence.

Pinheiro told jurors that Brand had told him he may have gone a "bit too far" with a woman when visiting the Labour Party conference in 1999.

"He said that things got a little bit heated and a little bit out of hand, and he thinks that maybe he did go a little bit too far.

"Those were his words - 'I think I may have gone a bit too far'."

Pinheiro was pressed under cross-examination about whether he accurately remembered the comment, but he told the court he was sure Brand had said "things may have gone a little bit too far" or "I may have taken things a little too far".

The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.

Brand was accompanied by his wife Laura to the court on Wednesday.

He rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. In recent years, he has turned to podcasting and now lives in Florida in the United States.

News.title: Sally Rooney books withdrawn in UK over Palestine Action support
News.content:
Normal People author Sally Rooney has said her novels will no longer be supplied to booksellers in the UK as a result of her support for Palestine Action.

The Irish novelist said last year she intended to carry on using her royalties to support the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK.

In a statement to BBC News, Rooney said further publication of her work could constitute a "serious criminal offence", so she had agreed with her publisher Faber not to continue supplying her books in the UK.

"I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences," she said.

Ebook editions have already been removed from sale in the UK, although many book shops still have existing stock of physical copies.

Waterstones confirmed to the BBC that Faber had advised there were no restrictions on booksellers keeping their current copies on the shelves.

Rooney has sold more than six million books globally, including 2.3 million in the UK, according to NielsenIQ BookData.

Normal People was released in 2018 and turned into a hit TV series two years later, effectively launching the acting careers of Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones.

Rooney's other novels are Intermezzo, Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You.

Publisher Faber told BBC News: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work.

"To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.

"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format."

Faber added: "We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories."

News.title: Drop-off charges at UK airports to be reviewed after sharp increase
News.content:
Airport drop-off charges are to be reviewed by the government following sharp price increases in recent years.

Prices at major UK airports have risen by a third since the summer of 2025 on average, according to one analysis, with Gatwick and Stansted drop-off charges found to be the most expensive, jumping from Â£7 to Â£10.

Such charges at Edinburgh Airport have risen from Â£6 to Â£8.50, while fees at Bournemouth increased from Â£5 to Â£8, the same price as Leeds Bradford and London City.

The Department for Transport confirmed it had committed to a review, saying it was "vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly".

The government added it hoped airports would "exercise restraint on rises, particularly where there are limited public transport alternatives".

News.title: What we know about the Pope's lung cancer diagnosis
News.content:
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer but had a successful surgery to remove part of his right lung, the Vatican has confirmed.

The Pope, 71, underwent a 90-minute surgery on Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, where he is expected to stay for about a week.

BBC Southern and Eastern Europe Correspondent Sarah Rainsford is in St. Peter's Square in the Vatican as people sent their well wishes to the pontiff.

News.title: Family pays tribute to 'warm and engaging' man killed in tiger attack
News.content:
The family of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure at a wildlife park has paid tribute, describing him as "bright, warm and engaging".

William Chapman, 23, visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday and was attacked after going into the animal's pen. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

In a statement, his family said that he had suffered from "significant mental illness" over a number of years and had been prescribed "strong medication".

His family added: "It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death. We would ask everybody to respect that process."

City of Doncaster Council has launched a health and safety investigation into Chapman's death.

The park remains closed and a reopening date has not yet been confirmed.

"William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved - and William loved them back," a statement released on Tuesday evening said.

The family also asked for privacy, saying "the publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time".

"The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened," the statement continued.

"The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did."

News.title: Container ship hit by projectile sinks in Strait of Hormuz, Singapore says
News.content:
A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporean authorities.

All 21 crew members of GFS Pride were evacuated and no injuries were reported after the attack on Tuesday, which caused damage and a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said.

Another Singapore-flagged container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage after being hit by a projectile on Wednesday but was able to reach a safe anchorage with all 22 crew, it added.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines and sank while passing through what they called an "unauthorised" route in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Guards released photos that appeared to show a plume of black smoke rising from a container vessel that was still afloat but down by the stern. In other photos, dozens of containers and their contents could be seen floating in the water.

The Hydrographer of Pakistan warned mariners that GFS Pride had sunk 4 nautical miles (7.4km) north-west of Ras al-Sheikh Masud in Oman's Musandam Peninsula.

Meanwhile, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said that two unnamed container ships had reported being struck by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz between 16:40 and 17:00 GMT on Tuesday.

Both vessels sustained minor damage and were able to continue their passages, it added.

News.title: Civil servant faked illness with make-up to juggle five jobs, court hears
News.content:
A civil servant is accused of earning almost Â£350,000 by juggling five full-time public sector roles - using sick notes and working from home to cope with the workload.

Kashim Chowdhury allegedly held multiple government jobs between February 2020 and September 2023, earning Â£350,000 overall.

The jury at Southwark Crown Court has been told he wore white make-up during a video call with his boss to try to look ill, but the make-up began peeling off his skin.

Chowdury, a 55-year-old from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud, which he denies. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.

The jury was told that Chowdhury got jobs by making ''false representations'' about his employment status whilst applying. Over three years he held overlapping jobs at Tower Hamlets Council in east London, the Home Office, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the UK Health Security Agency and the Department of Health and Social Care.

The jury was told that in 2023 his manager at the Health Security Agency, Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him to discuss his sick leave.

Ms Adams claims Chowdhury was wearing make-up on his face to appear ill - and that during the meeting the make-up started to separate on his forehead showing his real skin underneath. At the time of the call he is alleged to have been paid for five full time jobs.

Lucy Organ, for the prosecution, told the court: "There could be no doubt about it, the defendant had applied make-up to his face for this Teams meeting to try and pretend to his line manager that he was unwell.

"This almost laughable incident demonstrates, we say, quite how far the defendant was willing to go in his deceit."

Prosecutors say Chowdhury "exploited" the work from home culture that began during the Covid pandemic. The court was told that Chowdhury had told his employers that he had to work from home to care for his "unwell" mother.

But the prosecutor, Ms Organ, said his workload eventually became "too much to cope with" and his performance suffered.

The court heard that he was signed off work from some jobs due to "mixed anxiety and a depressive disorder", but he did not hand his sick note to all his employers.

Jurors heard that the alleged fraud came to light after the National Fraud Initiative alerted Defra to them.

The trial continues.

News.title: I do not have confidence UK is safe from Russian threats, says Swinney
News.content:
Asked about the MI5 chief's comments, the first minister said he was "very worried" about a "lack of coastal and offshore protection".

He identified waters north of Shetland as an area of significant Russian activity.

"I don't think we've got nearly the presence in those areas that we require today," he told BBC Scotland News.

"There's an obligation on the United Kingdom government to make sure that the country is safe. And I don't think the defence posture of the United Kingdom enables me to have that confidence."

Scotland is home to the UK's nuclear submarine fleet at Faslane, west of Glasgow. The SNP wants those weapons to be removed, but is in favour of an independent Scotland joining Nato.

Swinney insisted that independence would not hamper Scotland's security, but rather give the country "more choices".

The SNP leader said he had "always been a believer in defence co-operation between Scotland and other countries", citing Canada joining the EU's SAFE defence programme, external.

Responding to the first minister's comments, a Ministry of Defence Spokesperson said:

"The first duty of government is to keep its citizens safe, and this government is investing Â£298bn over the next four years to ensure we can tackle rising threats.

"The Navy is helping to patrol Nato's northern flank, with this year's carrier strike group deploying to the Arctic and the high north.

"To tackle these threats, we're also investing in new frigates for the Navy and high-tech uncrewed vessels as part of our Hybrid Navy, backed by Â£1.5bn in funding."

Delivering a speech at the UN General Assembly, external last month, Burnham said his government would invest in defence and build up the UK's "hard power and deterrence".

He added: "But we will not play Russia's game of trading escalatory rhetoric. Unlike Russia, we do not seek confrontation."

News.title: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show
News.content:
Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City football club's chairman while mayor of Greater Manchester, it has emerged.

The PM dined with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches in 2017 and 2018 - but this was not detailed in a statement on Monday by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) about his meetings with the club.

Burnham has been under pressure to clarify his previous discussions with Man City since the club was found guilty of having "systematically" broken Premier League rules, which it will appeal.

The PM, who was mayor until June, sparked widespread controversy when he said last month he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners now sold up.

On Monday, the GMCA released a statement about Burnham's meetings with Man City in his role as mayor for the region for almost a decade.

The statement said he had a formal meeting with Al Mubarak in October 2021 at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit, arranged by the Department for International Trade; and that he met the club chairman "informally in the stands" at a testimonial match in 2019 for former player Vincent Kompany.

It also said that "in his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions".

But the statement did not specify that this referred to, external two hospitality dinners he had with the Manchester City chairman at separate matches.

A previous GMCA register of declarations for Burnham, seen by the BBC, detailed a "dinner with [then-Manchester City Council leader] Richard Leese and Chair of Man City" for an Everton match at the Etihad stadium in August 2017, valued at Â£300 for hospitality.

Below is another entry for "dinner with the Chairman at the Man City/Man Utd derby at the Etihad" in April 2018, valued at approximately Â£699.

Burnham previously declared those dinners, alongside a Â£150 pair of tickets to see Ed Sheeran perform at the stadium in May 2018.

But the register of declarations has since been deleted from the GMCA website, as first reported by The Sun. The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term.

News.title: Driving test waits fall to two-year low - but still average 20 weeks
News.content:
Waiting times for driving tests have dropped below 20 weeks for the first time since November 2024, according to official figures.

But learner drivers in September still had to wait an average of 19.7 weeks, or around five months, for a practical test.

The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) has been trying to cut waiting times and clear a backlog which began during the Covid pandemic in 2020.

Commenting on the agency's progress, one driving instructor told the BBC: "I don't think this is anything to boast about."

The DVSA initially had hoped to reduce the average waiting time to seven weeks by the end of last year.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander pushed the target back to summer 2026, but subsequently admitted even that would not be possible - with waits not expected to fall to seven weeks until next autumn.

The DVSA conducted 191,682 practical driving tests in September, with more than half of those passing.

Learner drivers have repeatedly told the BBC how a lack of access to driving tests has limited their freedom, education and job prospects.

Until earlier this year, many learner drivers chose to pay inflated prices to access driving tests being resold by third party providers who'd used automated programmes, or bots, to block book tests before learners could access them.

But a number of changes were made to the test booking system earlier this year by the DVSA to stop the system being exploited. Now, only the learner driver is able to book their driving test.

News.title: Teen shot friend by mistake, inquest told
News.content:
A teenager told an inquest he fatally shot his friend with an air rifle at a house party after mistaking the trigger for the safety catch.

Connor Bell, 17, from Tadley, had been drinking with friends at a house in Chineham, near Basingstoke, on 8 November 2025 when he was hit by a pellet fired by Jack Beechy, the Winchester inquest heard.

The pellet entered through his right eye socket, causing an "unsurvivable" brain injury and cardiac arrest. He died at Southampton General Hospital two days later.

Coroner Jason Pegg recorded a conclusion of accidental death, exacerbated by a lack of weapons-handling skills.

The inquest heard Joshua Brown, now 18, had agreed with his parents that only a couple of friends would come round and the air rifle would stay locked in a cupboard.

But he said more friends came than he had told his parents about, and the group drank vodka, cider and beer.

He took out the .177 calibre rifle and it was used to shoot at bottles in the garden from the conservatory.

Beechy, now 18, said he was "a little bit drunk" when Brown asked him to put the rifle away.

He fired off the remaining pellets from the conservatory because he "thought it would be safer", believing the gun was then empty.

Beechy said that as he walked into the kitchen, with Bell standing nearby, he fired the rifle by mistake.

News.title: 'Dark day for Lewis' as one fisherman dead and two missing
News.content:
Police say a body has been found in the search for three men who were onboard a fishing boat that has gone missing off the Western Isles.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) said the alarm was raised about 21:20 on Tuesday when it emerged the boat, called the Kilda, was overdue from Lewis.

A plane, two helicopters, two lifeboats and volunteers searched off the Port of Ness in north Lewis. Police have warned the public not to make their own searches due to bad weather.

Local councillor Kenneth Macleod said it was a "very dark day" for islanders, and their thoughts were with the families of the three men, and First Minister John Swinney said his heart went out to those involved.

Police Scotland said the man's body was found about 02:45, but the remaining two men and their boat remained unaccounted for.

News.title: Swimmer Archie Goodburn thanks prime minister as brain cancer review announced
News.content:
Swimmer Archie Goodburn has been successful in his efforts to improve brain cancer care for patients as the UK government announce new measures.

The Scottish athlete, who was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours two years ago, met Prime Minister Andy Burnham after making a tearful TV appeal for more investment to be put into brain cancer research.

After the meeting, Burnham announced a new national brain cancer clinical lead and promised a review of brain cancer progress and action to get patients treatment sooner.

Goodburn, 25, thanked the prime minister and said all three of his requests have been "promised to some extent" but "fleshing out" needs to be done on the details.

The prime minister described the swimmer an "inspiration to us all" and said he was "delighted" to welcome him to Downing Street.

Burnham said: "He has spoken passionately about the need for change on brain cancer, and he's right: progress hasn't been good enough, here or anywhere else.

"Families facing this disease can't afford to wait."

Goodburn reached the final of the 50m breaststroke at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

He said he went for medical tests after suffering from numbness and seizures during training for the 2024 Olympic trials.

He was diagnosed with three large oligodendrogliomas, a rare type of cancer which can affect the brain and spinal cord.

The Edinburgh-born athlete underwent chemotherapy and radiotherapy to treat the tumours, but surgery to remove them was found to be impossible.

News.title: Semenyo 'froze' after alleged racist abuse, court told
News.content:
Footballer Antoine Semenyo "froze" after he was allegedly racially abused by a Liverpool fan during a Premier League match at Anfield, a court has heard.

The Manchester City winger, who was playing for Bournemouth at the time, was preparing to take a throw-in when Mark Mogan, 47, allegedly shouted a racist insult at him on 15 August 2025.

Prosecutors said Semenyo was "clearly hurt and upset" and reported the incident to referee Anthony Taylor when the ball next went out of play.

Mogan, of Dovecot, Liverpool, denies racially aggravated behaviour.

Liverpool Magistrates' Court heard Mogan, who uses a wheelchair, shouted an offensive slur about 30 minutes into the opening match of the Premier League season.

Prosecutor Simon Jones said: "Mr Semenyo briefly froze as he couldn't believe what the male had said."

News.title: Man City v PSG LIVE: Bizarre Donnarumma blunder punctures momentum of City’s Champions League comeback
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Manchester City were left stunned by a “ridiculous” performance from Paris Saint-Germain as the Champions League holders ran riot and scored three first-half goals at the Etihad, in front of the former City manager Pep Guardiola.

Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha struck for the visitors and Achraf Hakimi hit the post in a rampant 17-minute spell, as PSG became the first team to score three first-half goals against Manchester City away from home since Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool in November 2015.

City were playing their first match at home since they were found guilty of almost all of the club’s breaches of the Premier League financial rules. With City appealing the decision and continuing to maintain their innocence, Enzo Maresca’s side were supported by former manager Guardiola, who returned to the Etihad for the first time since his departure in May.

But PSG were too good for City in a stunning first half and former England international Owen Hargreaves said: “The quality of the touches and finishing [from PSG] is exquisite. That is as good as I’ve seen live maybe ever. Technically this is best of what the Premier League has to offer and they’ve put on a masterclass.”

Follow updates from Man City v PSG, below

News.title: ICE rejects suggestion that its officers wear body cameras that automatically activate
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Federal immigration officials need to ensure that body cameras worn by officers are uniformly activated when needed, a government report released Wednesday said, following a series of contentious shootings and aggressive arrests by ICE officers.

The agency rejected the recommendation, saying that using cameras that automatically activate when an officer pulls their weapon or activates a car siren could risk privacy concerns.

ICE has come under intense scrutiny after numerous incidents where officers have opened fire during enforcement operations and the agency has claimed they were under threat but officers weren't wearing body cameras. Critics say the cameras could help hold officers accountable and promote transparency at a time when the agency is operating at a high tempo across the country and increasingly accused of excessive use of force. The report by the Government Accountability Office covers the period from February 2025 until September of this year. The report, conducted at the request of Democratic members of Congress, delves into policies governing the use of body-worn cameras by ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection and details improvements both agencies can make to improve their programs. But it did not go into any of the high-profile ICE-involved shootings that have focused attention on the agency’s body-worn camera usage, such as the shooting deaths of Renee Good in Minneapolis or Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston.

A fatal shooting exposed gaps in ICE’s camera rollout

Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem announced in February that every Homeland Security officer on the ground in Minneapolis would be issued body-worn cameras. Noem, who was later fired by Trump, said officers across the country would receive them as funds became available.

The department later received $20 million from Congress to finish the ICE body-camera rollout plan. But then came a shooting in July of Salgado Araujo, when Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers shot and killed the Mexican man who lived in the U.S. for more than 35 years. Those officers were not wearing body cameras, raising questions about why the agency still hadn't gotten the cameras out to officers in the field. Homeland Security said after Salgado Araujo’s death that body cameras had been deployed to more than half of ICE field offices and that the remainder would get them in the next 60 days. In the GAO report, DHS said all ICE offices had received the body-worn cameras as of Aug. 5 and that officers were being trained on their use.

In a statement Wednesday, DHS said that while they'd purchased devices for all ICE officers across the country, the required training was still ongoing and that they expected to be finished “soon.”

DHS rejects automatic recording, citing privacy concerns

The report recommended ICE take additional steps such as “automated camera activation” that it said would be particularly helpful in situations where “unexpected and unplanned incidents, unrelated to sensitive operations, result in use of force by or against personnel.” The report said this would improve transparency and public trust. But DHS disagreed, saying that cameras that automatically activate could result in “the unauthorized recording of sensitive interactions with informants or victims.” The agency said the body-worn cameras are required to be turned on at the beginning of pre-planned enforcement activities.

Confusion over camera rules kept one ICE office from using them

The report also said some of the officers they talked to at both ICE and CBP were confused as to when they should activate the cameras. For example, some officers told the GAO they didn't know whether to activate the cameras during vehicle searches or when transporting detainees. The report noted that at one ICE office, staff was so uncertain about when they were supposed to use the cameras that they hadn't begun using them even after they'd been trained.

The report also found that neither agency had updated the plans that oversee their body-worn camera programs even as their staff had grown significantly.

News.title: Diddy’s prison injury was result of fight with drug lord: report
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

New details have come to light about Sean “Diddy” Combs’ reported hospitalization over the weekend.

According to TMZ, the disgraced music mogul was left with a head injury after he got into a fight with convicted drug lord known as Dudus.

Combs, 56, was reportedly treated at the hospital for a non life-threatening injury and taken back that night to the Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey, where he is serving 50 months behind bars after he was convicted on two counts of transportation for prostitution last July.

The reported altercation occurred Friday night after Dudus, whose real name is Christopher Coke, confronted Combs about getting their fellow inmates in trouble, according to TMZ.

Dudus and other inmates were reportedly “pissed” that Combs was exposed by a recent NBC News report for allegedly living a lavish life in prison that included using a contraband phone and drugs.

open image in gallery Diddy reportedly got into a fight with fellow inmate Christopher Coke ( Getty )

The outlet said that after the bombshell report, prison officials raided the facility twice and confiscated cell phones from Dudus and other inmates, leaving them furious.

Dudus, a kingpin who was arrested on drug charges and extradited to the U.S. from Jamaica in 2010, has been serving a 23-year prison sentence since 2012.

The Independent has reached out to Combs’ representatives for comment.

Regarding Combs’ hospitalization, a spokesperson for rapper previously told The Independent: “We are aware of the reports concerning Sean Combs and are working to confirm the circumstances. Sean’s health and well-being are our immediate concern, and we appreciate everyone who has reached out.”
