World.title: These workers help train robots who could one day steal their jobs
World.content:
These workers help train robots who could one day steal their jobs

Faven Mulugeta for NPR

KARUR, India — Three men stride across a cavernous textile factory floor of Texworth in the southern Indian city of Karur, handing GoPros and smart glasses to workers, including 40-year-old Shoba Kirubakaran. She's packing yellow aprons decorated with chickens into plastic wrapping for the brand Designs By Danica. It's the third time Kirubakaran says she's been told to don a GoPro.

It's recording her every hand gesture, to train AI robots to take over this job — a fact that she says the company did not share with her. NPR informed her when they interviewed her on a recent day. "Nobody told me anything about it," she says.

Sponsor Message

Kirubakaran has worked in the factory for 10 years, six days a week, from around 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. She makes $90 a month. With that money, she's helped her husband, a rickshaw driver, raise their two sons. And she adds, "I only know how to do this job."

Scenes like these shook the Indian public in April after a video went viral showing rows of textile factory workers wearing these headsets. "This is not a scene from a science fiction film," warned one news anchor from outlet News9Live. "That is happening right now on factory floors across India." Another outlet, AsiaNet News warned: "Indian workers are training AI robots to take their jobs."

Seeking "egocentric data"

India is emerging as one key place to record this kind of footage because of its large population, relatively low wages and relative openness to new tech. And developers need millions of hours of this footage, what the industry calls egocentric data — data gathered from the perspective of a human with a camera to train AI robots.

"That can be obtained only by emulating or collecting data from real human beings that does the job," says Prathosh A.P., a professor at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru. Like many other Indians, he uses initials to refer to his family name. "Think of today's AIs as brains without a body," he says. "Now you have to give them all motor skills ... to do all kinds of intricate motions that we do using a physical body."

Sponsor Message

Some workers are signing up because they're paid by the hour for the data. But it appears many others, like Kirubakaran, are simply made to record herself working without any explanation. "Call it what it is, which is exploitation of labor," says Astha Kapoor, co-founder of the Aapti Institute, which studies the impact of technology on people.

What will the impact be for India's workforce — the world's second largest, with 600 million people working or seeking work? "Training workers, retraining workers, absorbing them into new occupations," says Amit Basole, economics professor at Azim Premji University. "Do we have the policy agility to do that? I doubt it."

The power question

But that vision of a future full of factory and domestic robots isn't exactly around the corner, say some experts. AI robots are unlikely to be deployed at scale in India — in the near future at least — because they cost a lot of money and consume a lot of power, which is both unreliable and costly across parts of India. "We may be able to make the robots, but they're bloody expensive to run, right?" says Kapoor of the Aapti Institute. "Humans are cheaper to run than robots."

That power crisis is evident even in Karur, where an Indian tech company, Objectways, gathers egocentric data to sell onto AI developers. Massive generators loudly rumble to ensure seamless electricity in the buildings it powers. The company appears to be one of the town's biggest white-collar employers, occupying at least four building blocks in the town.

The CEO, Ravi Shankar, is a Karur native who migrated to Arizona decades ago. He's in perhaps unlikely agreement with Kapoor about the deployment of AI robots in India. "I think it will be more expensive," he says of AI robots, in comparison to human labor. "I don't think it's going to be cheaper."

Sponsor Message

He says his Indian clients want help designing AI robots for jobs that they can't find people to do, like tapping rubber from rubber trees; jobs that are geographically isolated, like dusting off solar panels in rural areas, and jobs that are physically grueling, like destemming chiles for processing.

Inside Objectways, employee Rajeshkumar Ramaswamy shows us how they are training other robots to do repetitive industrial jobs for foreign clients, through what he calls collecting exocentric data — that's data collected from the point of view of a robot. Instead of filming hands of actual workers, young men with GoPro cameras strapped to their heads record themselves doing jobs while holding and manipulating what look like grippy robot claws. One man records himself using the claws to screw bottle lids off and on.

There are dozens of bottles — big, small, plastic, metallic. Ramaswamy says it's to teach robots how to identify all the different shapes and sizes of this thing called a water bottle. The "robot needs to learn what is [a] water bottle," he says.

Ramaswamy says they'll repeat this process of screwing bottle tops about 100 times and feed that data into an AI robot, so it can see for itself how to use its own grippy hands to do the job.

"The robot is like a child," Ramaswamy says. "We are the humans. We are teaching the robots what needs to be done."

The company also trains robots to do household tasks — like folding towels, putting away books and unpacking bags. It sells that data to AI companies hoping to create domestic robots — there's already a few on the market, including one prominent model that looks like a faceless servant and retails for $20,000.

Working in a fake kitchen

Up a few flights of stairs, Ramaswamy shows us where they have humans recording themselves doing domestic jobs, on a floor kitted out to look like an Ikea-style three-bedroom house. In a fake kitchen, a woman, Rani N., records herself chopping onions.

Sponsor Message

Most clients who want first-person recordings of domestic chores are in the U.S., so Ramaswamy says they also pay Americans to record themselves doing housework — so their clients can train AI robots on American-specific data.

For instance, in India, many folks use stainless steel plates to eat. A robot trained to pick up a stainless steel plate could use a lot of pressure to grip it, and could drop it — no harm done. But if the same robot tried to pick up a ceramic plate, which is what many Americans use, the same pressure would cause it to "be separated into minute particles," Ramaswamy says — that is, smashed to bits.

And to amass recordings of humans doing work with their hands for clients who request ecocentric data, Ramaswamy says, they pay hundreds of people across India to undertake domestic jobs, like Sneha Jegadish, a 24-year-old who lives on the edge of town.

Jegadish clipped her smart phone to a headset and began chopping a carrot, her phone recording her every hand movement.

She records herself doing housework for a few hours a day, for about $2.60 an hour, and makes around $120 a month. Jegadish folds clothes, wipes the floor, does the dishes — jobs she was never expected to do growing up, because her mother wanted her to focus on her studies. So when she got this gig a few months ago, "my mother had to show me how to do those jobs," she smiles.

Money or not, it's still drudgery, says Jegadish. One day, she hopes, she'll have a robot to do her housework. "The work we are doing now is going to be done by robots in the future," she says.

That's the same conclusion that 42-year-old textile worker Kannagi Periyasaamy has come to.

At the textile factory, Periyasaamy was folding and packing aprons with a GoPro fastened to her head.

Sponsor Message

She's one of the few workers who is paid about $2.60 an hour to record herself, and she's been told why. She explains: "We are training them [the robots] on how to package the aprons, how to do a quality check, how to fold the aprons."

Periyasaamy says she's been doing this for the past three months, enough for her to be convinced that someday, a robot will take over her job. When that day comes, she says, "I'm thinking about taking up farming" — the family owns a scrap of land where she could raise cattle. Meanwhile, Periyasaamy thinks of AI robots as her students and says, "I'm proud I can teach it to do a good job."

With additional reporting by Vinodh Arulappan

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: Trump's ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigns after allegations of improper conduct
World.content:
Trump's ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigns after allegations of improper conduct

toggle caption i Jacquelyn Martin/AP

WASHINGTON — The White House publicly asked for U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle's resignation on Tuesday as she faced mounting accusations of improper conduct, and she announced within two hours that she was quitting, ending days of talk and speculation about her professional fate. Guilfoyle insisted that she would "vigorously defend" herself.

President Donald Trump's administration had said earlier Tuesday it had asked Guilfoyle to leave her post after she faced severe criticism over allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.

That revelation came in response to a question to freshly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia at her first media briefing Tuesday morning. Zacharia said Guilfoyle "has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well."

"She went to Greece. She was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump said just after Guilfoyle's resignation, which was posted on her X account. He said he had not spoken to her but "she will not be there."

Sponsor Message

Guilfoyle's departure comes after its possibility was previewed to The Associated Press over the weekend and Trump registered his unhappiness on Monday at reports about her alleged conduct. Those comments came a day after the AP, citing a senior U.S. official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were "extremely pissed off" by Guilfoyle's reported conduct.

Guilfoyle denies the accusations and cites her 'decades of public service'

In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the Republican administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.

Guilfoyle addressed the accusations directly in her resignation post on X, saying, "These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity."

"I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional," she said. "I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."

In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle's lawyers denied that she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid.

Sponsor Message

The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle's travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she "sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department's travel regulations."

They did not immediately return calls Tuesday.

The allegations began surfacing weeks ago

After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. Last week, Rubio said: "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."

But after another report appeared later, Rubio — speaking Thursday before leaving Athens — berated journalists for asking about the allegations. He said that he didn't know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them.

"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things," Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.

A second U.S. official, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department's inspector general was looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.

The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers, and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal. The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.

There was no immediate response to Zacharia's statement from the Greek government or Cabinet members.

Ahead of Tuesday's announcement, Greek opposition parties had called on the Foreign Ministry to summon Guilfoyle to respond to the allegations made against her. "This, most importantly, is an issue of national dignity," Sia Anagnostopoulou, a former deputy foreign minister, said in parliament Friday. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis responded that Guilfoyle had been treated "the same way as every other ambassador" and argued that an official summons had not been necessary.

Sponsor Message

Hours earlier, Guilfoyle had posted photos of her meeting this week with the Spanish ambassador to Athens as well as birthday wishes for Lara Trump, the president's daughter-in-law, accompanied by Dua Lipa's "Dance the Night," from the 2023 soundtrack of the movie "Barbie."

Greece has taken on an increasingly important and influential role because of its geographic location in Southeastern Europe and the Eastern Mediterranean, particularly on energy issues as the war with Iran has spiked global oil prices. Besides the vast number of Greek-registered oil tankers that regularly ply the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, Greece is well positioned to be a pipeline conduit for liquefied natural gas imports into the Balkans and beyond.

As the U.S. ambassador to Greece, Guilfoyle had put an emphasis on energy issues, although her close association with executives in that sector was part of what got her into trouble.

Democrats call for an investigation

The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.

Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the United States could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.

While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported — citing text messages — that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.

Sponsor Message

The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.

Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the U.S. government to Greece.

Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was married to Democrat Gavin Newsom when he was San Francisco's mayor, before he became California's governor. She later was engaged to Trump's son Donald Trump Jr.

World.title: In Kansas, a newly competitive Senate race tests limit of Trump's unpopular policies
World.content:
In Kansas, a newly competitive Senate race tests limit of Trump's unpopular policies

toggle caption i Stephen Fowler/NPR

📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App

DODGE CITY, Kan. — If ever there were a place to symbolize both opportunities and obstacles that Democrats and Republicans face politically this midterm election, it would be Kansas.

Two years after President Trump earned 57% of the vote, Kansas Republicans are grappling with the possibility that a Democrat could win a U.S. Senate race for the first time in nearly a century.

Adam Hamilton, a self-billed "independent-minded Democrat," has led in several polls against Republican Sen. Roger Marshall.

Both parties have redirected tens of millions of dollars in recent weeks to try and shape the surprising toss-up race. The president announced Tuesday he would campaign in Wichita next week for Marshall and other Republicans on the ticket.

Sponsor Message

But after eight years of Democratic governor Laura Kelly who is term-limited, Republicans are also hoping to retake control of the state's top office as one of the few pickup opportunities in an otherwise daunting midterm environment.

State Senate President Ty Masterson, the Republican candidate, leads in polls against Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher in a race that is less nationalized than other competitive gubernatorial races around the country.

The last-minute shift in national attention to the Sunflower State is reflective of how unpopular Trump's second term agenda has become with voters, especially in typically Republican states in the Midwest that have been disproportionately affected by rising fuel prices and tariffs.

As early voting gets underway in Kansas, neither side is taking the voters for granted.

'It's about decency'

toggle caption i Stephen Fowler/NPR

At a get-out-the-vote event in Lawrence Monday, Hamilton told the crowd that his priorities if elected are tackling affordability and health care, but also restoring "human decency" to politics.

"Now listen, I had somebody say to me, 'Look, I don't want somebody who's going to build bridges, I want somebody who's going to crush the Republicans,'" he said. "But here's the thing: if you want that in a state with only 25% of the population who are Democrats, you'll never get them elected.

Sponsor Message

"And if you did, they become part of the problem instead of part of the solution."

Hamilton is the founding pastor of Church of the Resurrection, the country's largest United Methodist Church congregation across its multiple campuses, and positions himself as a moderate voice seeking to tame rabid partisanship that has dominated modern politics.

"We've got to find solutions that will be a compromise between what the Republicans want and the Democrats want, but are going to end up getting something done as opposed to right now, where that doesn't happen very often," he said.

At a time when the Democratic Party brand is unpopular with voters, too, Hamilton is quick to point out that he's not a Democrat you might find in a blue state.

"We've been trying to make clear in our commercials that a Kansas Democrat is a bit different than a New York Democrat or a Los Angeles Democrat, and not just a little — a lot different," Hamilton told NPR.

That's also reflected in the slew of endorsements from conservatives, including former Republican Kansas governors Mike Hayden and Bill Graves.

Hamilton also told NPR of a recent event where Republican Party leaders said they were crossing over to vote for him.

"There were Republicans who were saying, 'We've got to do better,'" he said. "You represent our values. You represent the character we're looking for in somebody in leadership. And we know you're going to fight for both Republicans and Democrats. And they're exactly right."

Most of his stump speeches wrap with a callback to "The Wizard of Oz," with Hamilton saying Washington needs more senators "who have a brain and use it, who have a heart and feel empathy with it, and who have courage and speak up because of it."

Hamilton's campaign is also bolstered by backlash to many elements of President Trump's second term, including tariff policies and rising fuel prices, that have proven unpopular, causing the Republican Party's favorability ratings to plummet.

Sponsor Message

A Republican contrast to lead the state

toggle caption i Stephen Fowler/NPR

Even as Republicans sweat the closer-than-expected Senate race, the party is optimistic about winning back control of the governor's office after eight years of Democrat Laura Kelly's leadership.

The Kansas Republican Party is on a weeklong bus tour across the state, bringing a message of contrast that is more state-focused than dealing with the challenging national environment for the party.

Masterson, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, said in Dodge City that tackling issues like affordability and lower energy prices would come from putting a Republican back in the state's top office.

"There's never been a clearer choice than we've had in this election," he said. "If you want working families to be able to afford to live, if you want to stop taxing people out of their homes and out of their businesses and off their farms, if you want safe communities, lower energy prices, i.e. then lower grocery prices… It's not really a choice. You need to vote Republican."

On the trail, the nominees pointed to Kelly's frequent vetoes of measures from the Republican supermajority in the legislature — and overrides of those vetoes — as a motivating factor to get voters to the polls.

State Rep. Pat Proctor, the Republican nominee for Secretary of State, said aside from the state's history of alternating support for governors from both parties, there is strong precedent for still supporting Republicans.

"We are closer to where Kansans are on all the individual issues," he said. "And when they hear us talk and they look at what we actually do, we're just closer to where they want Kansas to be."

While Republicans in other states may have to deal more with Trump's shadow over their own campaigns, campaign speeches rarely mentioned the president or his unpopular policies. Instead, it was all about painting the Democratic nominees as extreme and out of touch.

Sponsor Message

For his part, Marshall has painted Hamilton as too liberal, saying he would destroy Kansas' cattle, agriculture, oil and gas industries if elected.

"Kansans need to know that my opponent, Adam Hamilton, is the most radical liberal person that ever got through a primary in the state of Kansas," he said to cheers.

Still, Marshall has been dogged by negative headlines over the last month, starting with a debate at the Kansas State Fair where the senator was shouted down by the crowd repeatedly.

Marshall's campaign also faced pushback after releasing an attack ad that claimed Hamilton "protected a pedophile" used images of two unrelated businesses, and paid an outstanding invoice from a cookie shop after a viral social media post claimed the campaign failed to pay for six years.

Kansas is one of only a few states that currently have a senator from one party and a governor from the other party, and is one of nearly ten states where voters could also split their choices for those key positions next month.

World.title: Civil rights advocates plan to send thousands of observers to midterm polling places
World.content:
Civil rights advocates plan to send thousands of observers to midterm polling places

toggle caption i Olivier Touron/AFP via Getty Images

It was loteria night at the offices of Living United for Change in Arizona, or LUCHA, in Phoenix.

A small group of young people were playing this bingo-like card game in the hopes of taking home an array of prizes: a camping chair, reusable water bottles and coolers.

Conveniently, the prizes would be useful if you plan to camp out somewhere for a while. Which happens to be what these players were getting trained to do last week.

LUCHA, a left-of-center community organizing group, has been training volunteers to be what they call "constitutional observers" ahead of this year's midterms. This was the first of many in-person sessions the organization plans to hold as Election Day nears.

Sponsor Message

Carime Rodriguez, who led the training, told volunteers that their main job will be to just observe.

"Monitor the polling environment," she said. "Stay aware of what's happening on the ground … just make sure you are kind of keeping your eyes open."

For many election cycles, groups have fanned out to monitor polling places, but the charged midterm environment has many organizations stepping up efforts. They plan to have thousands of individuals with eyes on this election.

Fears of ICE at the polls

For LUCHA's Rodriguez, immigration is a concern. She told her training volunteers that during Arizona's primaries earlier this year, there was an uptick in immigration enforcement — including around polling sites in Maricopa County, where Phoenix is located.

And in case this happens again, LUCHA and other similar groups want to have people on the ground, to keep an eye out for anything they think could intimidate voters. Chiefly, groups say they are worried about Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, agents at election sites.

"I feel like these last two years, everyone has been holding on by the edge of their seats," said Alejandra Gomez, LUCHA's executive director. "And so that has made us incredibly forward thinking and making sure that we are preparing. We're hoping for the best, preparing for the worst."

Sponsor Message

It would be illegal for the Trump administration to send armed agents to polling sites. And administration officials have said ICE has no plans to target polling locations. But right-wing political figures close to Trump like Steven Bannon have been calling for the president to send them anyway, and Trump officials have said ICE could serve warrants at polling places.

Mary Corcoran, co-founder and executive director of the left-leaning Save America Movement, said that's enough for her to take this potential threat seriously.

"The point is to scare people and use fear as an intimidation factor to keep people home," she told NPR. "So, our perspective was that the way that we could make a difference in this election was working in communities that would be most likely impacted by the threat of ICE coming to the polls this fall."

Corcoran's group is partnering with the Rev. Al Sharpton's National Action Network, as well as various unions, like the American Federation of Teachers, in an effort they are calling Vote Safe.

She said members of the effort plan to be in major population centers with large and growing Black, Latino, Asian and immigrant populations — particularly in states with key Senate races, like Ohio, North Carolina, Georgia and Michigan.

"The volunteers are not there to engage with any ICE folks that could show up," she said. "It's really about having a de-escalatory impact by way of really bearing witness."

She said the presence of clergy, veterans, teachers and nurses from the community will hopefully have a "de-escalatory impact and a deterrent impact."

DOJ election observers

Left-leaning groups won't be the only folks at the polls. The Republican National Committee, for one, recruits observers to keep elections secure and transparent. And leaders of the Justice Department, which regularly monitors polling places, say they plan to step up their usual presence.

toggle caption i Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

Harmeet Dhillon, the head of DOJ's Civil Rights Division, said on Real America's Voice that she plans to send a thousand people from the agency to monitor polling sites.

Sponsor Message

"This is going to be the biggest DOJ election observer effort in history," she said. "And I'm so excited to be leading that effort."

She said that DOJ staff will play a similar role to other observers that will be at the polls, which is just to watch.

"They're not going to be interfering in any way or running the election, they're going to be observing, making notes," she said.

Wyoming's Republican governor criticized the actions of DOJ observers in the state in August.

"Not normal times"

Tammy Patrick with the National Association of Election Officials says election administrators have been hearing of big plans of large groups of observers for a while now. But Patrick said it's important to note that this is something they hear most election cycles.

"Every two years it seems, for at least the 20 or so years I've been doing this, we hear that there's going to be massive observation, and thousands of people are going to show up to observe at the polling place," she said.

"It hasn't manifested in that way in the past, but these are not normal times."

Which is why she says election administrators are educating the public. Rules about who can observe what, or how close you can be to a polling site, for example, vary from state to state.

Also, there is only so much observers can actually do at the polls. If something goes wrong, it's up to election workers and local law enforcement to sort it out.

Patrick said most years many observers get bored and leave.

"The actual process tends to be ... pretty dry," she said. "And one might even say boring to watch people walk in, give their name, sign their name, get their ballot."

But if things are not boring, Jane Kleeb with the Association of State Democratic Committees — which is part of the Democratic National Committee — said she wants people on the ground recording.

Sponsor Message

For political parties, the stakes of problems at the polls are high — particularly in close elections, where lawsuits are common.

"We're going to record any bad behavior," she said. "So that might be on audio. It may be still pictures, and it will be video that will then be sent to each state party. So, then they can get that information up to the DNC. So, we have a very clear process to make sure that we're documenting all of this in case lawsuits have to be filed."

World.title: Who else besides Danielle Smith is saying 'yes to the nine' in Alberta's referendum?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It’s long appeared that the pro-unity side in Alberta’s referendum would prevail; polling suggests the separatists will lose by a three-to-one margin next week.

Polling is closer on the other nine questions, but Danielle Smith put them to voters, believing she had sure winners.

While she has repeatedly advocated for the “stay” option when asked, she’s focused most of her rhetoric — and the $4 million government advertising campaign — on the referendum’s proverbial undercard, the questions proposing immigration and constitutional reform.

But aside from that taxpayer-funded push, there’s been little public advocacy for Questions 1-9.

Contrast that with the more visible “No to the Nine” campaign that has cropped up alongside maple leaf emblems on many federalist lawns to push against Smith’s questions and the premier herself.

Though Smith designed the questions to be easy wins among her base and the general public alike, they’ve become a target of both the premier’s anti-separatist detractors, as well as prominent separatists, who treat the questions with either scorn or indifference.

Senior officials in Smith’s United Conservative Party privately say they’re concerned that voters could reject at least some of the questions. If it’s a really bad night, they could lose all of them.

Smith announced the nine questions back in February, months before she added the 10th — the referendum to hold a referendum. She’d crafted them based on some of the most popular ideas from her Alberta Next panel in 2025, which was created to suggest future referendum topics that weren’t stay-or-leave.

Opposition to the nine immigration and constitutional questions has become a central part of some pro-Canadian referendum campaigns. (Jason Markusoff/CBC)

In provincially commissioned polls and an online survey last year, the Smith government found wide support for wresting more control over immigration from Ottawa, denying non-permanent residents access to provincial programs, and trying to amend the Constitution to tilt the scales toward the province — and higher opposition to an Alberta-only pension plan, police force or tax collection agency.

“We think we've done that initial culling of the questions to make sure that we found the ones that are likely to get majority support,” Smith told reporters in April.

Translation: the premier crafted these questions because she believed they’d arm her with fresh ammunition against Ottawa, and that voters would rally around her tough-on-immigration stance.

But aside from her own government’s TV ads, billboards and booklets, there have been scant few voices trying to push the nine into the winner’s column. That said, the $4 million spent amounts to more than double the combined $1.8 million raised as of last week by the various pro- and anti-independence groups, according to Elections Alberta disclosures .

Few prominent conservative Albertans, on either side of that stark independence divide, echo Smith’s call to endorse action on immigration and constitutional measures.

The lesser-known group Alberta Women for Independence is one of the few organizations whose blue pro-separation signs also encourage yes votes for the nine questions.

But after its leader Kathy Flett treated a pro-independence town hall in Medicine Hat to a detailed slide presentation on the merits of all nine referendum proposals last week, the more prominent separatist leader Keith Wilson brushed off their importance.

“These other nine questions are — I’m sorry, they’re a political gimmick. They mean nothing,” Wilson said, before later noting he’d vote yes to them, anyhow.

One of the few pro-independence signs that also urges yes votes on the other referendum questions. (Jason Markusoff/CBC)

Some separatists are frustrated because they don’t like the abstract nature of the independence ballot question, or that Smith diluted the referendum with questions that she didn’t have to put directly to voters.

Jeffrey Rath of Alberta Prosperity Project is urging people to “decline the 9” entirely — even as APP itself is trying to educate voters about what those other questions are.

“The nine questions are a deflection from the independence question,” Rath wrote last week on social media . “They are Smith’s built in excuse not to pursue independence!”

Many conservatives have focused exclusively on Question 10, including Alberta’s federal Conservative MPs and former cabinet minister Monte Solberg’s group Vote to Stay.

Former premier Jason Kenney, one of the unity side’s most active conservative voices, has questioned whether the nine questions needed to be referendums, and said some of them even confused him, a former federal immigration minister.

Contrast all that to the array of people pushing against the nine questions, particularly the ones seeking to restrict the social services that non-permanent residents receive.

In a rare show of bipartisan unity, former Progressive Conservative premiers Ed Stelmach and Alison Redford joined NDP counterpart Rachel Notley in a newspaper op-ed Wednesday urging “no” votes on the immigration ballots, warning they’ll harm Alberta’s economy and ability to attract workers.

The Calgary Chamber of Commerce has also been highlighting immigrants’ contributions to society, while its CEO Deborah Yedlin has warned Smith’s suggested $1,900-per-migrant health care fee would be a burdensome “extra cost” for employers.

Christian leaders have taken the unusual step of weighing in , albeit without directly telling parishioners how to vote.

A joint letter from Alberta’s Catholic bishops called on people to “respect human dignity and avoid making any segment of our population the object of resentment or blame," while a letter from Anglican bishops reminded supporters of Scripture’s “call to welcome and care for strangers and sojourners in their midst.”

Labour unions have also argued for “no” votes down the line, including CUPE Alberta’s “no to scapegoating” video that emphasizes how little services for temporary residents cost the provincial treasury.

“It just reinforces that these questions were not wanted by anyone except Danielle Smith,” said Stephen Carter of Alberta’s Voice, the third-party advertising group behind the “No to the Nine” signs.

“She wrote them. She promoted them. And everyone else opposes them.”

Stephen Carter's group Alberta's Voice is behind one of the most visible opposition campaigns against the immigration and constitutional ballot questions. (Sam Martin/CBC)

As much as Smith believed they were winners, the nine questions haven’t been slam dunks in the polls.

Last month’s Janet Brown Opinion Research poll for CBC News said 52 per cent of respondents oppose limiting access to health and education to temporary immigrants, while 45 per cent agree. There was moderately more support for Alberta taking more control over its immigration (54 per cent agree, 42 per cent disagree) and for constitutional changes (49 per cent agree, 45 percent disagree).

A Research Co. survey in late August, meanwhile, found that support for the five immigration questions ranged between 58 and 66 percent, while views on the constitutional questions were more tepid — between 39 and 46 per cent support.

WATCH | Do Albertans know what they're being asked to vote on?: Many Albertans unaware of 9 other ballot questions | Duration closed caption 2:03 Less than three weeks ahead of Alberta's referendum on whether to seek a vote on separation from Canada, many Albertans seem unaware of the nine other questions on the ballot that involve thorny issues around immigration and constitutional reform.

But undermining those numbers is what appears to be widespread confusion and uncertainty about what those wordy questions are asking of Albertans. Brown’s poll suggested that close to half of Albertans didn’t know how they’d vote or weren’t familiar with the referendum ballot’s lesser-known nine.

As if to prove this confusion and lack of familiarity, the United Conservative Party issued its first message last week to its mailing list trying to explain and promote all nine questions. It was 1,708 words long. (It also didn’t tell the party’s backers how to vote on Question 10, perhaps unsurprisingly because of how split UCP ranks are on separation.)

The governing party doesn’t appear to have engaged in any door knocking or get-out-the-vote campaigns on the referendum. The opposition NDP, meanwhile, have been trying to activate pro-unity voters, with flyers that say “Vote to remain. No to the rest.”

The general lack of non-taxpayer-funded, on-the-ground campaigning may have already cost Smith. The Janet Brown poll showed that among Albertans who do know how they’ll vote on the nine, half will follow the “no the nine” mantra, while some will vote no to some and yes to others.

Only about one in 10 planned to fulfil Smith’s request and mark nine yeses.

Given that nearly half of committed voters would choose the UCP, that means a sizable contingent of Smith’s own political backers are not readily following her wishes into the ballot box.

World.title: Ottawa to announce over $350M for skilled trades worker training, recruitment
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The federal government will announce plans to help fund new infrastructure, equipment and recruitment efforts by unions and other organizations to train workers as part of a major funding announcement expected on Thursday.

Secretary of State for Labour John Zerucelli is expected to announce more than $350 million in funding, according to a senior government official speaking on background.

CBC News is not naming the official because they were not authorized to discuss the details of the announcement.

The funding aims to help fulfil an objective announced in the spring economic update called Team Canada Strong — a plan to recruit, train and hire 80,000 to 100,000 new skilled trades workers with the nationally recognized Red Seal certification by 2030-31.

The push is part of an ongoing effort to close a gap of more than 20,000 skilled trades workers per year. It comes as the Liberals' C-39, a bill intended to speed up major project approvals and construction, moves through Parliament.

The funding will be provided partially through the Union Training and Innovation Program (UTIP) and partially through the money earmarked in the spring economic update, and will include three different streams.

The first stream will help fund investments in equipment for unions, colleges and other organizations that train workers in the Red Seal trades. The federal government will temporarily pay up to 70 per cent of the cost of training equipment, up from 50 per cent.

The second stream, infrastructure, is intended to help unions and organizations training workers expand or build union-run training centres to increase capacity across the country. The government is looking to help finance shovel-ready projects that can begin construction by next spring.

The third stream, innovation, will offer funding for organizations and unions with ideas to recruit, retain and train Red Seal trades, including supporting apprentices in progressing toward certification.

This could include things like integrating artificial intelligence or helping recruit apprentices through new initiatives.

Part of $6B plan for workers

The formal announcement is set to take place on Thursday morning in Metcalfe, Ont., just outside of Ottawa.

In the 2026 spring economic update, the federal government pledged $6 billion over five years to recruit, train and hire workers.

It announced plans to offer wage subsidies for employers that hire apprentices, creating paid, entry-level trades-related work that leads to apprenticeship and offering apprentices with a weekly income top-up, as well as training completion bonuses.

The details of those plans — including when they are set to be rolled out — have not yet been released.

World.title: Image of mournful elephant mom wins 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

(Federico Veronesi/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

An Italian photographer's "heartbreakingly poignant" photo of a mother elephant carrying her dead calf has won this year's top Wildlife Photographer of the Year award.

Federico Veronesi captured "The Aftermath" while tracking elephants in the Huab River Valley in Namibia. He noticed unusual drag marks in the sand of the dry riverbed. When he caught up to a family of elephants, he saw an adult female with a calf's leg wedged between her tusk and trunk.

Kathy Moran, chair of the jury for the 2026 competition, described the photo as working on "so many levels."

"Emotionally it's a gut punch, heartbreakingly poignant. Intellectually, it's proof that animals have cognition," she wrote in a news release announcing the winners.

In addition to winning the grand prize, the photo also won the Behaviour: Mammals category.

Wildlife Photographer of the Year is developed and produced by the U.K.-based Natural History Museum in London, with a stated goal to share nature's stories and insights about environmental challenges that need our attention.

This year, the annual competition — the 62nd edition — attracted 65,403 entries from 121 countries and territories.

It awards top prizes to both an adult photographer and a young photographer under 18.

This year's Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year prize was won by Oscar Whitfield, a young British photographer who grew up in Zimbabwe and frequently returns there during school holidays.

His photo, captured while lying on the ground, shows a close-up of a dung beetle hard at work pushing a ball of dung. It was also the winner in the 11 to 14 years age bracket.

(Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife Photographer of the year)

Officially, there were no Canadian category winners this year. However, Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas, who lives in Germany and won this year's Rising Star Award, is a Canadian citizen who has previously told CBC News his parents were both born in Canada, and he has relatives in Ottawa and Nova Scotia.

His featured photo, "Afternoon snack," is a close-up of a robber fly preying on a flesh fly. "The bubbles forming in the victim's eyes indicate that the robber fly has injected digestive enzymes that liquefy its internal tissues before they are sucked out," the photo's description reads.

(Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

Canadians can see the 100-photo exhibition at the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto from Nov 7, 2026, to Feb 28, 2027, or at the Royal B.C. Museum in Victoria from Feb. 12, 2027, until April 18, 2027.

It opens at the Natural History Museum in London this Friday.

Here are some of the other category winners.

Amelie Davis, of the U.K., won the 10 years and under bracket with this photo of a common carder bee in southern England, captured with her father's smartphone.

(Amelie Davis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

A California newt lays eggs while clasping vegetation that already contains another newt's egg clutch in the winner of the Amphibians and Reptiles category, captured by U.S. photographer Anton Sorokin. The newt will stay like this until the egg mass swells to a size too large to be eaten by a predator.

(Anton Sorokin/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

Greek photographer Agorastos Papatsanis used UV light to make these fluorescent bonnet mushrooms glow brightly on a decaying log on the lower slopes of Greece's Mount Olympus. The image won the Plants and Fungi category.

(Agorastos Papatsanis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

A young bull elephant sprays water on a group of zebras at a waterhole in the Chyulu Hills of Kenya in this photo, the winner of the Animals in their Environment category, captured by James Lewin using a camera converted to infrared to soften harsh lighting.

World.title: Several organic cheese products recalled for possible Listeria contamination
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) is recalling several organic cheese products under the Farm Boy, L'Ancêtre, and Life Smart brands due to possible Listeria contamination.

The agency says the national recall was triggered by testing and there have been no reported illnesses connected to consumption of the products.

The affected products include Farm Boy organic Swiss, medium cheddar, old cheddar, extra sharp and three-year-old cheddar cheeses with a best before date of July 30, 2027.

Life Smart organic part skim mozzarella cheese with a best before date of March 30, 2027, is also being recalled, as are several shredded organic cheeses made by L'Ancêtre with best before dates of this December, next January and next July.

L'Ancetre's organic Swiss cheese with a best before date of July 30, 2027, is also included.

A full list of the recalled products can be found here. They were sold in stores across the country.

WATCH | Are food recalls becoming more common? Are food recalls in Canada becoming more common? | Duration 6:20 A string of product recalls, including some involving E. coli, Listeria and salmonella, has sparked concerns about food safety. Lawrence Goodridge, director of the Canadian Research Institute for Food Safety at the University of Guelph, says the data doesn’t indicate an increase in recalls but adds the pandemic did cause some disruptions in food safety.

The CFIA says people should not consume the product if they have it in their home, and to throw it out or return it to wherever they bought it. It warns that products that look and smell normal can still make someone sick.

Symptoms of Listeria include vomiting, nausea, persistent fever, muscle aches, severe headache and neck stiffness. Pregnant women, the elderly and those with weakened immune systems are at greater risk.

World.title: Trump says oil, gas and mineral exploration in Greenland is set to begin. It's not that simple
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump said "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration is set to begin in "our new and beautiful Greenland" early Wednesday.

It wasn't immediately clear what exploration or developments the U.S. president was referring to in his post, and Greenland is a self-governing territory of Denmark, rather than a part of the United States.

Trump posted on his Truth Social platform following a campaign event Tuesday in Wasilla, Alaska, to stump for Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan as he seeks his third term to represent the state in an election against Democratic former U.S. congresswoman Mary Peltola.

Rising energy prices — a direct result of Trump's war in Iran — are creating serious and sustained financial hardships for America's working class ahead of the midterm elections next month. Trump's comments Wednesday are likely aimed at addressing voters' concerns before they head to the polls.

But despite Trump's optimism, resource exploration and extraction in Greenland has stymied companies for decades thanks to the island's harsh climate, lack of key infrastructure and difficult geology. Previous efforts to extract so-called rare earth minerals, as well as oil and gas, have never progressed beyond the exploratory stage.

Recent deal doesn't include exploration rights

Trump's comments about the Arctic island come less than a month after he signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic following months of tensions with NATO allies over the U.S. president's repeated demands to take control of the semiautonomous Danish territory. It does not grant the U.S. any special exploration rights, but does place some limits on investments by non-NATO countries in strategic sectors.

A young boy walks in Nuuk, Greenland on Friday, Feb. 6, 2026. The self-governing Danish territory has consistently rebuffed Trump's calls for the U.S. to annex the island. (Christinne Muschi/CP)

The deal also paved the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and eased tensions over Trump's repeated calls for Greenland to become part of the United States. The agreement would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence.

Trump has expressed his desire to acquire Greenland since as long ago as 2019 and, during his second term, issued threats to seize the territory from Denmark, a NATO ally.

Representatives of the leaders of Denmark and Greenland did not immediately return requests for comment Wednesday.

Greenland has valuable resources

Greenland has large deposits of the rare earth minerals that are needed to make everything from computers and smartphones to the batteries, solar and wind technologies that will power the transition away from fossil fuels. China currently dominates the world's supply of these critical minerals and the Trump administration is seeking to break Beijing's chokehold on them.

The U.S. Geological Survey has also identified major potential offshore deposits of oil and natural gas.

But tapping these resources could be prohibitively difficult: the rare earth minerals are encased in rock, and the offshore oil and natural gas deposits are covered by Arctic ice.

Trump boasts about Greenland's strategic location

Trump's Truth Social post also touted Greenland's strategic location, saying that "from a security purpose in the defence and offence of both the United States of America, and Europe," the island is "second to none."

"Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our defence will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived," he wrote. "It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the world!"

The United States was prominent in Greenland for decades but, since 1945, the U.S. military presence in Greenland has decreased from thousands of soldiers on 17 bases and installations to roughly 200 soldiers on the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest. The base supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance operations for the U.S. and NATO.

Trump said last month that the U.S. would "immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations," including "building two very major military bases."

World.title: Kelly Clarkson bird saga takes another turn as store owner's footage is released
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Kelly Clarkson's feud with a Brooklyn shop over a mechanical bird just got a lot more expensive — $15 million more, to be precise.

Adam Rubin, the co-owner of Art of Play, chose to put the shop's automated bird, "Molly," up for sale for a whopping $15 million US amid the shop's ongoing viral feud with the pop star, according to USA Today.

The listing in the store now reads: "Molly. Designed and created by Bliss Kolb. The world's most famous singing bird automata! $15,000,000."

Rubin also told USA Today he'd give each shop employee $15,000 US and pay Kolb $1 million US if someone bought the bird. He said he'd use the rest of the money to buy other antique automata.

CBC News has reached out to Art of Play for confirmation but has not heard back.

It's the latest turn in a saga that has taken over the internet. It's also a dramatic increase from the $15,000 US price tag Clarkson says she saw when she stopped by the store on Oct. 10.

'Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger': shop owner

The shop owner spoke to several outlets at the Art of Play on Tuesday, saying the store has seen a large increase in foot traffic because of the publicity, but has also received a torrent of backlash from fans of the pop star.

"Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger," Rubin said. "We're concerned on behalf of our shopkeepers."

Clarkson's viral shopping experience can now be seen in footage obtained by independent journalist Pablo Torre on Tuesday, Oct. 13.

The four-minute, 50-second clip does not include audio. In it, Clarkson appears to enter the store wearing a baseball cap and a yellow T-shirt. She browses the store and appears to approach a clerk, who says something to her before walking away.

Later on in the video, Clarkson appears to put the items she had in her hands back on the shelves and speak to the person at the cash register before leaving the store.

How we got here

The online spat started on Saturday, when the singer posted that she visited the shop to buy "a few things," but "was looked at as if I couldn't afford it."

"But y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she wrote.

For context, Robert's character in the film is famously treated rudely by a snooty saleswoman in a boutique.

The store replied Sunday, stating that Clarkson had asked about buying "Molly," a one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird automaton which is "permanently attached to the wall and isn't for sale."

They said that Clarkson's version of events "would resonate with anyone who has ever felt judged," but said that all shoppers at Art of Play "are equally welcome."

"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," the shop wrote on Instagram.

Clarkson hit back later that day, posting a photo showing a $15,000 US price tag on the wall next to the wooden bird automaton.

"So you're not only rude, you're also a liar. [...] It's not that hard to be kind. I never blast people but you, my friend, were an exception," the star wrote.

Clarkson rarely makes personal posts on social media. Her previous post on X was two weeks earlier and promoted her coaching gig on NBC's The Voice.

On Monday, the shop said it told Clarkson the $15,000 US price referred to a nearly identical bird that could be made and sold, not Molly itself.

The store also said it offered to show Clarkson a different bird atomaton on sale for about $2,000 US, but that she didn't stick around long enough to see it.

In an interview with several outlets , Rubin said no one in the shop recognized Clarkson at the time, the store was "packed" and Clarkson was there for "less than five minutes." He also alleged that Clarkson scolded an employee.

"Everybody has a bad day. But things changed when she used her platform to attack us. It's asymmetrical social warfare," he said.

The internet weighs in

On social media, users have been closely following the online debacle and sharing their thoughts.

"This kelly clarkson situation is why everyone should work a retail job at some point in their life bc after u do u will never again care how store employees treat u," one user wrote on X

"Even if you buy kelly clarkson's entire narrative here... this doesn't feel like a pretty woman situation," wrote another , adding that "it seems perfectly reasonable that whoever she spoke to would not really be focused on selling it / expect to."

Molly, a singing and dancing mechanical bird, by Bliss Kolb, is displayed at Art of Play, on Tuesday, in the Brooklyn borough of New York. (Yuki Iwamura/The Associated Press)

"I think the funniest part about this situation is that for anyone to take a side they must either feel empathy for multimillionaire celebrity Kelly Clarkson or these multimillionaire shop owners," a third wrote.

World.title: 3rd victim dies following crash at B.C. mall on Truth and Reconciliation Day: police
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Delta police say another victim has died as a result of the vehicle crash at Tsawwassen Mills mall on Sept. 30.

Police said in a news release Wednesday that 64-year-old Gwenyth Brigit Dwyn of South Delta, one of two people who were hospitalized following the crash, has died as a result of her injuries.

Two other people were declared dead at the scene, where a house pole raising event had been taking place following a Truth and Reconciliation Day walk hosted by Tsawwassen First Nation.

Police initially said the vehicle's driver "may have experienced a medical emergency," but added Wednesday that investigators have not reached any final conclusions on the cause of the crash.

The two people killed at the scene were Tsawwassen First Nation elders Virginia Splockton and wilapiya (Barb Joe).

Police said Wednesday the second injured person has been released from hospital and continues their recovery at home.

"Our thoughts remain with the victims families and loved ones, and with everyone affected by this tragedy," Delta police said.

Cause remains under investigation

The department has faced criticism over a lack of public updates on the investigation. Before Wednesday, there had not been an update since Oct. 1.

In their new statement, Delta police Staff Sgt. Mike Whiteley said the responsibility of police is to ensure answers are based on an objective examination of evidence.

"Investigators are working through a significant amount of information, and it is important that we not reach conclusions before that work is complete."

First responders outside the mall after the collision. (Johna Baylon/CBC)

The release said investigators have reviewed a "substantial volume of evidence including cellphone and other video evidence," and completed a scene and collision analysis.

"This work includes examining the movements of the involved vehicle on the Tsawwassen Mills property before the pedestrians were struck, including an earlier collision. Investigators have not reached any final conclusions regarding the cause of the collisions," Delta police said.

"Based on the evidence reviewed to date, investigators have not identified evidence indicating that the collision was targeted or ideologically motivated."

Police said they continue to investigate the "possibility that the driver experienced a medical event prior to the collisions."

Anyone who witnessed the incident or who observed the vehicle on the mall property before the crash, and has not already spoken to investigators, is asked to contact Delta police.
