World.title: Sheinbaum signs decree blocking violent and hostile content from minors’ social media feeds: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📱 Sheinbaum signs decree to curb harmful online content for minors: Social media sites and online forums will be barred from displaying or recommending content to minors that “generates or promotes” hate speech, violent extremism, self-harm, eating disorders, cyberbullying and illegal conduct. Platforms must also verify users’ ages, classify content by age group and offer parental supervision tools. The decree, drawn up after an Oct. 1 machete attack at a school in Torréon, Coahuila, takes effect one month after its publication in the government’s official gazette today.

🚓 Sheinbaum orders CNDH probe into alleged police torture in Guadalajara: The president said the National Human Rights Commission must conduct a “very thorough investigation” into allegations that Jalisco police tortured people detained at Sunday’s water contamination protest. “How is it possible that in 2026, there is still torture of young people by police?” she asked.

⚖️ Sheinbaum defers to judges on ex-INM chief Garduño’s exoneration: Asked about Francisco Garduño’s exoneration over the 2023 Ciudad Juárez detention center fire that killed 40 migrants, the president said, “It’s what the judges determined.” Lawyers for the victims will challenge the ruling.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At her Wednesday morning press conference, President Sheinbaum signed a decree that will bar social media sites and other online forums from displaying or recommending content to minors that “generates or promotes” hate speech, violent extremism, sexual exploitation or violence, suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, cyber-bullying and illegal conduct in general.

The government drew up the decree after a fatal Oct. 1 machete attack at a school in Torréon, Coahuila, that was allegedly perpetrated by twin 18-year-old brothers who authorities say were exposed to violent content and extremist ideology online.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was Sheinbaum’s response to allegations that Jalisco state police tortured people who were detained in Guadalajara on Sunday during a protest against contaminated water. One woman said that police beat her and stepped on her bare feet, causing fractures.

Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus said Tuesday that all 39 people detained during Sunday’s protest had been released. He said that police used excessive force and made “unjust arrests.”

He also said that “serious mistakes that must be investigated and sanctioned” were made.

“… No one should have been exposed to violence,” Lemus said.

Sheinbaum signs ‘safe digital environments’ decree

Presidential legal adviser Luisa María Alcalde told reporters that she and other officials met with representatives of social media and other tech companies to discuss the “decree to guarantee safe digital environments for girls, boys and adolescents,” which was presented by the government last Friday.

“Far from demonstrating resistance, they perfectly understood the need for an instrument of this nature,” she said.

Alcalde said that the decree will be published in the government’s official gazette today and take effect one month later.

The decree will oblige social media sites to detect and “immediately” remove “accounts and content that promote or generate violent conduct,” she said.

📲 SHEINBAUM FIRMA DECRETO PARA QUE PLATAFORMAS DIGITALES EVITEN DIFUNDIR CONTENIDOS VIOLENTOS La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum da un mes a las plataformas digitales para avanzar en la regulación de contenidos que inciten a la violencia, contra niñas, niños y adolescentes. ⚠️ Advirtió que, si las medidas no funcionan, se promoverá una reforma legal que establecería SANCIONES. Aclaró que no se trata de censura, sino de garantizar espacios digitales seguros. 📱🫡🫡 — Isabel Uribe (@Isa_Uribe) October 14, 2026

Alcalde said that social media sites will also have to “classify content” by its appropriateness for different age groups, verify the age of their users and “establish supervision tools” for mothers, fathers and legal guardians of minors.

Before signing the decree, Sheinbaum noted that social media and “digital platform” companies agreed with the government’s initiative.

“The only thing they asked for was a month to prepare their platforms so that this is a reality,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the government’s Digital Transformation and Communications Agency will monitor social media sites to ensure that companies are complying with the decree.

“If we see they aren’t complying, we would move onto a law which would involve sanctions for the platforms,” she said.

Sheinbaum orders investigation into allegations of police torture in Guadalajara

Regarding allegations that police tortured people who were detained during a protest against water contamination in Guadalajara on Sunday, Sheinbaum said that the National Human Rights Commission (CNDH) has to conduct a “very thorough investigation.”

“Yesterday I was asked about the issue of torture in Jalisco. … What happened in Jalisco can’t be allowed,” she said.

“… In addition to the use of streams of water and tear gas [against protesters], the issue of torturing young people is something that has to disappear in our country,” Sheinbaum said.

“A police force cannot torture anyone,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the CNDH investigation should examine “who gave the order” to torture detainees and interview “the victims.”

“… How is it possible that in 2026, there is still torture of young people by police?” she asked.

“… We, who came from the fight against [government] repression, cannot allow there to be police forces in Mexico that repress and torture,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum responds to exoneration of former INM chief

A reporter asked the president her opinion about the exoneration of former National Migration Institute (INM) chief Francisco Garduño, who faced a charge of improper exercise of public service in connection with a 2023 fire in an INM detention center in Ciudad Juárez that killed 40 migrants.

“It’s what the judges determined,” Sheinbaum responded.

Garduño, head of the INM between 2019 and 2025, was exonerated at a court hearing in Ciudad Juárez on Tuesday. Lawyers for the victims said they will challenge the decision.

Sheinbaum said that “a very thorough investigation” that examined “the responsibilities of each person” in connection with the fire was carried out. She then reiterated that the exoneration of Garduño was a decision made by “judges.”

According to authorities, the fire started when two detained migrants set a mattress alight to protest poor conditions in the INM detention center. Those two men survived the blaze and face homicide charges.

The Federal Attorney General’s Office began criminal proceedings against Garduño in April 2023, alleging that he failed to fulfill his duty to “supervise, protect and provide security to the people and facilities” under his control.

In September 2025, the former INM chief issued an apology to victims and relatives of the deceased.

There were “human rights violations that never should have happened” due to “omissions by personnel of the [INM],” he said at the time.

The Associated Press reported that Garduño “called for ‘those responsible’ to be punished and for reparations to be made without recognizing his own responsibility in the tragedy.”

To date, no one has been convicted of criminal wrongdoing in connection with the deadly fire.

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Helping out after hurricanes, planning for Día de Muertos
World.content:
By the time you read this, Puerto Vallarta will be recovering from its third consecutive hurricane in the last few weeks. First came Polo, then Rachel, and now Simón — a Category 3 storm currently making its way up the Pacific coast. Luckily, the storms’ eyes stayed offshore, sparing the city the worst impacts. Still, our malecón and beachside resorts have taken a beating from intense tidal surges and waves; many neighborhoods have flooded, and we haven’t been able to safely enjoy the beach since Sept. 23, when the first red flags were raised.

Needless to say, many residents — myself included — are feeling a bit of a hurricane hangover these days and are thinking less about going out on the town and more about helping our communities recover.

So instead of entertainment listings, this week’s events roundup highlights a few volunteer opportunities and organizations that provide disaster relief and organize cleanup efforts after major storms and throughout the year. Whether you live in Puerto Vallarta permanently, seasonally, or just vacation here from time to time, there are ways you can help residents recover through these groups.

We’ve also thrown in what we know so far about Día de Muertos happenings. Even though we’ve been thrashed around by storms lately, this is still Mexico, so the celebrations will go on come hurricanes or high water.

Disaster relief, cleanup and community support organizations

Vallarta Cares

Vallarta Cares is a local charity that mobilizes food, water, hygiene and medical supply distribution to communities affected by natural disasters, including hurricanes, floods and other emergencies. The organization also operates a year-round soup kitchen that serves hundreds of meals daily, provides weekly medical services, including free dental services, and organizes medical brigades throughout the year.

Vallarta Cares was also recently awarded first place in the interior of Jalisco category for the 2026 Premio a la Generosidad Jalisco. You can inquire about volunteer opportunities and make a donation through its website.

Limpia Tu Mar

Limpia Tu Mar organizes trash cleanups along Vallarta’s beaches, rivers and at sea. Since its inception in 2017, the group’s cleanup brigades have removed more than 900 kilograms (1,984 pounds) of plastic, 125 kilograms (275 pounds) of styrofoam, 350 kilograms (771 pounds) of glass and 5,000 kilograms (11,023 pounds) of general garbage from the sea. Each week, volunteers set sail on boats from Puerto Vallarta to remove floating trash from the ocean.

Limpia Tu Mar also hosts one of Mexico’s largest environmental awareness events, the annual International Trash Fishing Tournament. This year’s tournament is coming up Oct. 18, and registration is still open if you want to participate or help sponsor the event. With all the recent storms washing tons of trash and debris into the bay, we could use all the help we can get to clean it up.

Local collection centers and cleanup brigades

If you are in Puerto Vallarta during hurricane season (June through November), local collection centers (centros de acopio) are often set up at community centers, fire stations and churches on short notice to organize relief efforts. Joining local community and business groups on social media is one of the fastest ways to find pop-up volunteering needs immediately following a storm.

One such brigade I join regularly is the Banderas Bay Project, started by local real estate agent Luis Salazar, which organizes monthly trash pickups around Boca de Tomatlán, one of the harder-hit areas from the recent storms.

Planning for Día de Muertos

Día de Muertos — Mexico’s annual celebration honoring departed souls — is around the corner, and that means Puerto Vallarta will again be pulling out all the stops.

This year, the city is participating in the statewide Festival de Las Almas (Festival of the Souls), featuring more than 350 free events across 11 municipalities in Jalisco from Oct. 24 through Nov. 2.

In Vallarta, the city is planning 28 free events and experiences Oct. 31 through Nov. 2 along the historic center, Los Arcos, Muelle de Los Muertos, Isla del Cuale, and, of course, the Malecón, which will again feature a monumental Catrina. The giant beauty has adorned the Malecón for the past several years, each time designed by a different Mexican artist. According to the Puerto Vallarta Tourism Board, this year she will be adorned with waves, whales, manta rays and bougainvillea.

If you do plan on heading downtown for the festivities, I recommend going early before the crowds get too big. Last year, we waited until after dark to go see the Catrina and were stuck in traffic for more than an hour trying to drive from the Marina to the Malecón.

Concierto de Día de Muertos

The Vallarta Symphony Orchestra will perform with the choirs of Puerto Vallarta and the University of Brasília for special Día de Muertos concerts on Oct. 30 at the Iglesia Reina de la Paz in Marina Vallarta at 9 p.m., and on Oct. 31 at the Haramara Auditorium at Universidad Tecnológica de Bahía de Banderas in Nayarit at 7 p.m. Tickets can be purchased from IAMPV.

Debbie Slobe is a writer and communications strategist based in Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco. She blogs at Mexpatmama.com and is a senior program director at Resource Media. Find her on Instagram and Facebook.

World.title: US congressional candidate says Mexico is where he gets healthcare as high costs dominate midterm debate
World.content:
Bobby Pulido, a singer and Democratic candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in Texas’s 15th District, recently said that he does not have health insurance and has had to go to Mexico to receive medical care.

Pulido, who is running against Republican Mónica De La Cruz, made the unexpected remark to Council President and CEO Javier Palomerez during a virtual discussion on Monday with the U.S. Hispanic Business Council.

“I’m going to start off by telling you that I don’t have health insurance, Javier. And I’m embarrassed to tell you that I’ve had to go to Mexico for my health care,” Pulido said, as cited by news outlet Border Report, reportedly the only journalism outlet that accessed the meeting.

Pulido, 52, whose full name is José Roberto Pulido Jr., lives in Edinburg, a border city located in southern Texas. According to Border Report, he also owns a home in Mexico.

During the conversation, Pulido contrasted U.S. President Trump’s reported plans to boost military spending with the difficulties U.S. residents face in obtaining affordable medical care.

“I live in the richest country in the world. Now the president wants to give a million and a half trillion dollars for our military budget when we cannot provide affordable health care to our people,” he said.

Pulido’s statements did not describe what specific illness, procedure or medical emergency has brought him to seek care in Mexico. Nor does the information shared by Border Report specify which Mexican city he visits for treatment, how much he pays or the reasons why he lacks insurance in the United States.

However, this isn’t the first time Pulido has publicly shared that he has traveled to Mexico for healthcare. On Sept. 27, he told Univisión he sought medical services in Mexico due to high costs in the U.S., while questioning the power of insurance companies in that country.

Before turning to politics, Pulido had a renowned career as a Tejano singer, with a fan base spanning Mexico and the U.S. Over the course of a three-decade career, he won two Latin Grammy Awards for Best Tejano Music Album — one of which he won in November 2025.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: The MND Peso Index™ for October: Is the peso approaching its fair value?
World.content:
Listen to this article

THE MND PESO INDEX™

Tracking the exchange rate people actually experience

MND Intelligence · Sixth edition

Welcome to the sixth edition of the MND Peso Index™, part of the MND Intelligence™ suite of data products developed by Mexico News Daily.

The MND Peso Index™ is a monthly purchasing power parity measure that assesses whether the Mexican peso is overvalued, undervalued or fairly valued against the US dollar by comparing the prices of a standardized basket of 20 goods and services in Mexico and Dallas, Texas.

Since we published the September index, the peso has been on quite a ride.

Between Sept. 2, the date on which we collected prices for the September index, and Oct. 6, the date on which we collected prices for this index, the peso depreciated 5.5%, trading at 16.98 to the dollar on the former date and 17.97 to the greenback on the latter date.

The peso’s depreciation was the decisive factor behind our first undervaluation finding for the currency since we launched the MND Peso Index™ in May.

Our headline finding for October 2026 indicates that the peso was undervalued against the dollar by 0.7%, a swing of 6.5 percentage points compared to the 5.8% overvaluation we determined in September.

For a detailed explanation of the purpose of the MND Peso Index™, the makeup of the basket and more, please refer to the index article we published in June. You can read even more about the index in our introductory article published in early May.

What did the MND Peso Index™ tell us in October 2026?

In October 2026, the MND Peso Index™ suggests that the USD:MXN exchange rate on the date we collected prices in various Mexican cities and in Dallas, Texas, undervalued the Mexican peso by 0.7%.

The Mexican and Dallas prices were collected on Oct. 6, 2026. The MND Peso Rate — the simple average of the 20 item-level implied exchange rates, rather than the rate produced by dividing the total Mexican basket cost by the total Dallas basket cost — came in at 17.84 pesos per dollar, compared with a Banxico FIX rate of 17.97 pesos per dollar on Oct. 6.

The gap between those two figures indicates that the peso — at a rate of 17.97 to the US dollar — was undervalued by 0.7% in early October.

In the table above, you can see the Mexico and U.S. prices for all 20 goods and services in the basket, the total costs of the two baskets, the implied exchange rate for each item, the MND Peso Rate (i.e., the overall implied rate), the Banxico FIX rate on the date prices were collected and the undervalued assessment for the peso.

Why did the peso go from overvalued to undervalued in just one month?

In contrast to September, the MND Peso Rate for October (17.84) is lower than the Banxico FIX rate on the date prices were collected (17.97).

As a result, the peso has gone from being overvalued against the dollar in early September, per the MND Peso Index™ methodology, to being undervalued against the dollar in early October.

The shift was primarily driven by the significant weakening of the peso, as mentioned in the introduction to this article.

The peso depreciated 99 centavos from 16.98 to the US dollar on Sept. 2 to 17.97 to the dollar on Oct. 6, per the Banxico FIX rates for those dates. The U.S. Federal Reserve’s Sept. 16 interest rate hike and increased investor risk aversion are among the factors behind the peso’s recent depreciation. The Fed’s hike narrows the gap between U.S. and Mexican interest rates, making peso carry trades less attractive to investors.

The MND Peso Rate declined 12 centavos from 17.96 in September to 17.84 in October, reinforcing the shift toward undervaluation. Had the MND Peso Rate increased by 1 centavo, rather than declined by 12, it would have been exactly the same as the Banxico FIX rate, indicating that the peso was trading at fair value under the index’s methodology.

In any case, the difference between the Oct. 6 Banxico FIX rate and the MND Peso Rate in October was just 13 centavos. Hence, the undervaluation assessment for the peso is minimal, indicating that it was trading close to fair value on Oct. 6.

The slight variation in the MND Peso Rate is due to month-over-month changes in the implied rates for some individual goods and services. The implied rates that changed due to price fluctuations are highlighted in the table above.

6 months of the MND Peso Index™

Through the use of the MND Peso Index™, we have now determined that the peso was overvalued against the US dollar by 2.8% in late April, 4% in late May, 2.9% in late June, 2.4% in early August and 5.8% in early September. That’s right — there were five consecutive overvalued assessments for the peso before this month’s determination that the currency was slightly undervalued in early October.

The difference between this month’s undervalued assessment for the peso and the highest overvalued assessment — that in early September — is 6.5 percentage points.

So far in 2026, the peso has depreciated around 2% against the US dollar. It closed at 18.00 to the greenback on the final day of 2025, according to the Bank of Mexico, while the closing USD:MXN rate on Tuesday, Oct. 13 was 18.38. If the Banxico FIX rate was 18.38 when we collected the prices for the Mexican and Dallas baskets on Oct. 6, the undervaluation assessment for the peso would have been 2.9%.

* Price sources: Mexico prices were collected from the websites and apps of Walmart México, Costco México, AutoZone México, Telmex, Cinépolis, Petco México, McDonald’s, Starbucks, Netflix, Spotify and Microsoft. Dallas prices were collected from their U.S. equivalents. The Banxico FIX rate of 17.97 published on Oct. 6, 2026, was used as the official exchange rate reference.

World.title: First migrating monarchs are spotted in Coahuila
World.content:
The monarch butterfly’s annual migration from southern Canada to central Mexico is in full swing, with the first sighting confirmed in the border state of Coahuila last week.

Linabeth Flores with the Mexican NGO Profauna confirmed, “We can now officially say that the migration is here.”

The monarch butterflies undertake a perilous southward migration each year from Canada, through the United States, and to Mexico starting in late August to reach their winter resting spot in the pine forests of Michoacán before the bacchanalian breeding season. New generations then migrate north to the Canadian Prairies for spring and summer.

Sightings so far have been concentrated in the cities of Acuña, Múzquiz, Monclova and Cuatro Ciénegas and are expected to increase in the coming days. At the Higher Technological Institute of Múzquiz, several monarchs were spotted feeding on polocote (Mexican sunflower) and pomegranate blossoms.

Before this year’s migration began, two dozen monarch butterflies were tagged with toothpick-sized radio transmitters in Winnipeg, Canada. The practice of tagging butterflies with tracking devices is common among conservation groups in Mexico, Canada and the United States, as it provides valuable information for the protection of the monarch population, which is endangered by climate change and habitat loss.

The first butterfly tagged in Winnipeg, known by the identifier MB26011, has already crossed the Mexican border, just five weeks after leaving Canada.

“She’s done about 2,300 kilometers in about 40 days,” said Laura Burns, the conservation program manager at the Assiniboine Park Zoo in Winnipeg. “It’s really incredible.”

Conservation researchers and members of the public can track the butterflies’ movements on the Project Monarch app.

Peak migration should occur within the next week, with most monarchs reaching overwintering sites in Michoacán and México state in early November. Profauna has asked the public to share photos and reports of the butterflies to help identify flight routes and locate the sites they use to rest and feed during their passage through Coahuila.

The eastern monarch population has fallen by an estimated 80% to 90% since the 1990s, although the number of butterflies in central Mexico this spring was around 64% higher than in the previous season, according to figures from Mexico’s Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat) and the World Wildlife Fund (WWF).

With reports from El Horizonte and CBC

World.title: I never thought of myself as Hispanic. Then I moved to the US
World.content:
A new Pew Research Center analysis asks who counts as Hispanic. For many Mexicans, the answer only arrives after they cross the border — sometimes shouted by a stranger.

I was on the phone with my mother — in Spanish, of course — when a woman who was clearly having a bad day shouted “f—ing South American” at me. My first impulse was to correct her: North American, actually. But I knew precision was beside the point. She wasn’t pointing at my exact origin; she was pointing at my culture.

And yes, unlike her, I am not Anglo-Saxon. So what am I?

The moment I became Hispanic

It is the question the Pew Research Center asked this month in its survey “Who Is Hispanic?,” published at the start of Hispanic Heritage Month. Pew’s answer suggests that it depends on who is counting.

Mine is that I only became Hispanic when I crossed the border.

It sounds naive, but until then I had no idea how many labels I could carry. It was, on a much smaller scale, a Frantz Fanon moment.

Fanon was a Martinican psychiatrist trained in France in the mid-20th century. In “Black Skin, White Masks” (1952), he recounts how a child in the street pointed at him and cried out, “Tiens, un nègre!” The moment forced him to confront everything his skin color meant in the France of his time. It opened a body of work on how such labels are produced by racial violence — territory I won’t step into here.

Labels and how they’re given

One detail of Fanon’s account stays with me, though. He argues that in Martinique, Antilleans did not think of themselves as Black; the label was waiting for them in Europe. Mine was waiting for me in the United States.

If we’re going by labels, I am North American (the region, not the country). I’m also Latin American, Mexican and chilanga, from Mexico City — and, to be precise, from the south of the city.

I know that people who did not grow up in an urban setting like mine are often far more aware of their ethnic origin, especially where an Indigenous language is still alive. Think of Oaxaca and the Mixe, Zapotec, Mixtec or Triqui peoples. I’ll confess that I was always more conscious of my socioeconomic context than of my ethnicity.

The state that made us Mexican

For those of us raised in cities, that blind spot is largely the legacy of the post-revolutionary state. After a decade of war, it decided that the best way to calm the waters was to insist that we were, above all, proud to be Mexican.

To make that true, the state launched an intense education campaign whose first goal was for everyone to speak Spanish, because once you erase the language that sets people apart, you erase the distinction between them. But the shift had started long before.

Around 1820, as Mexico was becoming independent, an estimated 60% of the population spoke an Indigenous language. By 1900, the figure was 15.4%. In the 2020 census, it was 6.1% of Mexicans aged three and older — and 87% of them also speak Spanish.

The project had a name for what it wanted to produce: a generalized mestizo. Anthropologist Manuel Gamio’s “Forjando Patria” (1916) and former education minister José Vasconcelos‘ “La Raza Cósmica” (1925) turned mixture into national identity.

So when I say I was never aware of my ethnicity, that is not entirely accurate. The state gave me one. I simply never noticed it, because the dominant category never needs to be named.

The painted castes

Mixture is not new in Mexico. Under Spanish colonial rule, a hierarchy of castas gave a name to each combination of Spanish, Indigenous and African ancestry, and that name could limit access to offices, guilds and rights. Historians note that daily life was more fluid than the system suggests, but the categories carried weight.

The independence movement explicitly rejected them. Miguel Hidalgo‘s 1810 decree abolished slavery and the tribute paid by the castes. In 1813, José María Morelos’ “Sentimientos de la Nación” called for abolishing “the distinction of castes.” The Plan of Iguala of 1821 declared all inhabitants citizens, regardless of origin.

From that era we keep the 18th-century casta paintings: picturesque and, to our eyes, a little terrible. Perhaps that is why it unsettles me when a society asks me to identify with a label. In Mexico, those labels still shape a person’s prospects. A 2016 survey by INEGI, Mexico’s national statistics agency, found that among Mexicans who placed themselves in the lightest skin tones, 10% had no schooling at all; among those in the darkest tones, the figure was 20.2%.

Who counts as Hispanic?

In the United States, the category was born as an administrative tool. Fifty years ago, Congress ordered the government to count Americans of Spanish-speaking background with roots in Mexico, Puerto Rico, Cuba, and Central and South America. The criterion is not geographic but linguistic — and, at bottom, colonial. Brazilians, Portuguese, Belizeans and Filipinos are left out.

The state does not always accept what people declare. If someone writes “Mexican” in the race question without checking the Hispanic box, the Census Bureau counts them as Hispanic anyway. If someone checks “Other Hispanic” and writes “Irish,” the bureau recodes them as non-Hispanic.

The race question itself fits poorly. In 2024, 23.4 million single-race Hispanics chose “some other race,” and most wrote in a nationality such as “Mexican” or “Latin American.” For those of us raised on mestizaje as national identity, race and nation are the same answer.

Most revealing is how Hispanics describe themselves. According to Pew’s 2025 survey, 53% use their family’s country of origin, 27% use “Hispanic” or “Latino,” and 18% simply say “American.” Most of the people the category covers prefer not to use it for themselves.

One figure seems to contradict my story: 97% of immigrants with Hispanic ancestry identify as Hispanic. I don’t think it does. The survey measures whether you accept the label when it is offered, not whether it existed for you before you arrived. The question assumes you have already crossed the border.

I also understand why the term exists, and why being counted matters to many. In a 2021 Pew survey, 57% of Latino adults said skin color shapes their daily lives at least somewhat.

A society of societies

I know the United States is a different case: a country made of many societies, with different customs coexisting in the same space. In 2024, its immigrant population reached a record 50.2 million, or 14.8% of residents. The only other time the share was that high was 1890.

The Census Bureau’s own breakdown shows how these labels overlap. Of the 341.8 million people it estimated for July 2025, 72.3% are counted as White alone, 13.5% as Black, 6.9 percent as Asian, 2.1% as American Indian or Alaska Native, 0.3% as Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, and 4.9% as two or more races. Hispanics, 20.5% of the population, are counted on top of those races rather than beside them, which is why non-Hispanic Whites are only 56.1%. The official estimates carry no “some other race” category at all — the box where millions of Hispanics write in their nationality.

The Hispanic population, now 70.1 million, is itself a federation of nationalities. In 2021, it included 37.2 million people of Mexican origin, 5.8 million Puerto Ricans and 2.5 million Salvadorans, with five other origin groups above 1 million each. “Hispanic” holds all of them in a single box.

Naming is classifying

When someone shouts my origin at me in the street — what a casta painter might have labeled mestiza — I become aware of what my features say, and of everything they tell another person before I open my mouth.

In 1952, the same year Fanon published his book, Jorge Luis Borges wrote in “The Analytical Language of John Wilkins” that every classification of the universe is arbitrary and conjectural. To name something is already to sort it.

So the question is not whether I am Hispanic. By the government’s definition, I am. The question is why it matters to name me that way — and what that classification says about us, and about those who do the classifying.

María Meléndez is a writer and art historian. She works at the Mexican Cultural Institute of the Embassy of Mexico in Washington, D.C.

World.title: San Luis Potosí auto cluster sees potential for Chinese manufacturing investment
World.content:
Could a Chinese automaker open a plant in the state of San Luis Potosí?

The president of the San Luis Potosí Automotive Cluster, an industry group, believes it’s possible.

Alberto Rosales Reyna, the cluster’s president, told the San Luis Potosí-based newspaper Plano Informativo that Asian automakers, including Chinese ones, have considered investing in the state, where BMW and General Motors have plants.

He acknowledged that no new automotive plant projects have been confirmed for San Luis Potosí, but suggested that could soon change.

“A very significant [possible] investment in the production of Chinese vehicles [in Mexico] has been spoken about as part of an effort to increase local content and have Chinese production in our state,” Rosales said.

He didn’t mention the names of any Chinese automakers that could open a plant in San Luis Potosí. However, Rosales asserted that the state has the capacity to welcome an automaker from China or any other country.

The geographical location of San Luis Potosí, the “technical ability” of its workforce, proximity to supply chains and “support that the local government could provide” all make the state an attractive place for automotive investment, he said.

Those things give San Luis Potosí “a great advantage,” Rosales said.

BYD is among the Chinese automakers that have expressed interest in opening a plant in Mexico. But neither that company — the world’s largest electric vehicle manufacturer — nor any other Chinese automaker has opened a plant in the country to date.

(However, a Mexican company, Giant Motors Latinoamérica, does assemble vehicles for Chinese automaker JAC at a plant in Ciudad Sahagún, Hidalgo.)

SLP automotive industry event could generate ‘business opportunities’ worth more than US $100 million

Rosales’ remarks about the possibility of a Chinese automaker investing in San Luis Potosí came ahead of Automotive Connection Potosí 2026, a business-to-business (B2B) networking event that will be held in San Luis Potosí city on Nov. 11 and 12.

The San Luis Potosí Automotive Cluster and the state Ministry of Economic Development are collaborating on the event.

According to the event website and media reports, Automotive Connection Potosí 2026 is projected to generate over US $100 million in “business opportunities” through meetings between automotive sector buyers and suppliers. Thirty buyers are listed on the event website, including BMW and Stellantis.

More than 500 suppliers are slated to attend the event, at which more than 1,500 B2B meetings will take place, according to the organizers.

According to a report by the news outlet Quadratín, San Luis Potosí Economic Development Minister Mario García Valde said that the event “seeks to facilitate local companies’ access to automotive sector buyers and open up opportunities for their incorporation in new productive projects.”

With reports from Plano Informativo and Quadratín San Luis Potosí

World.title: ICPC vs El-Rufai Aide Jimi Lawal: What We Know
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

The Federal High Court in Kaduna, where Jimi Lawal and Nasir El-Rufai face ICPC charges, pictured in July 2021. (Photo: Anasskoko, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

EXPLAINER · NIGERIA

Key Facts — The country Nigeria is Africa’s most populous country and a major oil exporter, heading into a general election in early 2027.

— Why it matters Nasir El-Rufai, Kaduna State governor from 2015 to 2023, is now a senior opposition campaigner. He and a former aide face corruption charges they deny.

— Why now On Wednesday 14 October, the anti-graft agency ICPC told a federal court in Kaduna it opposes bail for the El-Rufai aide Jimi Lawal.

— What happened Justice Hauwa’u Buhari set the bail hearing for Friday 16 October. The trial itself is due to start on 8 December.

— The numbers The case centres on a CCTV surveillance contract worth N8.68 billion (about US$6.5 million). El-Rufai has been held by the ICPC since 18 February.

— What it means for you Graft trials of opposition figures shape how investors read Nigeria’s rule of law before the 2027 vote. Testimony has also touched a New York-listed company.

— Still open Why the ICPC opposes bail, how ill Lawal is, and whether either man will be freed before trial.

The El-Rufai aide at the centre of a new bail fight is Jimi Lawal, a former senior special adviser to ex-Kaduna governor Nasir El-Rufai. On Wednesday 14 October, Nigeria’s Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) told a federal court it opposes his release.

The hearing took place at the Federal High Court in Kaduna, the capital of a large state in northern Nigeria. For foreign readers, the case is a test of how Nigeria handles corruption charges against a leading opposition figure ahead of the 2027 elections.

Lawal is the second defendant in a money laundering case in which El-Rufai is the first. Both men have pleaded not guilty, and the allegations against them have not been tested at trial.

What the ICPC Alleges Against the El-Rufai Aide

The ICPC is the federal agency that investigates and prosecutes graft by public officials, and it is led by Musa Aliyu, a senior lawyer. It filed the case on 17 April and arraigned the defendants in June on an amended 11-count charge, the commission said in a statement.

According to the charges as reported by Premium Times, El-Rufai approved a CCTV contract worth N8.68 billion (about US$6.5 million) in December 2015. The ICPC alleges the contract went to Singularity Network Security Limited, a firm it says lacked the experience the job required.

The April charge sheet also alleged that Lawal and two companies received N925 million (about US$694,000) in suspected illicit proceeds in October 2019. Lawal pleaded not guilty to counts six, seven and eight, while El-Rufai pleaded not guilty to count one.

Dollar figures in this article use the Central Bank of Nigeria’s official central rate of N1,332.09 per US$1 on 14 October. They are approximate and rounded.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Nigeria Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What Happened in Court on Wednesday

ICPC prosecutor Ibrahim Mukhtar told reporters the agency had filed a counter-affidavit against Lawal’s bail request. “We are opposing the application,” he said, according to Punch.

Mukhtar declined to give the grounds, saying the prosecution had not yet argued them before the judge. He described the charges as alleged financial misconduct involving about seven counts and said no witness had yet testified.

Lawal’s lawyer, Obong Okon, asked for bail on medical grounds, adding that only a living person could stand trial. He argued the ICPC could not reasonably object after it had earlier granted Lawal administrative bail, the News Agency of Nigeria reported via Peoples Gazette.

The prosecution asked for time to study a further affidavit from the defence, which was served on Wednesday afternoon. El-Rufai’s new counsel, Mustapha Abubakar, a senior advocate, said both sides agreed to the delay in the interest of a fair hearing.

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Why the Bail Fight Matters

El-Rufai himself has been in ICPC custody since 18 February under court-ordered remand, Premium Times and The ICIR report. On Friday 9 October, the Court of Appeal in Kaduna upheld a state court’s refusal to grant him bail.

He also faces a separate ICPC case at the Kaduna State High Court over alleged abuse of office and money laundering. Premium Times says the prosecutions stem largely from a 2024 Kaduna State House of Assembly probe of his administration.

In that state case on Tuesday, a forensic witness from the State Security Service alleged that El-Rufai planned to pay US$600,000 to stall an investigation by another agency, the EFCC. Premium Times stressed the claim is prosecution evidence that the court has not yet established.

El-Rufai’s lawyer, Paul Erokoro, objected that the defence had not been told the witness would appear, but Justice Darius Khobo allowed the testimony. That trial resumes on 30 November and 1 December.

El-Rufai maintains that his prosecution is politically motivated. He is deputy chairman of the campaign council of Atiku Abubakar, the former vice president running for the opposition African Democratic Congress (ADC).

What It Means for US Readers

Premium Times reports that the witness also described plans to keep the EFCC away from a company listed on the New York Stock Exchange, which it did not name. The April charge sheet, as reported by the same paper, named an executive of tower operator IHS, whose parent trades in New York.

That executive was not among the defendants arraigned in June, according to Premium Times and Daily Trust. No US company has been charged, and none has been accused of wrongdoing by a court.

For investors, the trials are a gauge of whether Nigeria’s anti-graft agencies act independently of politics before the 2027 elections. The US State Department rates Nigeria at Level 3, “reconsider travel,” citing crime, terrorism, unrest and kidnapping.

What Is Not Known

The ICPC has not said publicly why it opposes bail for Lawal, and the nature of his illness has not been disclosed. It is also unclear whether he is in detention, although he was brought to court under heavy security.

The number of counts is uncertain, because the prosecutor spoke of about seven counts while the June arraignment involved 11. It is also not known whether the judge will rule on Friday or reserve the decision for a later date.

Connected Coverage

For the wider picture of who holds power, read Nigeria Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026. The elites and regions behind it are mapped in Who Dominates Nigeria, Elites and Regions Explained.

Visitors heading to the country’s commercial capital can start with our Lagos City Guide for Expats and Visitors. The ruling party’s campaign line-up is covered in APC Campaign Council Adds Wike, Adeleke, Soludo.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the El-Rufai aide in the ICPC case?

The El-Rufai aide is Jimi Lawal, a former senior special adviser to ex-Kaduna governor Nasir El-Rufai. He is the second defendant in an ICPC money laundering case and has pleaded not guilty.

Why does the ICPC oppose Jimi Lawal’s bail?

The ICPC has filed a counter-affidavit against his bail request but has not yet given its reasons in court. Its prosecutor said the arguments would be made at the hearing.

When is the next hearing?

The Federal High Court in Kaduna will hear the bail application on Friday 16 October. The trial of El-Rufai and Lawal is scheduled to begin on 8 December.

What is the case about?

The ICPC alleges irregularities around a Kaduna CCTV contract worth N8.68 billion (about US$6.5 million) awarded in 2015. The defendants deny the charges, and no court has ruled on them.

Is Nasir El-Rufai in custody?

Yes, he has been held by the ICPC since 18 February under court-ordered remand. The Court of Appeal in Kaduna upheld the refusal of his bail on 9 October.

World.title: Petrobras Oil Output Hits 2.96 Million a Day
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

Sunrise over the Santos Basin, home of the pre-salt fields that drive Petrobras oil output, seen from a drillship in 2015. (Photo: Diego Vasconcellos Renato, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

ENERGY · BRAZIL

Key Facts — The country Brazil pumped 4.615 million barrels of oil a day in August, and state-controlled Petrobras dominates that output.

— Why it matters Petrobras shares trade in New York, and rising Brazilian output adds barrels from outside OPEC to the world market.

— Why now Preliminary regulator data for September reached the market on Wednesday 14 October, a day after a US$859 million settlement with partners.

— What happened Petrobras produced 2.96 million barrels of oil a day in September 2026, up 1% from August, a level Brazilian media called a record.

— The numbers Third-quarter oil output averaged 2.89 million barrels a day, up 6% on the quarter and above a 2.77 million consensus.

— What it means for you Holders of Petrobras ADRs may see higher profit and cash estimates, while more Brazilian crude can ease pressure on global prices.

— Still open The September figures are preliminary, and the regulator’s consolidated bulletin and the company’s own third-quarter report are still due.

— Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

Prediction markets · who wins the runoff Implied chance of winning Brazil’s presidency on 25 October, from traders’ prices. Polymarket Flávio Bolsonaro 85% · Lula 14.5% (US$182 million traded) Kalshi (regulated in the US by the CFTC) Flávio Bolsonaro 86% · Lula 15% As of 14 October, 3:00 pm ET (20:00 Lisbon), updated every 20 minutes. Prices are bets, not polls, and can move fast. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Petrobras oil output reached 2.96 million barrels a day in September 2026, according to preliminary regulator data compiled by Bradesco BBI. The figure, up 1% from August, was described by Brazilian financial media on Wednesday 14 October as a new record.

For US readers, the number matters because Petrobras shares trade on the New York Stock Exchange as American depositary receipts. It also shows Brazil adding supply from outside the OPEC+ group of producers.

The data come from the National Agency of Petroleum, Natural Gas and Biofuels (ANP), the federal regulator that tracks output field by field. Bradesco BBI, the investment banking arm of Bradesco, one of Brazil’s largest private banks, compiled them in a note to clients.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 75.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Petrobras is Brazil’s state-controlled oil company and the operator of most of the country’s offshore fields. Its shares rose more than 1% on Wednesday morning in São Paulo, InfoMoney reported.

What Drove Petrobras Oil Output in September

The gain came mainly from two giant fields in the pre-salt layer, the deep reservoirs beneath a thick salt crust off Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. Output at Búzios rose 2% in the month, while Tupi grew 8%, according to the BBI note.

Tupi produced about 550,000 barrels a day in September, after running closer to 500,000 between May and August. Búzios stayed above one million barrels a day, the bank said.

Búzios is now Brazil’s largest producing oil field. The ANP’s August bulletin, published on Thursday 1 October, put its oil output at 1.172 million barrels a day.

The field has eight production units after the P-79 platform started up on 1 May 2026, three months ahead of plan. Petrobras said in July that the new unit lifts installed capacity at Búzios to about 1.33 million barrels a day.

Petrobras oil output in September 2026 topped both the third-quarter average and Bradesco BBI's 2027 forecast. Source: ANP preliminary data and Bradesco BBI, as reported 14 Oct 2026.

Over the whole third quarter, Petrobras oil output averaged 2.89 million barrels a day, up 6% on the quarter, BBI calculates. That beat the market consensus of 2.77 million barrels a day cited by InfoMoney and Guia do Investidor.

How September Fits Brazil’s Oil Boom

Brazil as a whole produced 4.615 million barrels of oil a day in August, the ANP said. That was 2.6% more than in July and 18.4% more than in August 2025.

Total oil and gas output reached 6.002 million barrels of oil equivalent a day in August. Fields operated by Petrobras, alone or with partners, accounted for 87.55% of everything produced.

The company had already reported record own production of 3.34 million barrels of oil equivalent a day in the second quarter. That figure, released on 28 July, includes natural gas and was 14.1% higher than a year earlier.

Our Petrobras company profile tracks the group’s results and dividends over time. Our earlier report, Petrobras Hits Record Oil Output Ahead of Q2 Results, covered the second-quarter numbers.

The Exploration and Production segment explores, develops, and produces…

The US$859 Million Partner Settlement

On Tuesday 13 October, Petrobras said it had signed cost and volume equalisation agreements for the shared Berbigão and Sururu reservoirs in the Santos Basin. It will receive a net amount of about US$859 million from its partners, to be settled by November 2026.

The partners are Shell, TotalEnergies and Petrogal Brasil, a unit tied to Portugal’s Galp, all members of the BM-S-11A consortium. The payment follows the ANP’s approval of production unitisation agreements, which split a reservoir that crosses contract boundaries.

Under the new split, Petrobras holds about 45.4% of Sururu and 62.9% of Berbigão, effective from 1 May 2026. The settlement reconciles revenue, investment, operating costs and royalties back to the original concession signed on 15 September 2000.

Analysts at XP Investimentos, a Brazilian brokerage, said the sum equals about 0.52% of Petrobras’s market value. They added that it should support cash generation and dividends in the fourth quarter.

What It Means for You

For investors holding Petrobras ADRs, BBI expects analysts to keep revising production, profit and cash flow estimates upward. The bank models oil output of 2.8 million barrels a day in 2027 and 3.05 million in 2028.

September’s level already sits above the bank’s 2027 forecast, which BBI called reassuring for its view. It warned, however, that one strong month should not be extrapolated directly.

For the wider market, more Brazilian barrels add to supply from non-OPEC producers. That can help to cushion prices, although demand, conflict and OPEC+ decisions weigh far more on Brent.

Readers new to the country’s resource economy can start with Brazil Natural Resources Explained 2026. For the political backdrop, see Brazil Explained 2026 for Newcomers on Politics and Economy.

Petrobras has its headquarters in Rio de Janeiro, the hub of Brazil’s offshore oil industry. Our Rio de Janeiro city page covers life and business in the city.

What Is Not Known

The September numbers are preliminary, and the ANP’s consolidated bulletin for the month has not been published yet. Petrobras has not released its own third-quarter production report, which could show slightly different totals.

It is also unclear whether the 2.96 million level will hold in the coming months. BBI noted that planned stoppages, maintenance, well work and the pace of new platforms can all move monthly output.

Petrobras had not published its own September figures by Wednesday afternoon. The company has not said how it will use the US$859 million settlement.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much oil did Petrobras produce in September 2026?

Preliminary ANP data show Petrobras produced 2.96 million barrels of oil a day in September 2026. That was 1% more than in August.

Which fields drove the increase?

The Búzios and Tupi fields in the pre-salt layer led the gain, rising 2% and 8% in the month. Búzios stayed above one million barrels a day.

What is the US$859 million payment?

It is a net settlement Petrobras will receive from Shell, TotalEnergies and Petrogal Brasil over the shared Berbigão and Sururu reservoirs. The money is due by November 2026.

Why does this matter to US investors?

Petrobras ADRs trade in New York, and stronger output can lift profit and cash flow estimates. Analysts also expect the settlement to support fourth-quarter dividends.

Are the September figures final?

No, they are preliminary regulator data compiled by Bradesco BBI. The ANP’s consolidated bulletin and Petrobras’s third-quarter report will give the final numbers.

World.title: Russia War Recruitment Scams: How Dominicans Are Lured
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

EXPLAINER · DOMINICAN REPUBLIC

Key Facts — The country The Dominican Republic is a close US partner in the Caribbean, with a large diaspora in New York, New Jersey and Florida.

— Why it matters Offers of civilian work in Russia have pulled Dominican men towards the war in Ukraine, and the same bait has surfaced in Peru and Cuba.

— Why now On Wednesday 14 October the Labour Ministry told citizens to have any foreign job offer checked before signing or travelling.

— What happened The foreign ministry gave Russia files on 20 Dominicans on 6 October and had 22 complaints and requests by Friday 9 October.

— The numbers Rights researchers estimate Russia has recruited at least 27,000 foreigners from more than 130 countries since February 2022.

— What it means for you Relatives in the US who see Russia job offers shared online can ask Dominican officials to check them before anyone travels.

— Still open How many Dominicans are in Russia, who recruited them, and whether Moscow will release any of them from their contracts.

Russia war recruitment scams follow a simple script: a well-paid civilian job abroad, a quick trip, then a military contract, often written in Russian. On Wednesday 14 October the Dominican Republic’s Labour Ministry warned citizens about this pattern after families said relatives had been drawn into the war in Ukraine.

For US readers, the offers matter because they spread through social media and family networks that reach Dominican communities in New York, New Jersey and Florida. They also show Moscow’s hunt for foreign soldiers reaching countries that work closely with Washington on security and migration.

Our news report, Dominicans Get 3 Red Flags for Russia Jobs, sets out the ministry’s three warning signs. This explainer looks at how the scheme works, why Latin Americans are targeted and what remains unclear.

How Russia War Recruitment Scams Work

The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), a Paris-based network of rights groups, studied the system with Ukraine’s Truth Hounds and a Kazakh rights bureau. Their report of 29 April estimates that Russia has recruited at least 27,000 foreign nationals from more than 130 countries since February 2022.

In sub-Saharan Africa, Nepal, Cuba and Yemen, the study says, middlemen promised well-paid civilian jobs in construction, security or cleaning, plus Russian citizenship. Within days of arriving in Russia, some of those recruits found themselves in uniform and on their way to the front.

The report says up to 20% of such fighters did not survive their first four months of deployment. It adds that Russia widened foreigners’ access to military contracts by law, created fast routes to citizenship and introduced sign-up bonuses.

The authors do not claim that every recruit was deceived, and they say many knew to some extent what they were joining. Others were tricked or coerced, which is where military service can shade into human trafficking under international law.

Peru shows how one alleged recruitment chain can reach court. On 1 October prosecutors in Lima North obtained the preliminary detention of a 54-year-old man, Pocho Pinto, on suspicion of aggravated human trafficking.

Prosecutors say he offered four Peruvians about US$2,300 a month and a US$20,000 bonus after a year as guards at a military base. They also say he assured the men they would not be sent to a war zone or the front line.

One of them, Julio Salazar, was taken to military facilities, trained and made to sign a contract in Russian he did not understand, according to the prosecutors. He died at the front in April, and by 11 October a Lima judge had ordered Pinto held for 14 months while prosecutors investigate.

Pinto is presumed innocent, and the case against him has not been tested at trial. Prosecutors said the route ran from Lima through Paris, Istanbul and Moscow to Ufa.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why Dominicans and Other Latin Americans Are Targeted

Dominican families describe the same bait in the cases now before their government. Trinidad Campusano told the newspaper Hoy that her brother Héctor, 52, went to Russia for a job welding trucks and was then put into training for the war.

Jacqueline Félix told Hoy that her son Maicol, 33, left the country on 19 August with the promise of work in Panama and is now in Russia. She said he has asked for help to leave, and that he never agreed to travel for a war.

The foreign ministry says the men signed their contracts individually on Russian soil. Some of them and their relatives told the ministry that what they found did not match the work they say they travelled for.

Russia’s ambassador in Santo Domingo, Alexey Seredin, gave a different picture on the El Día programme on Telesistema, the newspaper reported on 5 October. “Russia considers these volunteers heroes,” he said, describing enlistment as a personal choice that foreigners may make under Russian law.

The FIDH study says recruiters focus on people in economic, social or legal hardship, from undocumented migrants to workers in insecure jobs. Many, it says, were drawn by promises of citizenship and wages far above anything available at home.

Relatives have kept up a protest outside the National Congress in Santo Domingo, Hoy reported on 9 October. Their main fear, relatives told Hoy, is that the men now in training will be sent to the front.

What the Dominican Government Has Done

The foreign ministry first warned publicly about these offers on 24 September. That day Foreign Minister Víctor “Ito” Bisonó raised the issue with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at a meeting in New York during the UN General Assembly.

On 6 October two vice-ministers handed Russia’s ambassador, Alexey Seredin, the files on 20 Dominicans formally identified by their families. By Friday 9 October Bisonó said his ministry had 22 complaints and requests, some from relatives and some from men who had come back.

Bisonó warned that the state’s room to act is limited when contracts were signed between private parties. In some cases, he said, relatives need a power of attorney before officials can act on behalf of a family member abroad.

On 14 October Labour Minister Eddy Olivares Ortega, a vice-president of the governing Modern Revolutionary Party (PRM) of President Luis Abinader, added his own warning. He said the country has no bilateral labour migration agreement with Russia, though that alone does not make every individual contract abroad illegal.

Olivares listed three warning signs: extraordinary pay without clear duties or employer, unjustified fees in advance, and middlemen whose identity cannot be confirmed. He also urged people not to hand passports to intermediaries or sign contracts they do not fully understand.

What It Means for You

For Dominican families in the United States, the practical step is to check an offer before anyone books a flight. The Labour Ministry in Santo Domingo reviews foreign job offers, and the foreign ministry handles the cases of people already in Russia.

The foreign ministry’s citizen protection desk can be reached on (809) 987-7001, extensions 7595, 7597 and 7100. The Dominican embassy in Moscow also takes calls and e-mails from nationals in Russia who need help.

The warning signs look similar wherever the offer comes from: high pay, vague duties, upfront fees, unknown middlemen and a contract in Russian. Peru’s case adds two more, namely guard work at a military base and promises that the worker will never see combat.

For Washington, the cases show Russian recruitment reaching partners in its own neighbourhood. Bisonó said other governments in the region have also warned their citizens, so the problem is not confined to one country.

What Is Not Known

It is not known how many Dominicans are in Russia, or how many signed contracts knowing they would serve in the military. The figure of 22 is a count of complaints and requests, not of confirmed recruits.

Dominican officials have not said who recruited the men or whether prosecutors have opened a case. Russia has not said publicly whether it will release any of them from their contracts.

Earlier coverage is in Dominican Republic Seeks 22 Citizens in Russia’s War and Peru Seeks 18-Month Jail for Alleged Russia Recruiter. Wider context is in Dominican Republic Geopolitics 2026, US, China, Gulf, Dominican Republic’s Role in Latin America Explained and our Santo Domingo city page.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are Russia war recruitment scams?

They are offers of civilian work in Russia, such as construction, security or technical jobs, that end in military contracts. Rights groups say some recruits know what they are joining, while others are deceived or pressured.

How many Dominicans are affected?

The foreign ministry handed Russia files on 20 Dominicans formally identified by their families on 6 October. By 9 October it had 22 complaints and requests, but the total number in Russia is not known.

Is it illegal for Dominicans to take a job in Russia?

The Labour Minister said the lack of a bilateral labour deal with Russia does not by itself make every individual contract illegal. Hiding the true nature of a job or sending someone without telling them the risks can, however, seriously violate their rights.

What warning signs should families watch for?

Officials point to extraordinary pay with vague duties, demands for upfront fees and middlemen whose identity cannot be checked. Peruvian prosecutors describe two more: offers of guard work at a military base and promises that the worker will not reach the front.

Where can Dominican families get help?

The Labour Ministry checks foreign job offers before people travel, and the foreign ministry assists nationals already in Russia. Its citizen protection desk is on (809) 987-7001, extensions 7595, 7597 and 7100.

Sources: Ministerio de Trabajo, 14 October 2026 (mt.gob.do); MIREX, 25 September 2026 (mirex.gob.do); MIREX, 7 October 2026 (mirex.gob.do); Ministerio Público del Perú, 1 October 2026 (gob.pe); FIDH, 29 April 2026 (fidh.org); Listín Diario, 9 October 2026 (listindiario.com); Hoy, 9 October 2026 (hoy.com.do); Hoy, 11 October 2026 (hoy.com.do); El Día, 5 October 2026 (eldia.com.do); Correo, 11 October 2026 (diariocorreo.pe); MIREX, ambassador’s credentials 2025 (mirex.gob.do).

World.title: De La Espriella and the ACSN: His Santa Marta Offensive
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

PROFILE · COLOMBIA

Key Facts — The country Colombia, a close US security partner, has been led since Friday 7 August by President Abelardo de la Espriella, a conservative former criminal defence lawyer.

— Why it matters His fight with the ACSN, an armed group based above Santa Marta, is the first big test of his promise to crush armed groups by force.

— Why now Forty-one detainees escaped in Santa Marta on Monday 12 October, and he fired the city’s police commander the same day, calling cowardice unacceptable.

— What happened He rejected talks with the group on 12 September, then sent troops into Santa Marta after the ACSN called an armed strike on 21 September.

— The numbers A reward of COP 3 billion (about US$943,000) is on offer for ACSN leader alias Pinocho; 12 escapees were back in custody by Tuesday night.

— What it means for you The offensive overlaps with US anti-drug work, and visitors to Santa Marta and Tayrona face more troops, checkpoints and occasional road blockades.

— Still open Whether force alone can dismantle a group rooted in the Sierra Nevada, and whether Pinocho and the fugitives will be caught, remains unresolved.

— Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

De la Espriella and the ACSN have been locked in an open confrontation since September, and the Santa Marta jailbreak of Monday 12 October has raised the stakes. Colombia’s president, a conservative who took office on 7 August, has made the armed group the showcase of his hard-line security policy.

For US readers, the fight matters because authorities link the ACSN to cocaine shipments bound for the United States. It also plays out around Santa Marta and Tayrona National Park, one of Colombia’s main destinations for foreign tourists.

Who Abelardo De La Espriella Is

Abelardo de la Espriella was born in Bogotá on 31 July 1978 and grew up with family roots in Montería, on the Caribbean side of the country. He studied law at Universidad Sergio Arboleda in Bogotá and built a career as a criminal defence lawyer, according to Blu Radio and Noticias Caracol.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

His clients included the Colombian-Venezuelan businessman Alex Saab and David Murcia Guzmán of the DMG pyramid scheme, Noticias Caracol reported. In July 2025 he founded Defensores de la Patria, a movement that campaigned on an “iron fist” against criminals and corruption.

He won the runoff on Sunday 21 June 2026 with 49.66% in the electoral authority’s preliminary count, against 48.7% for Iván Cepeda of the left-wing Pacto Histórico. He was sworn in as President of the Republic for 2026 to 2030 in Cali on 7 August, with José Manuel Restrepo as vice president.

His wider agenda is covered in Who Is Abelardo de la Espriella? Colombia’s President.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

De La Espriella and the ACSN, From Ultimatum to Offensive

The Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada, also called Los Pachenca, are an armed group active in Magdalena, La Guajira and Cesar. Authorities name Fredy Castillo Carrillo, alias “Pinocho”, as their main leader.

Under former President Gustavo Petro, the group took part in exploratory legal talks, and Pinocho held the status of a “peace manager”. The new government dismantled those talks in late August and early September, and a Bogotá judge later rejected his legal challenge, NTN24 reported.

On Saturday 12 September, after Pinocho offered to surrender on conditions, the president gave his defence and justice ministers one week to arrange it. “Here there are no negotiations, delays or demands,” he wrote on X, warning that otherwise the order would be to kill him, Vanguardia reported.

The deadline passed, and on Monday 21 September police killed alias “Cholo”, described as the group’s second in command. The ACSN answered with an armed strike that shut shops and transport in Santa Marta for several days.

De la Espriella ordered the city militarised and on Wednesday 23 September told the prison service INPEC to move 76 detainees linked to the group. He said they would go to maximum-security wings in other regions so they could no longer give orders from Caribbean jails.

In a national address on Sunday 27 September, he offered COP 3 billion (about US$943,000 at the official rate of 3,181.74 pesos per dollar on 14 October) for Pinocho. He reported 2,500 security personnel in Santa Marta and 23 arrests of alleged group members, according to Minuto60.

He also said he would lead operations in person, carrying and if necessary using “the legitimate weapons of the Republic”. “We are breathing down his neck and we are going to find him,” he said of Pinocho, who remains at large.

The Santa Marta Escape Tests His Strategy

At about 1 a.m. on Monday 12 October, 41 detainees escaped from a police holding centre in Santa Marta. Among them was Mario Alejandro Méndez Aguilar, alias “Mongolo”, whom authorities describe as a senior ACSN figure and who is presumed innocent.

The president removed the metropolitan police commander, Colonel Jeyson Haird López Puerto, within hours. “In this government, cowardice has no place,” he wrote, citing the escape and a road blockade at Tasajera that police failed to handle, Blu Radio reported.

The Magdalena government offered up to COP 50 million (about US$15,700) for Mongolo and a second fugitive, alias “El Guajiro”. Santa Marta Mayor Carlos Pinedo Cuello said on Tuesday night that 12 escapees were back in custody and 29 remained at large.

On Tuesday 13 October, the president announced that police and soldiers working with the US Drug Enforcement Administration had seized about a tonne of cocaine near Tayrona that he attributed to the ACSN. “We keep hitting the criminal income of the narco-terrorists,” he wrote, as quoted by Semana.

The escape and the seizure are explained in detail in Santa Marta Jailbreak: What We Know About the ACSN. The September stand-off is covered in Alias Pinocho Gets One Week to Surrender, and No Deal in Return.

What Critics Say

Lerber Dimas Vásquez, who heads PDHAL, a human rights platform in the Sierra Nevada, links the escape to the hurried prisoner transfers. He told El Espectador that some detainees were moved to a temporary centre that was not ready, and that police guards are not trained like prison staff.

Luis Fernando Trejos, a conflict researcher at Universidad del Norte, told the same paper that the escape showed a deep lack of capacity among city authorities. He said the ACSN benefits directly, because it recovers members and may be able to recruit.

The president’s style is also personal and highly visible, from ultimatums on X to patrolling Santa Marta with a pistol on his belt. Supporters see resolve, while critics question whether public threats and rapid transfers produce lasting results.

What It Means for You

For US readers, De la Espriella’s campaign against the ACSN runs alongside joint anti-drug work with Washington, as Tuesday’s DEA-backed seizure showed. A government that publicly targets cocaine routes to the United States is likely to keep that cooperation close.

Travellers to Santa Marta, Tayrona, Minca or the Lost City trek should expect a heavy military and police presence. Visitors should follow alerts from the US Embassy in Bogotá and local authorities, and avoid road travel during announced strikes or blockades.

For investors, the episode shows a president willing to act fast and in public, but also the cost when institutions lag behind. The economic toll of the armed strike is covered in Santa Marta Armed Strike Cost Colombia’s Tourist City US$30 Million.

Wider context is in Colombia Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026 and Colombia Explained: The Country, Its Politics, Its Economy and What to Watch. Practical background on the city is on our Santa Marta city page.

What Is Not Known

Pinocho’s whereabouts are unknown, and reports in September said troops were reinforcing the Venezuelan border in case he tried to flee. Whether he will be captured, killed or surrender has not been settled.

Counts of the Santa Marta fugitives still at large have varied since Monday, from 33 cited in early reports to 29 given by the mayor on Tuesday night. No investigation result into how guards lost control has been published.

It is also unclear how much the offensive has weakened the ACSN’s finances and command. The government reports arrests and seizures, but independent assessments of the group’s strength are not yet available.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the President of Colombia in October 2026?

Abelardo de la Espriella is President of Colombia, sworn in for the 2026 to 2030 term in Cali on 7 August 2026. He is a conservative former criminal defence lawyer who founded the Defensores de la Patria movement.

What is the conflict between De la Espriella and the ACSN?

De la Espriella and the ACSN have clashed since he rejected negotiations with the group in September and ordered a military offensive. The group, also called Los Pachenca, answered with an armed strike that paralysed Santa Marta for several days.

What reward is offered for alias Pinocho?

The government offers COP 3 billion, about US$943,000, for information leading to ACSN leader Fredy Castillo Carrillo, alias Pinocho. He remained at large as of 14 October.

How did the president react to the Santa Marta escape?

He removed the city’s police commander on Monday 12 October and ordered priority efforts to recapture alias Mongolo. Regional authorities also offered rewards for the two most wanted fugitives.

Is Santa Marta safe to visit?

Security forces have been reinforced in the city since September, but armed strikes and road blockades have disrupted travel in recent weeks. Visitors should follow US Embassy and local alerts before travelling to Tayrona or the Sierra Nevada.

World.title: How Cartel Sanctions Affect US Investors in Nuevo León
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

The San Jerónimo district of Monterrey, the capital of Nuevo León, seen from the Obispado hill. (Photo: Rick González, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

GUIDE · MEXICO

Key Facts — The country Nuevo León is a northern Mexican industrial state with Monterrey as its capital and a short border with Texas at the Colombia crossing near Laredo.

— Why it matters US cartel sanctions now reach businesses registered inside Nuevo León, a manufacturing base for many US companies and their Mexican suppliers.

— Why now On Tuesday 13 October the US Treasury blacklisted four people and 11 entities tied to the Cartel del Noreste, including a builder and a horse barn in Anáhuac, Nuevo León.

— What happened The listed builder CEGESA had won three Nuevo León state contracts worth about US$6 million in 2022 and 2023 for works at the Colombia border crossing.

— The numbers US holders of blocked property must report it within 10 business days and file an annual report by 30 September; firms 50% owned by listed persons are blocked too.

— What it means for you Companies with Mexican partners, contractors, carriers or fuel suppliers need to screen them and their owners against the US sanctions list before any payment or shipment.

— Still open Which Mexican politicians allegedly received cartel campaign money is not public, and Mexico’s president says Washington has shared no evidence.

— Power Index Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 71.4 points (October 2026 edition).

Cartel sanctions announced by the US Treasury on Tuesday 13 October now reach companies in Nuevo León, the industrial state around Monterrey. For US investors, suppliers and lenders with Mexican partners, the listing creates legal duties that apply immediately.

The Treasury’s sanctions unit, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), listed 15 people and firms tied to the Cartel del Noreste. Several are registered in Anáhuac, the Nuevo León municipality that hosts the Colombia border crossing to Laredo, Texas.

This guide explains what US rules require of American companies and investors, and how firms check their exposure. It summarises published rules and is not legal or investment advice.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 71.4 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the Cartel Sanctions Changed on 13 October

The Cartel del Noreste is a Los Zetas offshoot based in Nuevo Laredo, Tamaulipas, across from Laredo, Texas. Washington named it a terrorist group in February 2025, as our explainer Cartel Del Noreste: What We Know After US Sanctions sets out.

The 13 October package covers a racetrack, construction and fuel firms, a horse barn and a trucking company. It was issued under Executive Order 14059 on the drug trade and Executive Order 13224 on terrorism.

The Nuevo León names are Gamaliel Garza García, his son Gamaliel Garza Elías, his builder CEGESA and his barn Cuadra San Dibanh, all in Anáhuac. Treasury calls Garza García, a businessman and racehorse owner, a cartel associate whose firm funnelled money to election campaigns.

Treasury also says CEGESA corruptly won public works contracts and subcontracted the work to cartel-linked people. Seven more of his firms in Nuevo Laredo, in building materials, construction, fuel and gas, were listed as well.

No criminal charges over this action have been announced, and a sanctions listing is not a conviction. Hacienda, Mexico’s finance ministry, said the listing is a preventive administrative measure and not a final finding of responsibility.

Our first report, US Sanctions 11 Firms Tied to Mexican Cartel, lists every name in the package. The cartel sanctions were the fourth and largest US action against the group’s networks since May 2025.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Mexico Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why Nuevo León Is Exposed

Nuevo León’s border development agency, Codefront, awarded CEGESA three contracts worth about MXN 110 million (about US$6 million) in 2022 and 2023. The work was at the international trade centre of the Colombia border crossing in Anáhuac.

The anti-graft group Mexicanos Contra la Corrupción y la Impunidad (MCCI) found the contracts in national transparency records, La Silla Rota reported. Peso amounts here use Banco de México’s FIX rate of 18.3528 per US dollar for Tuesday 13 October.

The largest contract, about MXN 70 million (about US$3.8 million), paid for booths and access lanes in July 2023. Codefront belongs to the state government of Governor Samuel García, of the centre-left opposition Movimiento Ciudadano party.
