World.title: Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg to build anti-drone factory in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg has announced plans to build a new factory in Poland producing counter-drone systems. The firm will invest over 200 million zloty (€46 million) in the facility, creating more than 100 long-term jobs. “The new facility will support Polish industry and defence capabilities and strengthen Kongsberg’s presence in Poland,” declared CEO Eirik Lie alongside Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz at the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year serving as the official partner nation. In January, Kongsberg signed an agreement to supply a new anti-drone system to Poland in partnership with Polish state defence group PGZ. The project comes in response to growing fears over the threat of Russian drones, around 20 of which violated Polish airspace on one night in September last year. Norwegowie inwestują w Polsce. Duża inwestycja #Kongsberg na Pomorzu ogłoszona właśnie na #WSF2026. Szybka budowa fabryki i nowe miejsca pracy. pic.twitter.com/msI2FWGym8 — Beata Górka-Winter (@BeataGWinter) October 12, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz thanked Kongsberg for its investment and emphasised that Polish-Norwegian relations are at their highest point in history, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The announcement of the counter-drone plant came as Poland and Norway’s prime ministers, Donald Tusk and Jonas Gahr Støre, signed a declaration on strategic partnership that pledged to deepen security ties, including joint defence production and strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks. While the exact location of the plant has not been revealed, Kongsberg stated that it would be in northern Poland, near the Tricity area (consisting of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot) on the Baltic Sea coast. Construction of the facility is scheduled to begin this year, with production at the site scheduled to commence in the first half of 2028. Counter-drone technology has become an increasing priority for Poland following Russian airspace violations and also the growing use by Moscow of jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border, including recently a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw. Polish spending on drones and counter-drone systems combined rose from 100 million zloty in 2023 to 26 billion zloty in 2026, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk announced in August, quoted by news website Interia. The summary report of this week’s Warsaw Security Forum suggested the use of counter-drone systems to create a “controlled fly-zone” over the Suwałki Gap, a strategically important choke point along the Polish-Lithuanian border that sits between the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and Russia’s ally Belarus. Poland has signed an agreement for a new anti-drone system that it claims will be the first of its kind in Europe. The network is intended to protect Poland’s eastern borders, where last year around 20 Russian drones crossed in an unprecedented incursion https://t.co/WhWhJxDwXA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 30, 2026 Poland has in recent years moved to strengthen its defence ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland. In 2024, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab. Saab this year also signed a strategic collaboration agreement with PGZ that will see them cooperate on naval production, servicing and technology. On Monday this week, Norway’s defence ministry announced that Poland will join an initiative recently launched by 11 European countries and Canada to cooperate more closely on security in the North Atlantic, Arctic and Baltic Sea. World.title: New Polish constitutional court judge takes oath in defiance of president
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The standoff between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president. Berek is now the fifth judge to take their oath without presidential approval. The previous four have been denied entry to the TK, and speculation is rife that the government may soon take action to ensure that the excluded judges are able to take up their positions. PILNE 🚨 dr Maciej Berek złożył w Sejmie ślubowanie na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego! pic.twitter.com/sZlzLnsL3M — Bogdan Zdrojewski (@BZdrojewski) October 14, 2026 Under Polish law, a new TK judge must swear an oath “before the president”. However, since Berek was elected to the TK by the government’s majority in parliament in early September, Nawrocki has refused to swear him in. The president claims that Berek has not presented evidence that he meets the statutory requirement of having practiced as a legal counsel for at least 10 years. Berek says he has done so. Nawrocki has also expressed his opposition to the fact that Berek has gone from serving in Tusk’s cabinet, where he was minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy, to becoming a TK judge. Even some members of Tusk’s ruling coalition opposed Berek’s candidacy, saying that it contradicted the government’s earlier pledges to “depoliticise” the judicial system, including by banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. With no invitation from Nawrocki forthcoming, on Wednesday morning Berek instead swore his oath at a ceremony organised in parliament. He declared that he was directing the oath towards the president, despite Nawrocki not being present. The development came a day after the Venice Commission, an advisory body to the Council of Europe on constitutional law, had issued an opinion effectively supporting the government’s position on the crisis around the TK. The commission found that the Polish president should swear in TK judges chosen by parliament “without delay” and does not have the power to review their election. It added that, if the president refuses to receive a judge’s oath, they are justified in taking it without him being present. The opinion was welcomed by Tusk and his government. However, Nawrocki’s spokesman, Rafał Leśkiewicz, pointed out that the Venice Commission’s opinions are advisory and not legally binding. 1294/2026 Poland – Opinion on the powers of the President in the context of the oath-taking of the judges of the Constitutional Tribunal and of other judicial appointments.https://t.co/vcpfNeteWo — Radoslaw Szewczyk (@SzewczykRadek) October 13, 2026 Earlier this year, four other TK judges chosen by parliament similarly organised their own swearing-in ceremony in parliament after Nawrocki failed to invite them to take their oaths before him. However, when they arrived at the TK to take up their positions, they were prevented from doing so by the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government (and had previously served as a minister in that government). Święczkowski argues that the judges cannot take up their positions unless they swear an oath in the presence of Nawrocki, who was elected as president last year with the support of PiS. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the four judges be accepted onto the TK. However, Święczkowski has so far refused to comply, arguing that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision. In a further escalation of the crisis around Poland's constitutional court, prosecutors have charged two officials for preventing new judges from taking up their positions. Meanwhile, the chief justice has launched proceedings against three other judges https://t.co/aeKKue37oN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026 Since replacing PiS in office in December 2023, Tusk’s government has refused to recognise the legitimacy of the TK, pointing to the fact that some of its judges were unlawfully appointed under PiS. It has ignored all rulings issued by the tribunal. Until this year, the ruling coalition refused to fill new vacancies that resulted from the expiration of judges’ nine-year terms or their retirement. However, that position changed in March, when it began filling the backlog. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its candidates in theory now have a majority on the 15-person court. However, Nawrocki has only sworn in three of those judges, with the other refused entry to the TK. Prime Minister @donaldtusk has succeeded in having Maciej Berek, whom he recently described as his “right-hand man”, elected by parliament as a constitutional court judge, staving off a rebellion from some members of his own coalition https://t.co/VAVbkGL8xS — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 4, 2026 Speculation has been rife that the government will take action to ensure that the excluded judges can gain access to the court, perhaps even using the police to force entry. Speaking to broadcaster Polsat today, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said that “the state must do everything to enable these judges to adjudicate”. He added that Berek’s swearing-in “brings us much closer to launching the tribunal’s work”. However, Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, told Polsat that today’s ceremony in parliament was “grotesque” and “a sad day for Polish democracy”. This morning has also seen some clashes between police and supporters of PiS and Nawrocki, who have been camped out outside the TK in order to defend it from any takeover by force. ❗️Policja szarpie posłów oraz zgromadzonych obywateli pod TK ❗️ pic.twitter.com/eGPRFQJnAX — Oskar Szafarowicz (@Szafarowicz2001) October 14, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Man charged with plotting attack on Polish PM
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A 66-year-old Polish man has been charged with planning an attack on Prime Minister Donald Tusk as part of an attempt to overthrow the government. A search of his home revealed improvised explosive devices that he allegedly planned to use in the plot. The suspect, who can be named only as Krzysztof N. under Polish privacy law, has also been charged with a number of other offences, including promoting a war of aggression in Ukraine and inciting hate crimes. Media reports have identified the man as a radical-right extremist. Do Prokuratury Okręgowej w Warszawie został doprowadzony 66-letni Krzysztof N., zatrzymany w związku z planowaniem zamachu na @donaldtusk i @KosiniakKamysz ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/rjcR3rNvyW — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 13, 2026 On Sunday, Poland’s security services announced that they had received what they described as “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Tusk and his defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. Later that day, a 66-year-old suspect was detained in the city of Wrocław, southwest Poland, and his property was searched. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński told broadcaster TVP that the man was “very active in groups promoting extreme views”. On Tuesday, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw, where Krzysztof N. has been transported, announced that he had been charged with nine offences. “The most serious charge is for planning to forcibly overthrow state authorities, including the prime minister and cabinet, using explosives,” said spokesman Piotr Antoni Skiba. That crime carries a potential prison sentence of up to 15 years. Skiba revealed that “a dozen or so” improvised explosive devices, which appeared to be similar to fragmentation grenades, had been found in the man’s home. There was also a crossbow, sharp-tipped metal bolts, and what are believed to be blank-firing or pneumatic guns. Skiba said that Krzysztof N.’s plans had been discovered after an anonymous person sent a message to the State Protection Service (SOP), which is responsible for the security of high-ranking officials, that included a recording of a conversation purportedly with the suspect. Krzysztof N. could be heard claiming that he had gathered “sevel hundred people” who shared his ideological beliefs and would help him overthrown the Polish government by force. At the moment, there is no indication that Krzysztof N. or the group around him were inspired in any way by foreign intelligence agencies, but the issue is still being investigated, added Skiba, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Poland’s security services say they have received “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz https://t.co/zl3vt6mah3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 11, 2026 Among the other charges Krzysztof N. has heard are “promoting a war of aggression, including in Ukraine, as well as incitement to commit crimes based on nationality, ethnicity, race and political views”, added Skiba. The suspect has so far pleaded not guilty on all counts. On Monday, Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading daily, reported that Krzysztof N. had for months been posting videos online calling on fellow right-wing extremists to fight against the authorities. He also expressed antisemitic and anti-Ukrainian sentiment. Another newspaper, Rzeczpospolita, found that he runs a Facebook page called Radical Polish Resistance Movement that has almost 8,000 followers and claims Poland’s two main political parties – Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) – are “in the hands of globalists and Judeo-communists”. "Patriota do przesady". Kim jest Krzysztof N., Wrocławianin podejrzewany przez służby o planowanie zamachu na premiera Tuska Mężczyzna, który miał planować zamach na premiera Donalda Tuska Od kilku miesięcy nagrywał w mediach społecznościowych filmiki i skrzykiwał prawicowych… — Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 12, 2026 In a separate case, government spokesman Adam Szłapka announced on Tuesday that a 46-year-old man in the town of Oborniki in western Poland had been detained on suspicion of publicly calling for the murder of Tusk and the speaker of parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty. A spokeswoman for the district prosecutor’s office in Oborniki told PAP that the man had been charged with inciting murder, for which he could face up to three years in prison. “He admitted to publishing content insulting various government officials, but denied the charge of inciting their murder,” she revealed. “He expressed regret and remorse.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland and Norway sign declaration on deepening security ties
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland and Norway have signed a declaration on deepening security cooperation, including joint defence production, strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks, and continuing to support Ukraine. “In a world where the international order, laws and principles are being violated by the world’s biggest players, Poland and Norway show how partnership can be built on shared values and interests,” said Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, alongside his Norwegian counterpart, Jonas Gahr Støre. 🇵🇱🤝🇳🇴 Strategiczne partnerstwo Polski i Królestwa Norwegii oficjalnie przypieczętowane. ✍️ Podpisano deklarację o strategicznym partnerstwie między obu państwami, stanowiącą efekt wieloletniej współpracy oraz wspólnoty interesów biznesowych, geopolitycznych i moralnych. 🛡️ W… pic.twitter.com/vBrWrdC8oT — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 12, 2026 The two leaders signed a declaration on strategic partnership during a visit by a Norwegian delegation to the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year’s partner country. The agreement sets out a framework for closer long-term cooperation between the two countries. Among the commitments made by the two countries are “deeper operational cooperation” and expanding joint procurement and production between their respective defence industries. Warsaw and Oslo also pledged to work together on strengthening NATO’s eastern and northern flanks, as well as to coordinate responses to cyberattacks, hybrid operations and foreign information manipulation. “The point is that Europe should take on greater responsibility for security,” said Støre. “We must invest in it more coherently and consistently, so as to avoid duplication, but invest in such a way that regional defence systems are stronger.” The declaration also promises continued support for Ukraine in its defence against Russia, as well as efforts to ensure a just and lasting peace and to “hold Russia accountable for its war of aggression”. Although security issues dominate the declaration, the two countries also pledged to deepen economic ties, including in the energy and maritime sectors. Robin Allers, a scholar at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the move to sign the declaration with Poland was part of a broader Norwegian strategy to deepen mutual commitments with key NATO partners amid uncertainty over US engagement in Europe. “Today’s agreement demonstrates your country’s increasingly important role in Europe,” said Allers, pointing to Poland’s growing economic and military strength, as well as its role in supporting Ukraine. Poland has unveiled its first frigate to enter service in decades at a ceremony in the Baltic port of Gdynia, where the ship was constructed. It will be followed by two more new frigates as part of a €3.5bn programme to modernise the ageing Polish fleet https://t.co/093Fx2WSM7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Poland has in recent years also moved to strengthen its ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. This year, Polish and Norwegian companies announced plans to develop a new anti-drone system for Poland in the wake of incursions of Russian drones into Polish airspace. Last year, Norway opened a facility in Poland, Camp Jomsborg, for training Ukrainian military personnel. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland. The two countries also have close energy ties. In 2022, the Baltic Pipe began delivering Norwegian gas to Poland, helping the country reduce its reliance on Russian supplies. Norway’s Equinor is also involved in developing one of Poland’s first offshore wind farms in the Baltic. Poland will manufacture the missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is buying from South Korea. The Norwegian government says that Polish production "will strengthen security of supply for Norway and other European customers of the system" https://t.co/NIJj7owK45 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 29, 2026 Poland has also moved closer in recent years to Sweden, with which it signed a strategic partnership in 2024. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab. Last year, at Poland’s suggestion, NATO launched a new military mission to protect critical infrastructure in the Baltic Sea. On Monday this week, Norway’s defence ministry announced that Poland will join an initiative recently launched by 11 European countries and Canada to cooperate more closely on security in the North Atlantic, Arctic and Baltic Sea. World.title: Germany detains Turks suspected of sabotaging Starlink station in Poland on behalf of Russia
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Two Turkish men suspected of carrying out last month’s arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink have been detained in Germany. The Polish authorities say that the sabotage was carried out on behalf of Russia. On Monday evening, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk first announced that the pair had been taken into custody “at the request of the Polish security services”. He said that the Turkish men’s actions had been “a further act of hybrid warfare” – the term used for sabotage and other hostile activity carried out in Europe by Russia – and that “the perpetrators will answer before the Polish justice system”. Na zlecenie polskich służb niemiecka policja zatrzymała dwóch obywateli tureckich podejrzanych o podpalenie stacji Starlink na Mazowszu. To kolejny akt wojny hybrydowej. Sprawcy sabotażu odpowiedzą przed polskim wymiarem sprawiedliwości. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026 Shortly afterwards, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński revealed that the arrests had taken place in cooperation between Poland’s police and Internal Security Agency (ABW) and Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA). He said that the charge the suspects are likely to face in Poland would be “sabotage on behalf of a foreign intelligence service”, a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of 10 years, ranging up to life. Later on Monday, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, confirmed that Poland believes the attack was carried out “on behalf of the Russian security services”. The incident in question took place on 23 September at a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company. The facility is used to provide internet services across the region, including in Ukraine, which has relied heavily on Starlink connections since Russia’s full-scale invasion. Firefighters were called out that evening to a fire at the facility, which is owned by Polish state telecommunications operator Exatel. The next day, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gakowski revealed that the blaze had been started deliberately and “the modus operandi is clearly Russian”. Poland has been one of the primary targets for Russian sabotage operations in Europe. Those have included a series of arson attacks, including one that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre and another at a drone factory that is used to supply the Ukrainian military. A fire last night at a Starlink ground station in Poland that is used to provide internet services to Ukraine was caused deliberately and "the modus operandi is clearly Russian", says digital affairs minister @KGawkowski https://t.co/p2DEn7XexF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026 On Monday evening, at a press conference alongside Kierwiński and Siemoniak, the commander of Poland’s police, Marek Boroń, revealed that one of the two Turkish suspects had resident status in Germany while the other did not. He said that the Polish authorities had been able to document their movements in Poland, and had recordings, fingerprints and DNA of the suspects. Simoniak added that there was a “high probability” that other individuals were involved in the attack, but that he could not divulge further information about them currently. He also thanked the German authorities for their cooperation. “We have no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage,” said the minister, quoted by the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “And it’s worth adding that Russian intelligence services are increasingly using people connected to the criminal world. They never use their own citizens.” Russia uses individuals already present in Europe – and often already involved in criminal activity – to carry out most of its hybrid operations. On Monday, in a separate case, three Ukrainians and one Belarusian went on trial in Warsaw accused of being behind a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania. Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 On Tuesday morning, German newspaper Handelsblatt reported confirmation from the State Criminal Police Office (LKA) in Baden-Württemberg that two Turkish men had been detained on Monday in the town of Nürtingen at the request of the Polish authorities. The office did not provide further details, but Handelsblatt reports that the two suspects are due to be brought before a judge today. World.title: Four go on trial in Warsaw over arson attacks carried out on Russian orders
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Four men have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. The accused – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – can be named only as Oleksandr H., Stepan K., Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. under Polish privacy law and their trial is taking place behind closed doors for security reasons. Polish prosecutors say that they were part of an organised group tasked with “committing acts of sabotage and terrorism” on behalf of Russia’s foreign intelligence service in April and May 2024. Those included a fire that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, Marywilska 44; another at a store in Warsaw belonging to home improvement chain OBI; and a third at an IKEA store in Vilnius. They also allegedly planned an arson attack on an IKEA store in the Latvian capital of Riga. W Sądzie Okręgowym Warszawa-Praga ruszył proces grupy przestępczej, która miała na zlecenie Federacji Rosyjskiej podpalać markety wielkopowierzchniowe, w tym centrum handlowe przy Marywilskiej w Warszawie.https://t.co/0CFl1RyJvq — TVN Warszawa (@tvnwarszawa) October 12, 2026 According to an indictment issued against the men in March this year, Stepan K., the Belarusian, set fire to the OBI store. Oleksandr H. is accused of involvement in the arson attack on the IKEA store in Vilnius and preparations for further attacks. The pair have been indicted under Poland’s espionage law for carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism on behalf of foreign intelligence. That crime carries a minimum sentence of 10 years in prison, ranging up to life. Another Ukrainian suspect, Daniil B., had also been due to stand trial today on the same charge, with prosecutors finding that he had received an order from a handler in Russia to go to Marywilska on the night the arson attack took place and record footage of the fire and the response of the emergency services. However, Daniil B. was jailed in Lithuania last year for his role in the Vilnius IKEA fire and Poland has not yet managed to secure his extradition for the trial in Warsaw, meaning that it went ahead without his involvement. Polish prosecutors say they have determined that the Marywilska fire was also carried out on the orders of Russian intelligence, but have not been able to identify which individuals actually perpetrated the attack. Stepan K. and Oleksandr H. – as well as Vitalii K., whom prosecutors accuse of helping carry out the arson in Vilnius – are additionally charged with participating in an organised criminal group that aimed to carry out terrorist offences, a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison. Both Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. were also indicted in relation to an assault in the village of Wólka Kosowska, just outside Warsaw. Pavlo T. was already convicted in Poland last year along with two other Ukrainian men, Serhii R. and Vladyslav Y., over their role in the same criminal group tasked with carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism by Russia. They were handed jail terms ranging from 16 months to five and a half years. Two other alleged members of the group, Serhii Chalyi and Oleksandr Varyvoda, who prosecutors say were involved in coordinating sabotage activities, remain wanted. Three Ukrainians have been jailed in Poland for their role in a group tasked with carrying out sabotage and terrorism. That included the fire that destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, which Polish prosecutors say was carried out on Russia’s orders https://t.co/xuFx5T4HH9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 24, 2025 In response to evidence that Moscow was behind the Marywilska fire, Poland last year ordered Russia’s consulate in Kraków to close. It has since closed all Russian consulates due to Moscow’s ongoing campaign of sabotage, with Russia responding by shutting down all Polish consulates on its territory. A report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published earlier this year found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russian sabotage in Europe. Most recently, Poland has accused Moscow of being behind a fire at a drone factory that supplies the Polish and Ukrainian militaries. Last year, Ukrainian operatives working on behalf of Russia also used explosives in an attempt to derail a train in Poland. Most acts of sabotage ordered by Russia in Poland have been carried out not by Russians themselves, but by Ukrainians and Belarusians, large numbers of whom already live in Poland and other countries in the region. World.title: Israeli producer had access to data harvested by Poland using Pegasus spyware, say prosecutors
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Data harvested from mobile phones by the Polish authorities using Pegasus spyware were transmitted outside Poland and were accessible to the tool’s Israeli producer, Polish prosecutors have revealed as part of an investigation into the use of Pegasus under the former government. Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that the case is “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history since the fall of communism”, and that it is “beyond any doubt” that the Israeli firm behind Pegasus, NSO Group, cooperates with Israeli intelligence. Tego o Pegasusie jeszcze nie słyszeliście. pic.twitter.com/etvhTE9EWa — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026 Pegasus is a powerful and controversial tool that allows the extraction of large amounts of data from mobile phones without users’ knowledge. A number of countries have been found to have used it to spy on opposition figures. In 2017, Poland, under the government of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, purchased Pegasus from NSO. The spyware was subsequently used against hundreds of targets, including a number of PiS’s political opponents. Among them was the head of the 2019 election campaign of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party (which was then known as Civic Platform, PO). Last year, Tusk revealed that his own wife and daughter had been among those caught up in the surveillance. PiS, however, has insisted that Pegasus was a necessary tool to fight crime and ensure national security. It says the spyware was only used with court approval against targets legitimately suspected of wrongdoing. After a coalition led by Tusk took power from PiS in December 2023, it launched investigations into the use of Pegasus under the former government. Today, the National Prosecutor’s Office released its latest findings, based on analysis by experts at the forensic research office of Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW). The experts confirmed that Pegasus allowed the harvesting of emails, instant messaging and text messages; the content of telephone conversations, both via mobile networks and internet calls; browsing histories, calendars and contact lists; photos, videos and other files; and location data. “Additionally, Pegasus allowed the use of the device’s built-in microphone and cameras to record audio and video in real time and take screenshots,” reports the National Prosecutor’s Office. Czy to możliwe, że państwo traci kontrolę nad własnym systemem inwigilacji? I to nie była stara konsola… Z opinii biegłych ABW wynika, że CBA kupiło narzędzie, nad którym nie miało pełnej kontroli. Dane opuszczały Polskę, moduł infekujący kontrolował producent, a zagraniczna… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) October 12, 2026 The ABW experts also highlighted serious concerns over management and security of the harvested data, noting that Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA), which was responsible for using the spyware, “did not have full control over the Pegasus system”. “The CBA did not have passwords to access some accounts with administrative privileges and some system components remained under the control of the manufacturer [NSO],” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The server module responsible for infecting mobile devices remained under the manufacturer’s exclusive control.” Data transmitted through the Pegasus system travelled outside Polish territory, through “servers located in various parts of the world”, in a network managed by NSO and “beyond the CBA’s control”, found the experts. Meanwhile, NSO “had technical access to materials from operational surveillance”, although prosecutors say that the experts “did not determine whether the manufacturer actually obtained access to materials from specific operations”. The former deputy head of Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau has been charged with unlawfully sharing material obtained through surveillance using Pegasus spyware, including communication involving PM @donaldtusk's daughter when Tusk was in opposition https://t.co/LyTuqbq0KQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2025 In a video commenting on the latest findings, Tusk said that the investigation into Pegasus was “coming to a head”. He called it “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history after the fall of communism”. The former PIS authorities signed a contract for a spyware system “over which they de facto had no control, because control remained in the hands of Israel and an Israeli company…whose cooperation with Israeli intelligence is, of course, beyond doubt”, said the prime minister. “They paid money for a system that de facto transferred all possible data on Polish citizens, Polish opposition leaders and Polish independent prosecutors…to the Israeli side,” he added. “This is no longer [just] a scandal…We’re talking about a crime against the state.” Two former heads of Polish security agencies have been charged over the use of Pegasus spyware under the former PiS government. The pair, who deny wrongdoing, could be jailed for up to three years if found guilty of unlawfully allowing use of the spyware https://t.co/TWjQR74IYT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 26, 2026 Later on Monday, a separate parliamentary committee set up by the ruling coalition to investigate the use of Pegasus also revealed unclassified sections of a report on its findings. In addition to the information released by prosecutors, the commission also said that the CBA had never obtained the required IT security accreditation for Pegasus, meaning that it was used without meeting requirements for protecting classified information. The commission’s chairwoman, Magdalena Sroka, also said that courts granting authorisation for the use of Pegasus were not informed of its full capabilities, such as the ability to access the entire contents of phones, reports broadcaster RMF. 💬 Jest to dokument o tym, jak władza publiczna w Polsce sięgnęła po narzędzie ingerujące w prawa obywatelskie – powiedziała przewodnicząca komisji śledczej ds. inwigilacji systemem Pegasus @MagdalenaSroka, prezentując raport z prac komisji.https://t.co/MzA9gj4M0Y — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) October 12, 2026 Legal proceedings are already underway against a number of former officials in relation to Pegasus. In February, prosecutors charged the former heads of the AWB and Military Counterintelligence Service (SKW) with abuse of power for approving the use of Pegasus despite being aware of legal shortcomings. Previously, the former head of the CBA was charged with the same offence, while one of his deputies was charged with unlawfully disclosing material from surveillance of Roman Giertych, an MP from Tusk’s KO party who has also worked as a lawyer for Tusk and his family. Last year, a former deputy justice minister from the PiS government, Michał Woś, was indicted to stand trial over his role in the alleged illegal use of justice ministry funds to help the CBA purchase Pegasus.
