World.title: Aussie cyclists begin World Championships with silver medal
World.content:
Australia has claimed a silver medal in the men's team sprint on the opening night of the UCI Track Cycling World Championships in Shanghai.

The Australian trio of Leigh Hoffman, Ryan Elliott and Danny Barber finished runner-up to the Netherlands in the final.

It was Australia's fifth consecutive World Championships medal in the event.

"For the final, we made a minor change in strategy," Hoffman said.

Richardson withdrawn from world champ squad British track cyclist Matthew Richardson, who defected from Australian cycling at the end of the Paris Games, has been withdrawn from this week's UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai.

"We just tried to have a little gamble, and it almost paid off.

"We were up to the 500-metre mark, so we definitely gave the Dutch a run for their money.

"It's definitely bittersweet to miss out on the [winner's] rainbow bands, but considering last year was a bronze and this year we have silver, I think this team is on the way up."

Australia won a first-round duel against a British team missing Matt Richardson.

He was withdrawn from the British squad earlier in the week over alleged misconduct.

Richardson won three Olympic medals for Australia before switching allegiance to Great Britain after the 2024 Paris Games.

In other results in Shanghai, Australia's Kristina Clonan, Molly McGill and Alessia McCaig finished seventh in the women's team sprint.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Top gymnastics coach fined after assaulting two female teen athletes
World.content:
A gymnastics coach with more than 30 years' experience has avoided conviction and instead been ordered to pay a fine after assaulting two teenage female athletes.

Over the length of his career, Jamie Glen Cannon, 49, has trained athletes at clubs on the Sunshine Coast, in Cairns, and at Brisbane Grammar School.

Mr Cannon was sentenced in Maroochydore District Court last week, after pleading guilty to four charges of common assault against the two teen gymnasts, each aged between 13 and 16.

Jamie Cannon has coached athletes at clubs on the Sunshine Coast, Cairns and at Brisbane Grammar School over his 30-year career. (ABC News: Alex Papp)

Coach touched athletes

Crown prosecutor Alex Stark described Cannon's behaviour as "a breach of trust, both professional and personal" and tendered an agreed statement of facts about the offending.

The court heard Cannon was a senior coach at a Sunshine Coast club when the incidents occurred in 2022 and 2023.

The two girls were under his supervision as athletes.

One of the assault charges related to Cannon smacking the bottom of a 13-year-old as she performed handstands with other gymnasts at the club.

One athlete's victim impact statement said the offending led to her "quitting gymnastics entirely". (Pexels: Ivan Samkov / CC licence)

Three more offences occurred at the same club, involving Cannon touching and rubbing the inner thigh of a second athlete, aged 15 at the time.

The court heard that in one interaction, Cannon asked the teenager if she wore make-up, told her she was pretty, then put his hand on her inner thigh.

In another, he asked if he could touch the teenager's leggings, and before she could respond, he put his hand on her knee.

The fourth charge involved Cannon approaching the 15-year-old as she prepared to coach a class, standing in between her legs before placing his hands on her knees and rubbing her thighs as she attempted to move away.

The court heard it was accepted that Cannon's behaviour had "no sexual intent".

Gymnast left the sport she loved

The 15-year-old athlete's victim impact statement was read to the court at his sentencing by Mr Stark.

The teenager wrote that the offending led to her "quitting gymnastics entirely".

She described problems falling asleep and how it damaged "many friendships", particularly at the gymnastics club.

"[It] affected the development of a romantic relationship with partners due to fear and sensitivity to certain actions and situations," Mr Stark read to the court.

Mr Stark said there was a "vulnerability" in the situation because the teenagers were under his supervision.

He said both teenagers had been clear about their boundaries to Cannon, including the request not to be touched.

"It was really that sense of breach of trust that was at the heart of the impact for both of them," he said.

Cannon declined to be interviewed by police.

The court heard he has not been involved with the sport since being charged.

Decades as a top coach

Cannon's lawyer Ambyr Cousen described how her client had been involved with the sport for 30 years both as an employee and as a volunteer, including as a committee member with Gymnastics Queensland (GQ).

"He has won a number of awards for peer service within that industry," Ms Cousen told the court.

Cannon was working with Brisbane Grammar School as a senior coach in 2019 when he received GQ's Individual Service Award for his service to gymnastics in Queensland.

He also spent more than a decade leading GQ's Men's Artistic Gymnastics Sport Committee.

Ms Cousen also supplied the court with several character references for her client.

Court accepts 'no sexual intent'

Cannon provided a written apology to the court for his actions, and offered to pay $1,000 to each of the victims as compensation.

Jamie Cannon was sentenced on four counts of common assault in the Maroochydore District Court last week. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques)

In sentencing, Judge Amanda McDonnell told Cannon he treated "these young, vulnerable girls in a way that they didn't wish to be touched".

"I have no doubt that they looked up to you for guidance," Judge McDonnell said.

" I accept that there was no sexual intent, but that you acted in an overly-familiar way. "

Cannon was ordered to pay a single fine of $2,500 for the four offences, plus the promised compensation.

No conviction was recorded.

World.title: Live: Labor scraps controversial ministerial discretion in digital duty of care bill
World.content:
Anika Wells says the government's digital duty of care bill will place the onus of responsibility on big tech companies.

Labor will be introducing its digital duty of care bill to parliament today. It will require big tech companies to mitigate and protect under 18 users from harmful content on their platforms.

The government's legislation will also give social media users the ability to opt out of the social media algorithm.

But Labor has dropped controversial ministerial powers in the legislation which would have given the minister the power to designate harms.

Asked on ABC News Breakfast if she's worried health information could be caught up in the law, the communications minister says the bill isn't targeting that.

World.title: Some older Australians embrace downsizing and apartment living despite costs
World.content:
An inner-city apartment and a lack of mowing suits 72-year-old John Turner down to the ground, especially after two knee operations.

He and his wife, Kathryn, moved eight years ago when they retired, downsizing from the family home on an 850 square metre block they had lived in for four decades and raised their children in.

Other older Australians have told the ABC that the costs of downsizing, including stamp duty, are a barrier to making the move.

But the Turners love their two-bedroom apartment for its proximity to everything from public transport to markets to the cinema, as well as a hospital.

John Turner says being close to a hospital, medical facilities and transport was a priority. (ABC News: Liz Pickering)

There is less maintenance and when they travel, they have more peace of mind about security.

Just across Brisbane, downsizer Bryan Worn agrees wholeheartedly with the Turners' experience.

Bryan Worn downsized from a large home to an apartment a year ago. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

The 78-year-old moved from his large home to a two-bedroom apartment last year, motivated by concerns about his ability to manage the maintenance his old Queenslander required.

"I'd been living on my own in a large house for five years … and my kids were getting a little bit antsy about me being on my own in a house," he said.

Mr Worn does not miss the work the home required, including after storms when he was often left with a mess to clean up.

Having previously lived in an apartment and worked in finance, Mr Worn said he was aware of the extra costs he would have to factor in for things like strata.

But he believes more information about future apartment-living costs, such as whether future building work would need to be funded, could encourage others to make a similar move.

The Turners wished they had known how much development would pop up around them before they moved in. (ABC News: Liz Pickering)

Costs and changes worth it

Like in Mr Worn's case, the additional costs of living in an apartment, and move-related costs like stamp duty, were not ultimately a barrier for the Turners.

What shocked them was how much their strata fees increased over the years, and how much development, including much taller buildings, sprung up around them.

And while they love the lifestyle their home offers, they confess to making the long drive south of Brisbane for their old doctor and Ms Turner's hairdresser.

Housing advocates believe emotional connections to a home and place can be a major barrier to older Australians moving.

Curtin University's Steven Rowley said most older Australians ultimately chose to stay in place and in their homes for as long as possible.

Professor Steven Rowley is Director of the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute’s Curtin Research Centre. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"There are those emotional ties to a dwelling, and also just a lack of housing choice," he said.

"You just don't have the options available to really allow a quality downsizing move for a lot of people who want to downsize in their local community."

Professor Rowley, director of the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute's Curtin Research Centre, said the country lacked a supply of larger apartments, such as three-bedrooms, which downsizers often find more attractive.

Edgar Liu is a housing policy expert at the UNSW City Futures Research Centre. (Supplied: UNSW)

Edgar Liu, at UNSW's City Futures Research Centre, agreed the research he had conducted showed many older Australians wanted something bigger than a one or two-bedroom apartment.

"Once you retire, you tend to spend more time at home, " he said.

"There are also considerations in terms of family staying or coming back to live."

He suggested greater government intervention or oversight in terms of mandating a particular mix of different sized units or apartments could help facilitate that kind of development.

Professor Rowley was concerned the housing industry couldn't deliver affordable, larger apartments given construction costs.

"There really doesn't seem to be a tremendous solution to that at the moment," he said.

"You need a real rebalancing of prices and costs."

World.title: Universities justified job cuts with numbers no one could check
World.content:
Adam Lucas spent decades marking students down for conclusions they could not support.

But when the University of Wollongong told him his job was no longer viable it would not show him the financial model it used to reach that decision.

"We saw the outputs, but we never saw the model, and we were never given the chance to test whether the numbers actually added up," he said.

A spokesperson for UOW said staff were informed of the criteria and data sources used, but detailed data was withheld to protect personal privacy.

"We would fail [management] for providing this kind of material," Dr Lucas said.

" If [they were] our students there's no way that they would pass any of this stuff. "

After unsuccessfully challenging the figures, Dr Lucas accepted a voluntary redundancy.

Former University of Wollongong professor Adam Lucas said being made redundant was a degrading experience. (ABC Illawarra: Tim Fernandez)

"It soon became clear to me that it didn't make any difference what I said. So at that point I figured, okay, the number's up," he said.

" It was demeaning, it was degrading going through this process. "

Dr Lucas is one of hundreds of academics who have lost their jobs in restructures across Australian universities over the past two years.

Universities have said the cuts were unavoidable, citing falling international student numbers and changes to federal policy.

But an NSW parliamentary inquiry into university governance has questioned that rationale.

It found UOW and five other universities appeared to overstate their financial problems and went too far in restructures and staff cuts.

The finding also covered the University of Technology Sydney (UTS), Macquarie University, the University of Newcastle (UON), Charles Sturt University (CSU) and Western Sydney University (WSU).

Dr Lucas said the findings reflected his experience, but did not go far enough.

"They confirmed what many of us had been saying for months," he said.

" The crisis was manufactured and not just at Wollongong, and that the restructure was designed at Wollongong to produce a predetermined outcome. "

The inquiry did not make that finding.

A spokesperson for UOW rejected the claim its financial crisis was "manufactured", saying it faced a projected $35 million revenue shortfall in 2024 because of falling international enrolments and rising costs.

It also denied the framework produced predetermined outcomes, saying only four of the 25 disciplines initially assessed as unviable were ultimately discontinued following consultation.

The university said the changes delivered $22 million in recurrent savings.

'Faux crisis narratives'

The inquiry accepted universities were operating in a difficult environment, but questioned the accuracy of the financial information used to justify restructures.

It found the way some universities calculated their finances painted a worse picture than their official audited accounts.

The committee found some forecasts used to justify cuts were later significantly revised.

In at least one case the university's own modelling showed job cuts were not the only option.

At Macquarie University, internal modelling obtained by the National Tertiary Education Union included a "no workplace change" scenario that the union said could have achieved the university's $55 million savings target.

Management instead selected the full-redundancy scenario, accompanied by the words: "Why not go all the way?"

Macquarie said the no-cuts scenario was hypothetical and did not represent a formal plan or decision.

The NSW parliamentary inquiry was critical of the role of consultants found to have benefited from the crisis at universities. (Four Corners: Nick Wiggins)

Inquiry chair and Labor MLC Sarah Kaine has described some of the financial cases as "faux crisis narratives".

Speaking on a recent Australia Institute webinar she said university councils had displayed a "lack of genuine inquisitiveness" and sometimes failed to adequately challenge the information presented by senior management.

Dr Kaine was also critical of the role played by consultants, describing them as "at best complicit in the crisis" and "at worst architects of it", while benefiting financially from reform programs.

NTEU NSW secretary Vince Caughley said the findings vindicated union members who had challenged the cuts and pushed for the inquiry.

"People lost jobs, courses and careers while university managements repeatedly failed to make a defensible case for the damage they were inflicting," he said.

"These aren't accounting quirks or transparency problems.

" They're evidence of a governance crisis across institutions entrusted with billions of dollars and an enormous public responsibility. "

What were the findings?

University of Wollongong Read more Read more What happened? UOW used a Discipline Viability Assessment Framework to classify academic disciplines as "viable", "marginal" or "unviable". It cut the equivalent of 92 full-time academic jobs and 100 professional and support staff jobs. What the inquiry found: UOW appeared to overstate its financial problems and go too far in its cuts. What the university says: UOW rejects the findings and the claim that its financial crisis was "manufactured", citing a $35 million projected revenue shortfall in 2024. It says consultation reduced the number of disciplines to be discontinued from 25 to four, and the changes delivered $22 million in recurrent savings. UOW has not committed to publishing the complete model and says detailed data was withheld to protect personal privacy. Macquarie University Read more Read more What happened? Macquarie University cut 61 full-time teaching positions in its arts, science and engineering faculties. That included 45 voluntary redundancies, nine forced redundancies and seven pre-retirement contracts. What the inquiry found: Internal modelling included a no-cuts scenario which, according to the NTEU evidence, could have achieved the university's $55 million savings target. Management instead selected a full-redundancy option accompanied by the words: "Why not go all the way?" The committee found Macquarie appeared to overstate its financial problems and overreach in its cuts. What the university says: It rejects the findings, saying the no-cuts scenario was hypothetical and the cuts fixed a mismatch between staff, teaching and research needs. University of Technology Sydney Read more Read more What happened? UTS pursued a $100 million savings target and proposed cutting about 134 full-time-equivalent academic positions. It scaled back, moving primarily to voluntary separations with no clear final figure on the number of job losses. What the inquiry found: Six UTS academics developed an alternative financial plan to avoid the proposed cuts. Inquiry chair Sarah Kaine said councillors were shown the analysis but declined to reconsider their decision. The committee found UTS appeared to overstate its financial problems and overreach in its restructure. What the university says: UTS said it trusted its finance team's modelling and declined to have the competing plans independently assessed. It said the disagreement reflected different risk appetites and strategic judgements, and that consultation led to changes to its proposal. University of Newcastle Read more Read more What happened? The University of Newcastle says its Business Improvement Program saved more than $28 million and resulted in a net reduction of fewer than seven ongoing permanent full-time-equivalent positions. What the inquiry found: Newcastle used its own measure of its finances, leaving out investment returns and some other income. It acknowledged this was "not prescribed by Australian Accounting Standards". It painted a very different picture from its audited accounts. What the university says: Vice-Chancellor Alex Zelinsky rejected the suggestion Newcastle maintained "two sets of books". He said the core result reflected the income and costs associated with teaching and research. Western Sydney University Read more Read more What happened? Western Sydney University's projected 2026 deficit increased from $6.5 million to $79 million. Vice-Chancellor George Williams said the university had "no choice" but to cut between 300 and 400 positions. Ultimately, WSU said 187 of the employees covered chose voluntary redundancy with no forced redundancies. What the inquiry found: The committee remained unconvinced by the original financial rationale and described the "no choice" statement as ill-judged. However, it praised how WSU partnered with unions and contrasted it with more combative restructures at UTS, UOW, UON and CSU. What the university says: WSU says its financial pressures were documented in audited accounts. It said staff suggestions helped generate $23 million in non-salary savings, while one in four executive and senior positions were removed. A review of the restructure is underway. Charles Sturt University Read more Read more What happened? Charles Sturt University is seeking $35 million in savings, efficiencies or additional income by the end of 2027. It said about $7.5 million had already been saved through salary and operational measures, but has not provided a final job loss figure. What the inquiry found: CSU said its 2025 deficit was $30.4 million, more than twice the $12.4 million in its audited accounts after it removed one-off income and accounting adjustments. The committee remained unconvinced by the financial assumptions underpinning CSU's reforms. What the university says: A CSU spokesperson said, "We don't agree with their conclusion. The case for our change program is clear." It points to deficits since 2022 and a fall in international students from 8,500 in 2019 to 1,620 in 2025.

The use of consultants at UOW has also come under scrutiny from the state's corruption watchdog.

ICAC's Operation Scandi examined allegations involving recruitment, procurement, consultant contracts and the management of conflicts of interest.

Public hearings scrutinised UOW's $3.8 million contract with KordaMentha, including the tender process and former interim vice-chancellor John Dewar's relationship with the firm.

ICAC has not yet handed down its findings.

Students, staff and community 'paying the price'

Dr Lucas, a researcher in the history of technology, ran UOW's science and technology studies and environmental humanities programs.

He designed and taught their core subjects and supervised research students.

He said the viability model used to justify which disciplines would be cut relied on a single year of data, 2024, when he was on long-service leave.

By his own calculations his area fell about 1 per cent short.

The role of consultants at the University of Wollongong has been the subject of an ICAC inquiry. (Four Corners: Mark Hiney)

It also treated academics as if they spent all their time teaching, when most were contracted to teach 40 per cent of the time.

UOW said teaching was its primary source of revenue while it subsidised research and other university activities, and it could no longer justify existing staffing levels in some teaching areas.

Dr Lucas said his subjects were eventually discontinued, forcing some students to find alternatives or change their study plans.

"They'd entered uni, they'd paid for a degree that they could no longer complete," he said.

" One student told me that she'd enrolled in environmental humanities because she wanted to work in climate policy. Now the core subjects that she needed aren't being offered. "

Dr Lucas said the restructure had also increased pressure on those who remained.

"They're doing more with less, covering subjects they didn't design, supervising students they didn't recruit, watching their colleagues disappear," he said.

"The people paying the price are current and former students, staff and the Illawarra community."

UOW disputed Dr Lucas's account, saying the assessment considered three years of data and was not affected by his long-service leave.

It said science and technology studies was found to be unviable across all three measures, rather than narrowly missing a single threshold.

The university said 140 students were significantly affected.

It said the majority were able to adjust their study plans and remained at UOW, although some transferred elsewhere.

Calls for transparency

The committee recommended banning universities from publicly using their own adjusted figures to justify restructures when they differ from their audited financial statements.

Where universities do use adjusted figures, they would need to disclose material differences from their audited results.

The NTEU wants all six universities to publish the models, assumptions, consultancy reports and council papers used to justify their restructures.

"If your financial case is strong enough to dismantle part of a university it should be strong enough to survive daylight," Mr Caughley said.

Dr Lucas wants UOW's model independently audited by the NSW auditor-general, and the decisions to cut disciplines reopened.

"That doesn't necessarily mean reinstating every position, but it does mean reopening the process," he said.

"If the model can't withstand scrutiny it shouldn't have been used to eliminate academic positions."

" The inquiry was right, but the damage is already done. "

World.title: Schutt stars as Aussies sweep Bangladesh in ODI series
World.content:
Australia has coasted to an eight-wicket ODI win over Bangladesh to secure a clean sweep of the three-match series.

Ellyse Perry (65 not out off 64 deliveries) and Annabel Sutherland (74 not out off 52) added 137 for the third wicket, guiding Australia past Bangladesh's total of 172 all out inside 23 overs.

Australia lost openers Georgia Voll (11) and Beth Mooney (21) early in the run chase at Allan Border Field.

Mooney, in her 100th ODI match, was cleaned up by Bangladesh debutant quick Disha Biswas.

Mooney wants to go well beyond 100 ODIs Beth Mooney is still smarting over Australia's World Cup loss to India last year, and as the star prepares for her 100th ODI against Bangladesh, she still has her eyes set on a couple of long-term goals.

From that moment, it was plain sailing for the hosts as Perry and Sutherland went through the gears.

Earlier, fast bowler Megan Schutt, who was named player of the match and the series, produced another masterclass.

Schutt bowled an incredible 10 overs straight to snare 4-16 and restrict Bangladesh after it was asked to bat first in the third and final ODI.

She bowled 53 dot balls in her spell and took her series haul to 10 wickets at a miserly average of 7.1.

Schutt now has 28 wickets in 14 ODIs at Allan Border Field, the most of any bowler in history.

Australian opener Phoebe Litchfield was ruled out of the match with a low-grade hip strain.

The star batter was replaced by all-rounder Nicola Carey.

World.title: Sally Rooney pulls books from UK over her support for Palestine Action
World.content:
Books by Sally Rooney will no longer be sold in the UK because of the Irish novelist's support for Palestine Action, an organisation that has been banned in the country.

The move was confirmed by both Rooney and her publisher, Faber, and means titles such as Normal People, Conversations with Friends and Intermezzo will disappear from UK bookshops.

She has also cancelled an upcoming trip to the UK over fears she could be arrested.

Rooney has previously expressed support for the group, which the UK government banned as a "terrorist" organisation in July 2025. It is not banned in Ireland, where Rooney lives.

The proscription, which the organisation is appealing, puts Palestine Action on the same blacklist as militant groups Hamas and Hezbollah, making it illegal in the UK to be part of, support or finance it.

"Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work," Faber said in a statement.

"To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.

Loading...

"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format."

The bestselling author of Normal People and Intermezzo previously said she would donate earnings to Palestine Action and told the High Court in London that the proscription would affect freedom of expression.

"As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence," Rooney said in a statement shared with AFP.

"After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK."

Britain's Supreme Court is set to hear an appeal against the ban from the group's co-founder, Huda Ammori, next month.

Thousands have protested the ban and been detained in the process, while rights groups and some public figures have condemned it as criminalising dissent.

Palestine Action's stated goal on its website is to end "global participation in Israel's genocidal and apartheid regime".

Its proscription came after a series of high-profile stunts protesting the war in Gaza, including targeting weapons factories, especially those belonging to Israeli arms group Elbit.

AFP

World.title: Flinders University admits to $965k underpayment of casual staff
World.content:
Flinders University has apologised for underpaying more than 1,400 casual staff over several years, in a case the higher education union has labelled a "massive breach of trust".

The underpayments were worth $965,827 and impacted 1,405 current and former staff, the university said, equating to roughly $687 underpaid per person.

The issue occurred between 2020 and 2025, the university said.

In an all-staff email on Friday afternoon, Flinders University vice-chancellor Professor Colin Stirling said the issue was identified by a university review into payment practices for casual employees.

He said the university was now contacting affected staff, who would be repaid with superannuation and "applicable interest".

"We accept responsibility for it, and, on behalf of the University, I sincerely apologise to all those affected," Professor Stirling wrote.

The National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU) SA said the underpayments affected professional, non-academic staff who were "precariously employed, low paid [and] predominantly women".

The university says it disputes that characterisation.

The repayments will "easily" exceed $1 million when factoring in superannuation and interest, the union said.

Three-hour 'minimum engagement' clause at fault

Flinders University said the issue was it had not paid some casual staff their three hour "minimum engagement period".

This is a workplace clause that stipulates a causal employee must be paid for at least three hours, even if their shift ends up being shorter.

"This does not mean staff worked hours without being paid," the vice-chancellor said.

"Rather, some staff should have been engaged for a longer period of time to comply with the minimum engagement period."

Professor Colin Stirling says the university is now contacting affected staff. (Flinders University)

Professor Stirling added that not all casual staff were subject to the three-hour requirements, with "multiple exemptions" under the university's enterprise bargaining agreement (EBA).

"The issue occurred in the context of a complex enterprise agreement that includes a number of provisions and exceptions to the three-hour minimum engagement period," he said.

"While this complexity provides important context for how the errors occurred, it does not diminish the University's responsibility."

The university has now introduced stronger controls, monitoring, oversight and training, Professor Stirling added.

Underpayments 'massive breach of trust', union says

Flinders University's underpayment admission comes only a year after the old University of Adelaide revealed it had underpaid 838 casual academic staff $1.25 million over eight years.

The underpayments, which occurred between March 2017 and May 2025, were equivalent to nearly $1,500 per staff member.

NTEU SA division secretary Andrew Miller said underpayments were a "feature, not a bug" of Australia's higher education system.

He added that Flinders University's underpayments were "actually large for a small, bespoke university".

"This represents a massive breach of trust, a massive breach of entitlements and hardship for the staff throughout a period of time where there's been high inflation and cost of living pressures," he said.

The university says it accepts responsibility for the underpayment, and has apologised to staff. (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook )

Dr Miller also rejected the university's reasoning around complex EBAs.

"If they can't implement the enterprise agreements that they sign, there's a big problem in the governance of our universities," he said.

"Staff are due their entitlements, and vice chancellors must ensure those entitlements are paid and honoured in full."

A spokesperson for Flinders University noted that it was the university's own review that discovered the error, which it had "disclosed publicly and apologised for".

"Affected staff are being paid as quickly as possible, including applicable interest and superannuation," the spokesperson said.

"It is important to note that all affected staff were paid in full for the work they did. The error is that these individuals should have been engaged for a longer shift."

The NTEU SA and Flinders University are currently locked in enterprise bargaining negotiations.

Union members voted last month to take industrial action, including work stoppages.

World.title: ‘Obsessed’: The reclusive billionaire heiress who can’t stop getting richer
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesBillionaires ‘Obsessed’: The reclusive billionaire heiress who can’t stop getting richer Clara Hernanz Lizarraga October 15, 2026 — 7:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Sandra Ortega, Spain’s richest woman, has spent most of her life in the small northwestern town of Oleiros, a windy place overlooking the Atlantic Ocean. The 58-year-old is so intensely private and lives such an ordinary life that “for all they have,” there’s little that points to her immense wealth, says Ángel García Seoane, the town’s mayor. Zara heiress Sandra Ortega at her mother’s funeral in 2013. The reclusive billionaire’s fortune is growing. Alamy Stock Photo The second-largest shareholder of Zara owner Inditex after her father, the company’s founder Amancio Ortega, Sandra’s 5.05 per cent stake is currently valued at about €8.5 billion ($13.7 billion). Her half-sister Marta, Inditex’s chairwoman, is the more visible member of the next generation of Ortegas. But Sandra, Amancio’s daughter with his first wife, has amassed enormous wealth without ever playing a role at the business her parents started — now the world’s biggest fashion retailer. When 90-year-old Amancio, whose net worth stands at about $US127 billion ($182.2 billion), eventually passes on, Sandra’s wealth is set to grow substantially. Under local laws, at least a quarter of his estate’s value will go to his descendants. That would give his three children — Sandra, her disabled brother Marcos, and Marta — a minimum of $US10.6 billion each, based on Bloomberg Billionaires Index’s estimate of his fortune. The inheritance may not necessarily be in Inditex shares, but Sandra’s current stake already gives her unusual clout.



Sandra’s only direct connection to Inditex’s operations has been through her husband, who has held low-profile jobs at the company linked to facilities and innovation. Her three young-adult children have not been involved in the business, and there’s little to suggest that will change after Amancio Ortega. But Amancio’s descendants from his two marriages have had almost no relationship for decades, leaving investors with the question of how Inditex’s family shareholders will deal with one another once he — their common link — is no longer in the picture. Related Article Billionaires The family feud over the $65 billion Ray-Ban fortune “The vulnerability is not today; it is the day Amancio Ortega’s shares move,” said Martin Roll, a global family business strategist and senior adviser at McKinsey & Co. “A passive shareholder with a meaningfully larger stake, no board seat and no track record of how she would vote when it matters becomes a strategic variable for everyone around the table, including outside investors.” Granted, Amancio may already have in place an ownership architecture for the nearly 60 per cent stake in Inditex held by his holding firm Pontegadea, with a well-defined shareholders’ pact and family governance structure that has not been made public. Still, how family shareholders work together is often critical to such companies’ future, said Alfonso Chiner, a professor at IESE who specialises in such entities. “The shareholders of a family business need commitment and unity,” he said. “The predecessor, successor, the company and the family all have to comply with a joint, parallel and organised plan.”



Spokespeople for Sandra’s organisations, Inditex and Pontegadea declined to comment. Sandra didn’t accept requests for a meeting and didn’t make any of her staff available for interviews. But conversations with about a dozen people familiar with her world paint a picture of a reluctant billionaire who shuns the trappings of the rich even as Inditex continues to swell her coffers. Inditex is headquartered in Arteixo, just outside A Coruña, a port city of sandy beaches and cobbled streets where Amancio Ortega lives in a 19th-century building with glass-enclosed balconies overlooking the shoreline. Nearby, a similar façade houses Sandra’s family office. Zara founder Amancio Ortega with daughter Marta Ortega Perez in 2018. Getty Although a short distance sets the two buildings apart, father and daughter were long estranged, a reflection of the family rupture that shaped Sandra’s place in the Inditex story. More than four decades ago, her parents separated after Amancio’s relationship with an Inditex employee, Flora Pérez, resulted in the birth of a daughter — Marta. His two families had little to do with each other. Over time, however, Amancio and Sandra have rebuilt a relationship, people familiar with the matter said, declining to be named discussing private matters.



The story of Sandra’s fortune, which she now manages through her family office and a foundation, traces its roots to the creation of Zara by her parents in the mid-1970s. Sandra’s mother, Rosalía Mera, was born in 1944 in A Coruña and grew up in poverty. Mera’s home faced a beach where a slaughterhouse sewer emptied blood and scraps into the sea. Leaving school at 11, Mera took up jobs as a seamstress to support her family, eventually working at a haberdashery known as La Maja, where she met her future husband, Amancio Ortega. In the beginning, they were a team of four: Mera, Amancio, his brother Antonio and sister-in-law Primitiva Renedo, according to the Zara founders’ biographer Xavier Blanco. Mera and Renedo began sewing baby buntings, but it was a women’s padded housecoat — a cheaper version of a popular design — that became their breakout product. Production spread beyond Renedo’s home to a network of women sewing from workshops and homes, while Amancio and Antonio handled sales and distribution. Mera and Amancio had two children: Sandra, in 1968, and Marcos, born three years later with cerebral palsy. Mera soon assumed caregiving responsibilities while Amancio threw himself into the business. After a failed first attempt, they launched Zara in 1975, the flagship brand of what is today Inditex. As the business expanded through the late 1970s, the couple’s relationship deteriorated. By 1984, they split up after Amancio had formed a new family with Pérez and Marta. After their separation, Mera remained one of Inditex’s principal shareholders, even as her ownership declined over the years. Although she was largely removed from the company’s day-to-day operations, she remained a dedicated and opinionated board member, her biographer Blanco said. By the time of its public listing in 2001, Inditex had become enormous, with its valuation running into the billions. Mera sold half her position, keeping 7 per cent and remaining the second-largest holder after Amancio. Mera stepped down as board member in 2004, and when she died in 2013, Sandra inherited her stake.



Sandra largely followed in the footsteps of her mother, who had turned to philanthropy as her connection to Inditex faded. Mera defended abortion rights and focused on issues like education and social inclusion. Headstrong, she sparked a small outcry in 2011 when she publicly supported the “Indignados,” an anti-establishment grassroots movement that emerged after the financial crisis. Related Article Medicine She lost her sight. Her Wall Street billionaire father bet on a daring new treatment Despite her fortune, Mera was seen as austere, zipping around town in a small hatchback bearing the insignia of one of her organisations and negotiating every penny. Her stance on wealth was coloured by her childhood, says Antonio Pernas, a designer from A Coruña born the same year as Mera. Since emigrants returning from the Americas sometimes came dressed in bright colours and patterned scarves to show off their newfound prosperity, anyone clothed a little extravagantly would be mocked with shouts of “¡Hay barco!” – “The boat’s in!” – suggesting they were like the newly rich returnees, he said. Mera remained wary of ostentatious displays of wealth all her life. “Sandra is even more obsessed than her mother with making sure nobody could tell they were rich,” said Pancho Casal, a film producer whose company Mera had backed. The only photos of Sandra online are from her mother’s funeral more than a decade ago.



Her childhood was spent in a middle-class neighbourhood of A Coruña. Around the time her parents separated, she asked to swap her catholic education for a state school on the other side of town, where she met her husband. She studied psychology at a public university before joining Paideia, a charitable foundation created by her mother for social transformation. For all that, Sandra’s family office Rosp, which stands for Rosalía Patrimonio, has continued to make high-profile bets across the world. Its profit grew 2 per cent to €307 million in 2025, according to the most recent accounts available, and its assets were valued at over €11 billion. Her three children joined the family office’s board in 2024. Rosp’s largest holding is its Inditex stake, which will rake in €275 million in dividends this year. It also owns a 5 per cent of PharmaMar, a small Spanish company that specialises in oncology treatments, and invests in a broad range of venture capital and private equity funds that are mostly based in Spain. Although Sandra has avoided the lifestyle of the rich and famous, over the years her family office has built a vast portfolio of high-end hotels and real estate across the globe. Zara is the biggest fashion retailer in the world. Bloomberg Rosp’s holdings include such iconic hotels as the Waldorf Towers on Miami beach, a 1937 art deco-style building on Ocean Drive, and Palo-Alto’s El Prado, a hotel whose storied Italian eatery counted Steve Jobs, Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg among customers before closing this year. It bought the Radisson Blu on Leicester Square in London for €142 million a few months ago. In Portugal, Rosp has spent more than a decade backing the development of Na Praia, a luxury resort of villas and hotel suites overlooking one of the country’s most exclusive stretches of coastline.



Although Sandra has a small team running the show at her family office, she’s not entirely hands-off. That was demonstrated by her 2020 decision to fire its chief investment officer, who had worked first for her mother and then for her. Sandra later accused him of misappropriation and disloyal administration, among other things, drawing her into a series of legal battles. Her own activities revolve around the charitable foundation, which had a budget of about €3.5 million last year. Related Article Analysis

US midterms America’s billionaires are turning their backs on Trump Sandra rarely makes public appearances, even when it involves her foundation. Under the “contact” tab, her foundation’s website states that its president “does not maintain profiles or engage in any activity on social media,” nor does she take part in “any public dialogue regarding social or philanthropic initiatives, business activities, or any other type of endeavour.” She provided a rare glimpse into her view on life when a park named after her mother was inaugurated in Oleiros in 2024. Financed by her, it preserved old trees, stone walls and uneven ground and included over 200 plant species, nest boxes for birds and a pond full of a croaky frogs. Certain areas in the park are not lit at night to protect the circadian cycles of animals. In a documentary on the park a year later, Sandra reminisced about her childhood and mulled over creating “a green space instead of building homes.”



“I think this is a space that allows people to pause and be in the world, for a little moment, in a different way,” she said in voiceover at the end of the film. World.title: Musk points to Trump in row with Ukraine over Starlink slowdown
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war Musk points to Trump in row with Ukraine over Starlink slowdown David Crowe Updated October 15, 2026 — 7:18am ,first published 5:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: Ukraine has suffered a severe disruption to Starlink networks run by tech titan Elon Musk after days of dispute with US President Donald Trump, raising fears the Pentagon is “throttling” services to help Russia. Ukrainian forces cancelled missions after losing access to high-speed services from Musk’s satellite company, government officials in Kyiv said, after the world’s richest man backed Trump in criticising Ukraine for attacking Russian targets. The warnings led Musk to declare that any military use of the Starlink network was a matter for the US government and the US president, while others said connectivity was being restored after the outcry. Victoria Deineko holds her daughter, Mia, in front of a multi-story residential building damaged in a Russian missile strike in Kyiv onTuesday. AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the surprise slowdown in speeds and warned that more civilians would be killed if Musk or the US government did not act to restore full Starlink services to Ukrainian forces.



“We understand what is going on – they switched off, it’s their decision,” Zelensky told media host Piers Morgan in an interview aired late on Wednesday in London (about 3.30am on Thursday, AEDT) amid escalating concerns about the risk to Ukraine’s military capacity. “People will die, of course, if attacks will continue and if Starlink will not work.” A technician repairing a damaged Starlink satellite terminal board at an undisclosed location in Ukraine in July. Bloomberg Zelensky urged Musk to undo the “mistake” and prevent a “huge tactical problem” from leaving civilians exposed to greater Russian attacks. Former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov entered the debate soon afterwards by claiming on X that the speed of the Starlink service was being restored and thanking Musk for his support.



Musk reacted by drawing a distinction between the Starlink civilian service and the related Starshield system owned and controlled by the US government. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he said, referring to the American president. View post on X “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.” The remarks from the world’s richest man appeared to leave responsibility for the issue with Trump.



The satellite problems came hours after Zelensky revealed a separate halt to the usual supply of western intelligence about looming Russian missile and drone attacks, saying there was “no warning” of some of the latest strikes. The two developments fuelled concerns about decisions in Washington that could restrict Ukraine’s military capacity at a time when Trump wants Zelensky to stop hitting Russian oil refineries. President Donald Trump, right, presents the National Medal of Science to Elon Musk this month. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Ukraine depends on Starlink, which is part of the SpaceX group controlled by Musk, to guide missiles and drones that strike targets in parts of Ukraine occupied by Russian forces, and to support defensive drones to intercept Russian attacks. “SpaceX implemented speed restrictions on Starlink terminals while in motion last night,” said presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov on social media on Wednesday morning (late that night, AEDT).



“Currently, the restriction applies to the StarShield ‘military service package’ and limits speed to 100 miles per hour [160 kilometres per hour]. “Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation.” View post on X While Musk has clashed with Trump at times, he backed the US president in recent days in calling on Ukraine to replace Zelensky. “I agree, time for Ukraine to get a new leader,” Musk said on Sunday. When Trump said the attacks on oil refineries should stop, Musk posted: “Zelensky has gone too far.”



The military-grade services on the Starlink satellite network are known as StarShield and are controlled by the Pentagon, leading to speculation that the “throttling” was the result of decisions by the US government rather than Musk. Polish Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski called on Musk to ensure Ukraine gained the services it needed. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, left, with Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky in London on Wednesday. Bloomberg “Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?” Sikorski asked on X. “As your European customers, we are watching you.” The disruptions increased concerns in Kyiv about more strikes on civilians when Ukrainian defenders lacked full capacity.



Access to Starlink is a key factor in Ukraine’s ability to aim drones and missiles at Russian targets, but Musk has been accused in the past of using his personal power to intervene in the war. Reuters reported last year that Musk gave an order to his staff in September 2022 that cut coverage to Ukrainian forces at a pivotal moment in their attempt to retake Kherson and other areas near the Black Sea. Zelensky meets with King Charles at Buckingham Palace. Getty Russian forces lost access to Starlink this year, although the full impact of this change was unclear. The service can be so vital that the BBC reported that Russian soldiers would try to bribe Ukrainian collaborators to gain access to a Starlink terminal. Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and 120 drones at Ukrainian targets on Tuesday night, Zelensky said on Wednesday. He said 600,000 people were without power as a result of the latest strikes, despite Trump’s claim that both sides had agreed to an energy ceasefire.



Six people were killed and thirteen injured in Lutsk in western Ukraine on Wednesday, Zelensky said, when a drone hit a residential building and store. Related Article Analysis

Russia-Ukraine war The president of pretence: Why Trump’s latest ceasefire ‘trick’ failed its first test Zelensky gained public support in the UK on Wednesday when he visited London and spoke with King Charles III at Buckingham Palace before holding talks with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street. Burnham announced a faster delivery plan for British missiles that could help Ukraine intercept Russian jet-powered drones, but he avoided any move that might provoke Trump. When Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey asked Burnham in parliament if he agreed that the latest moves in the US were “another shameful Trump betrayal” of the Ukrainian people, the prime minister was cautious in response.



Burnham said it was a “very dark and difficult moment” for Zelensky, but he made no criticism of Trump. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ASX set to fall, Wall Street slumps after inflation report
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to fall, Wall Street slumps after inflation report Stan Choe Updated October 15, 2026 — 7:16am ,first published 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. US stocks dropped to their worst day since July after a report showing inflation accelerated last month raised expectations on Wall Street that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates. The S&P 500 fell 1.1 per cent and had its fifth loss in the six days since setting its all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 1.9 per cent. Markets now see a 39 per cent chance that the Fed will raise the federal funds rate at its next meeting in two weeks, up from the 22 per cent probability seen just a day earlier, according to data from CME Group. AP Photo/Seth Wenig The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures pointing to a fall of 21 points, or 0.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.6 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was weaker at US69.66¢. US stocks felt pressure from rising yields in the bond market, where worries grew after a report said US consumers had to pay prices for fuel, food and other costs of living last month that were 3.7 per cent higher overall than a year earlier. That means inflation accelerated from its 3.4 per cent rate in August and was worse than the 3.6 per cent that economists expected.



Related Article Opinion

Bonds Trump’s America and Wall Street are in a dangerous spiral Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Inflation has remained more painful than anyone would like since the economy launched out of the crevasse created by the COVID-19 pandemic. It’s breathed in new life recently because of jumps in fuel prices caused by the war with Iran, and the price for a barrel of Brent crude added 1 per cent Wednesday to $US106.71. That has built on signals that the US economy is still growing, longstanding worries about fast-rising debt loads for governments and other factors to send yields to their highest levels in years or even decades in bond markets worldwide. The centrepiece of the US bond market, the 10-year Treasury, saw its yield rise to 5.23 per cent from less than 5.17 per cent just before the inflation report’s release. During the morning, it briefly jumped above 5.32 per cent and pulled back toward its highest level since 2002. Yields on shorter-term Treasurys had even bigger leaps as traders raised their expectations for coming hikes to interest rates by the Federal Reserve.



The Fed last month raised the interest rate that it controls, which affects very short-term loans, for the first time in three years in hopes of reining in inflation. Higher rates do that by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money and slowing the overall economy. Traders now see a 39 per cent chance that the Fed will raise the federal funds rate at its next meeting in two weeks, up from the 22 per cent probability seen just a day earlier, according to data from CME Group. “The consumer price index was a little hotter than expected, but not scorching hot,” said Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. “It was just hot enough to keep traders on edge.” Part of what’s keeping inflation high is that Americans broadly are continuing to spend, which in turn encourages businesses to keep raising prices for their own products and services. As Americans become more “price-sensitive” and the economy benefits from greater productivity by workers, Vanguard Senior Economist Adam Schickling said inflation should slow, but “patience will be required.” Higher yields in the bond market push downward on prices for stocks, and the main way companies can offset that is by delivering bigger profits. That’s exactly what analysts are expecting, and it’s how the S&P 500 has been able to set records despite the many challenges weighing on Wall Street.



BlackRock rose 0.7 per cent after the investment company reported stronger profit and revenue for the summer than analysts expected. Customers poured a net $US205 billion ($294 billion) into BlackRock’s funds, including iShares exchange-traded funds, from July through September to bring its total assets under management to $US15.5 trillion. BlackRock makes money by charging fees on those dollars. But the high expectations for profit growth also mean companies will likely get punished if they fall short of targets, which is what several other financial companies did Wednesday morning. Related Article Updated

Energy Gas exporters to be forced to prevent Australian shortfalls under new laws Bank of America dropped 4.7 per cent after reporting weaker profit and revenue for the third quarter than analysts expected. The profit would have fallen short even after ignoring the $US1.2 billion in fines that the US Treasury Department announced late on Tuesday for alleged violations of anti-money laundering and sanctions laws. State Street sank 4 per cent after reporting weaker revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, even though its profit was slightly above their forecasts.



The higher yields in the bond market, meanwhile, hurt some stocks in particular because of their effect on the cost to borrow money. Homebuilders are finding potential customers turned off by mortgage rates at their highest level in nearly three years. Their stocks sank further on Wednesday, including drops of 1.9 per cent for Lennar, 2 per cent for PulteGroup and 1.3 per cent for D.R. Horton. In stock markets abroad, indexes ticked higher in Europe following a weaker finish in Asia. Indexes rose 0.6 per cent in Paris and fell 0.9 per cent in Shanghai for two of the world’s bigger moves. A patient at a Sydney hospital allegedly poured petrol on his fellow patients before setting one on fire in a shocking attack detectives are treating as a murder attempt.

Raymond James Dungay, a 48-year-old man admitted to the spinal ward of Prince of Wales Hospital, is accused of orchestrating the attack at 10.45pm on Tuesday, in which he allegedly doused three patients, including 54-year-old Randovan Banic, in petrol hidden in a drink bottle before igniting his lighter.

Randovan Banic is now being treated for burns following the attack. Nine News

The flame failed to catch on the first two patients – a 63-year-old man and 64-year-old woman – before burning Banic, a spinal patient who suffered injuries across his body.

“[He was] coming towards me and all of a sudden, he f---ing douses me in petrol, I smelt it, but it was too late, he lit me up,” Banic told Nine News on Wednesday from his hospital bed.

World.content:

Warning: Graphic content London: Actor and comedian Russell Brand was a “ruthless” predator who was obsessed with sexual conquest and told friends of his aim to sleep with 5000 women over his lifetime, a court heard on the opening day of his trial on rape and assault charges. A crown prosecutor told jurors that Brand could be funny and charming but was also “childlike” in demanding what he wanted, leading one woman to tell him he had treated her like an animal. Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday for his trial. Getty Images Brand, 51, faces three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault. He denies all the charges and has insisted he never engaged in non-consensual sex.



The jury heard graphic statements about the allegations in the opening of the prosecution case at Southwark Crown Court in London on Wednesday (UK time). Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told the court that the six women at the heart of the case did not know each other and would give evidence about being assaulted by Brand between 1999 and 2009. A court artist sketch of Brand during jury selection earlier in the week. Elizabeth Cook/PA via AP “He was ruthless, he was calculating, he was manipulative. And, the prosecution say, he was a sexual predator,” Karmy-Jones said. The prosecutor said Brand was not deterred regardless of what the women said or did to try to stop him.



“His desire, strong desire, for some form of sexual contact was indiscriminate and voracious,” she told the jury. Related Article Courts What to know about Russell Brand’s rape and sexual assault trial Karmy-Jones outlined the allegations from the six women before calling the first witness, a former friend of the actor. The first complainant, said the prosecutor, met Brand in 1999 when he did a show in Bournemouth and she was in the audience. She was in her 20s, thought Brand was gay and was flattered by his interest in her. Later, in her hotel room, the prosecutor said, she grew scared when Brand forced himself upon her and raped her.



Karmy-Jones said the woman was left “in shock” and crying because she felt “dirty and stupid” and did not know what to do. The second complainant alleges Brand tried to force her into a toilet in 2001 by grabbing her arm with a “desperate wild-eyed look” on his face. She managed to drag herself out of his grip, the prosecutor said. Brand was met on Wednesday by a crowd of photographers and journalists. Getty Images The third complainant alleges she was at a party in 2004 when Brand pulled her into a toilet by grabbing her arm. He forced her to perform oral sex, holding her head, the court heard. Afterwards, the prosecutor said, the woman was in complete shock: “She also recalls walking around in a daze, thinking, ‘What just happened? What do I do?’”



The woman also alleges she was in a car with Brand and two men when the actor exposed himself to her. She rejected his advance but felt ashamed and blamed herself for what had occurred, the prosecutor said. The fourth complainant alleges Brand pushed her up against a wall and began kissing her at her workplace when she was working in broadcasting in 2004 or 2005. “During this assault he also grabbed her body, her breasts, her sides and her buttocks aggressively,” the prosecutor said. The woman tried to stop him, but he was too strong. Another woman who saw this happen did nothing to help, the court was told, and this complainant managed to push Brand away. The fifth complainant alleges she met Brand when he performed at a show in London in 2009. The court heard that she was 21 at the time and had consensual sex with Brand in his dressing room after the show. At a later occasion at Brand’s home in London, the prosecutor said, the complainant had consensual sex with the actor – but he then “flipped” her over and had anal sex “with full force” without consent.



“In her words, she hated herself for what had happened,” the prosecutor said. The woman alleges that when Brand texted her the following year and said he wanted to “push” her further, she replied by text: “I think you pushed me far enough – you treated me like an animal.” The sixth complainant alleges she was working in broadcasting in 2009 when Brand approached her and members of his team said he required a massage. The complainant alleges he fell to his knees in front of her with his face pressed to her groin, so she could feel his breath on her genitals. The prosecutor told the court that the woman “froze” but later pushed her fingertips into Brand’s shoulders and said he was “really bony” – a remark that ended the incident by making his team members laugh. The first witness in the trial was Mark Pinheiro, a former friend and flatmate of the actor.



Pinheiro told the court he had travelled with Brand to the Bournemouth show in 1999 when Brand boasted in the car of being a “ladies’ man” and talked of his goal of having sex with 5000 women during his lifetime.



Pinheiro also told the court that he remembered Brand leaving Bournemouth in a hurry and later saying “things may have gone a little bit too far” with a woman at the time.



He said Brand always sought to gain “some kind of conquest” with women.



Karmy-Jones said another friend from Brand’s early career described him as having a “goal and obsession” with women and sex.



Brand, dressed in a dark suit, arrived at the court with his wife, Laura. In police interviews ahead of the trial, he denied ever engaging in non-consensual sexual activity.



Speaking briefly to reporters outside the court on Wednesday, Brand said he felt “blessed.”



“I feel, of course, concerned, but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody involved,” Brand said. “That’s my prayer.”



Those making sexual assault accusations have the right to anonymity under British law. This masthead seeks to avoid reporting details that might identify witnesses in the trial. The trial is expected to continue for six weeks.

World.title: Which party is best placed to manage Qld’s economy? The poll results are in
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsQueenslandResolve Political Monitor Which party is best placed to manage Qld’s economy? The poll results are in Matt Dennien October 15, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Half of Queensland voters want to see the state cut spending if it is to embark on the budget repair needed to address the debt and deficit issues that drove last month’s first credit rating downgrade in 17 years. New Resolve Political Monitor polling for this masthead also shows that voters’ views of One Nations’ economic management do not align with the party’s heightened support in the state. The survey comes at the halfway point of the parliamentary term as both major parties shift their gaze to the 2028 state election, with a still-popular government and an ascendent One Nation in striking range of a lagging Opposition. Queensland Treasurer David Janetzki and Queensland Senator and One Nation leader Pauline Hanson. Jamila Filippone, Alex Ellinghausen But despite its heightened share of the primary voting intention in the state steadying at above 20 per cent, only 13 per cent of voters believe One Nation would be the best party to handle the state’s budget, rising slightly to 15 per cent in marginal seats.



A total of 35 per cent of voters named the Crisafulli LNP government as the better economic managers, while 21 per cent selected Steven Miles’ Labor. Only 8 per cent chose “someone else”, with 22 per cent saying they were undecided or that no party would be best. The survey involved 434 registered voters and was conducted between October 6 and 10. In September, ratings agency S&P Global announced it had downgraded the state from AA+ to AA amid heightened deficits driven by Olympic infrastructure spending and economic headwinds. While Treasurer David Janetzki, at the time, reiterated his belief that the outcome was the inevitable result of the former Labor government’s actions, he also conceded his government had shied away from politically sensitive actions that the agency – and economists – say would help.



“Although S&P would have preferred Queensland to raise taxes, reduce services and stop building, those are decisions we are not willing to make,” Janetzki said in a statement. In the context of the rating downgrade and justification for this, voters were asked to choose their preference among a list of potential options for attempting to reduce debt and the deficit if the state government were to attempt to do so. A total of 49 per cent nominated reducing spending as their preference, with privatising, selling or leasing assets a distant second at 12 per cent, and an increase in taxes and charges supported by 10 per cent of those surveyed. Another 29 per cent preferred neither of those three options, or were unsure. The split was almost identical among those in marginal seats.

World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaDonald Trump Trump shares AI video of himself wrestling tiger that killed British man at zoo Poppy Wood October 15, 2026 — 5:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Washington: US President Donald Trump has shared an AI video in which he wrestles the tiger that killed a British man at a South Yorkshire zoo. In the clip the US president, in a suit and tie, chases the male tiger and throws him to the ground, before the pair start hugging. Altai the tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park. Facebook The beginning of the 23-second video mirrors actual footage of William Chapman’s last moments, before he was mauled to death on Saturday. In the AI clip, which was posted on the president’s Truth Social network on Tuesday (US time), Trump sits on the ground and tries to fend off Altai, the 200-kilogram Siberian tiger, while the animal swipes with its paw.



Trump is seen jumping up and running after the big cat in the faked video. It is set to the song The Lion Sleeps Tonight. Trump appears to have taken a keen interest in the tiger attack. A screenshot of the AI video shared by Trump. Truth Social/@realDonaldTrump On Tuesday night, the US president shared the actual footage of the attack on his Truth Social platform, showing the moments before Chapman was mauled to death at Yorkshire Wildlife Park at the weekend. Trump posted the video, which showed a tiger clawing and biting at a man, with the caption: “Don’t ever mess with nature! President DJT.”



One minute after sharing the footage of the actual attack, Trump posted a compilation video of big cats mauling humans. It included an AI-generated video of a lion smashing through the glass of its enclosure to attack a zookeeper. South Yorkshire Police had asked the public not to share “distressing footage” of Chapman’s death. On Tuesday evening, Chapman’s family revealed their “severe distress” about footage and other content shared online. Tiger mauling victim William Chapman. South Yorkshire Police Relatives said in a statement issued before Trump’s post: “The publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time. We ask people to stop doing this.” Emergency services were contacted shortly after 1.30pm on October 10 (UK time) after Chapman climbed into the tiger’s enclosure and was attacked. He was pronounced dead at the scene shortly afterwards.



Chapman’s family paid tribute to him on Tuesday night, describing him as “bright, warm and engaging”. Related Article US election ‘We have guns too’: Democrat slurs her way through viral, car crash interview In their statement, the family said he had suffered from “significant mental illness” for a number of years and had been prescribed “strong medication”. “The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened,” the statement continued. Chapman’s parents said they were “hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their utmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did”.



Chapman had posted a video on his Instagram page from inside the enclosure moments before the attack, in which he filmed as he slowly approached the big cat and could be heard breathing heavily. Related Article Analysis

Trump's White House ‘My president ... excuse me, my husband’: Trump’s new spinner gets off to a rocky start The Telegraph understands that Chapman was a former child actor who attended the Jackie Palmer Stage School in High Wycombe, Bucks. As a child, he appeared in the ITV production May Contain Nuts alongside Shirley Henderson – best known for playing Moaning Myrtle in the Harry Potter films – and Darren Boyd. He also portrayed Edward Jenner in the BBC drama series True Stories. Jackie Palmer Stage School said: “We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer, during his time with us.



“It was a privilege to be part of his journey, and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him. William will be truly missed, and he will always hold a special place in our heart.” Editor's pick Animal rights New York’s famous Central Park horse-drawn carriages set to be banned In a blog post from 2014, Chapman’s mother described his time at stage school, saying: “He has learnt a great deal in his time there, and whilst he doesn’t enjoy singing and dancing so much now he’s a teenager, he is passionate about acting and drama.” She recalled that he had auditioned for May Contain Nuts at the age of five, adding: “Over the years he has attended many auditions, and I have a few stories to tell there… “The most notable one was when he went for the part of Alfie in May Contain Nuts, the ITV two-part drama adaptation of John O’Farrell’s satirical book.”
