World.title: Middle income, uni degree no protection from financial struggles - researchers
World.content:
Audio player for " Do I know enough about my financial state to retire? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/personal-finance/1913516%2Fmiddle-income-uni-degree-no-protection-from-financial-struggles-researchers

Do I know enough about my financial state to retire? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 17m

Having a degree, owning your own home and being in full-time work are not protection from financial hardship, new Otago University research suggests.

The University of Otago has released its latest New Zealand Consumer Lifestyles report, which is updated every five years.

It said 27 percent of respondents could this year be described as "financial strugglers". This was the largest of any group in the survey, and bigger than the 2020 report, when it was 16.5 percent of the population.

These people were, on average, 43 years old, earning $51,000 to $75,000, often with a university education, paying a mortgage and engaged in full-time employment. "This suggests that these economic and personal factors do not necessarily protect individuals from experiencing financial hardship," the report said.

They reported comparatively low satisfaction with their standard of living, health, achievements and future security.

Audio player for " Otago study tracks changing consumer habits since 1979 " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/personal-finance/1913516%2Fmiddle-income-uni-degree-no-protection-from-financial-struggles-researchers

Otago study tracks changing consumer habits since 1979 Morning Report Download MP3 5m

They were also less likely to describe their lives as purposeful, their relationships as rewarding or themselves as engaged with daily life.

People who were struggling were concerned about inequality and believed the gap between rich and poor was growing.

Associate professor Leah Watkins said financial pressure was affecting a much broader group of New Zealanders now. "Our financial strugglers segment has grown … the financial impact of the cost of living crisis is affecting a lot more people ... the segment, in terms of income, would be classed as middle income and many had university degrees, many had mortgages. It's not perhaps what we picture as those that would be financially struggling."

Associate Professor Leah Watkins from the Department of Marketing at Otago Business School Graham Warman

She said people were asked whether they thought things would improve but were not optimistic.

"A large percentage of people thought that this cost of living crisis was likely to continue. That has impacts on the other measures we are seeing. The number of people thinking they had to leave New Zealand to get ahead was significantly higher than it was in 2020. You can see how that financial insecurity is not just affecting what people buy but it's affecting their outlook, their lifestyles in broader ways."

Another 11 percent were "aspirational materialists" with a strong desire for achievement and upward mobility. Another 13 percent were "contented traditionalists" who were older on average with high personal wellbeing, optimism, traditional values and a positive view of the country.

Sixteen percent were "ethical pragmatists" who were values-driven and financially stable so they could prioritise ethical living and social responsibility.

Ten percent were described as disengaged drifters.

The researchers found 40 percent of all respondents said they had struggled to buy essentials, 52 percent went without something to buy essentials, 48 percent said economic uncertainty prevented them making purchases they would otherwise have made and 48 percent thought they needed to leave New Zealand to get ahead, which was up from 29 percent in 2020.

Watkins said there was a connection between frugality and sustainability that had come through in the report. "Durability and reuse, those were the sort of behaviours we were seeing people saying was important to them."

There was also a key theme around the digital environment, she said. "That's just ingrained in people's every day. Consumers were saying what remains important to them is personal recommendations from friends and family. It wasn't influencer culture and it wasn't celebrity endorsement, they were seeking information from tried and trusted personal sources."

The report said the growth of price-led global platforms such as Temu, Amazon, and eBay had intensified price transparency and enabled consumers to compare products across multiple sellers with minimal effort.

"As a result, consumers increasingly expect low prices, seamless purchasing experiences, rapid fulfilment, and personalised service. At the same time, advances in artificial intelligence are accelerating these trends through AI-driven recommendation systems, dynamic pricing, automated customer service, predictive logistics, and personalised marketing. However, there are also signs of consumer resistance, reflecting low levels of trust and growing scepticism about the adoption of these technologies."

World.title: Explainer: What are special votes and why they could change the election results?
World.content:
Explainer - Election Day is coming up fast, but don't expect complete clarity on 7 November, thanks to special votes.

Special votes, which are counted slower, have shifted preliminary election results the last several times. And they may well do it again in 2026.

Here's what you need to know about what makes a vote special, why they take longer to sort and why some may end up getting discarded.

What are special votes?

Special votes are made by anyone who isn't on their electoral roll at their voting place, on the unpublished roll, lives overseas or votes away from a polling place because they can't get to one.

When you cast a special vote, you must also sign a declaration form that must be witnessed by another enrolled person. (If you vote at a voting place, that witness can be an Electoral Commission volunteer or staff member.)

And if you have yet to enrol for this year's election - remember the absolute latest you can do that is by midnight on Sunday, 25 October - you will be casting a special vote.

The printed roll for this year's election closed on 4 October, which was Writ Day. Any voter who enrols after that must cast a special vote.

"The number of special votes, and the proportion they make up of the overall vote, have increased in recent elections," an Electoral Commission spokesperson told RNZ.

"Over 600,000 special votes were issued in 2023 - meaning 21 percent of voters cast a special vote."

Richard Shaw, professor of politics at Massey University, noted that in the last election many people enrolled during the early voting period - which will no longer be allowed due to the government changing the deadline so you must be enrolled 13 days before the election.

In 2023, "450,000 people enrolled or updated their enrolment during the voting period; 110,000 did so on Election Day itself," Shaw said.

Despite the changes to enrolment, the Electoral Commission expects as many as 700,000 special votes this year.

The number of special votes has been steadily rising in recent elections, up from 13.5 percent of the overall total in 2014.

Have special votes made a difference in past elections?

They have. In the last three general elections, the final results including special votes have seen National lose two party seats and some electorates have changed sides from the preliminary tally.

It means that even after Election Day on 7 November and preliminary results come in, we may not know the final, final results for a couple of weeks.

Special votes generally tend to benefit the left-leaning parties.

Shaw said that tends to reflect the demographics of those who cast them: "typically younger; typically more mobile (eg renters); typically a little less attached to institutional politics".

"Those groups don't always break left, but they tend to. Or they tend not to engage at all."

In 2017, 2020 and 2023, National lost two seats with special votes, while Labour gained one in 2017 and 2020, Te Pāti Māori gained one in 2020 and two in 2023, and the Greens gained one party seat in 2017 and 2023.

The Electoral Commission is predicting it will take up to 20 days to total special votes. The commission said it has found ways to improve the speed of its checks, but it's still a lengthy process.

"Our forecasts indicate we could receive around 700,000 special votes, which take up to ten times longer to check and count," the Electoral Commission spokesperson said.

"If our forecast is right, then we will need 20 days to do all the required checks and deliver final results."

This year's election does away with being able to enrol to vote and cast a ballot all the way up to Election Day.

That change is likely to affect special votes, Shaw said.

"There will almost certainly be a higher rate of rejection of special votes this time round."

"At this point, of course, we have no way of knowing how many people are going to show up and cast a special which won't be counted ... some specials will be tallied, of course, because they are overseas votes or people out of their electorate or whatever, but plenty won't."

Voting papers being printed in Petone, Wellington weeks ahead of the election. Samuel Rillstone/RNZ

Why do they take longer to count?

They have a stricter checking procedure, and any overseas votes can also take longer to process. In 2023 it took three weeks for special votes to be counted to confirm the election results.

By law, 10 days are allowed for votes to be returned from overseas.

Special votes have to be returned to the electorate they were cast for before they're counted. Every special vote declaration is checked to make sure the voter is enrolled and eligible to vote.

"We check the voter was enrolled in the electorate where they voted, and check that the special declaration form has been completed and witnessed," the Electoral Commission spokesperson said.

"Special votes that are allowed can only be counted after these checks have been done. Votes are tallied and quality assurance checks are made before we release the results."

Shaw said overseas votes, once they're counted, could also affect how the election shakes out.

"The overseas voting population is interesting this year: there are more of them than previously (and at least some of them are presumably people who have left the country while they might rather have remained, had the economic conditions been better), so that might count against the incumbent administration too."

The government pushed for this year's changes to enrolment deadlines and one of the reasons it gave was to speed up vote counting.

"I just think three weeks is way too long to count special votes, I think that needs to be sped up," Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said in 2023.

However, when those enrolment changes were still being considered last year as part of the Electoral Amendment Bill, Chief Electoral Officer Karl Le Quesne said it ultimately wouldn't make results arrive any faster.

"We're forecasting that there'll still be around 700,000 special votes we've got to run through all these integrity checks," he said then.

Some special votes in the election may be disqualified. RNZ / Nick Monro

Why can special votes be tossed out?

In the 2023 general election, 15,555 special votes were disqualified.

"Reasons special votes are disallowed include if the voter is not enrolled, the vote received was late, or the declaration was not signed by an authorised witness or not signed by voter," the Electoral Commission spokesperson said.

The Electoral Commission has a full breakdown of why special votes were disallowed broken down by electorate on their website.

By far the biggest reason was that voters were not actually enrolled at all, with 10,566 discounted for that reason. Far behind was having a declaration not being signed by an authorised witness, with 2384 rejections.

In last year's Auckland local body elections, nearly half of the special votes were disqualified.

Auckland Council said 4162 special votes were deemed invalid, due to incorrect or missing declaration details, or outdated enrolment details. Special votes were only 1.68 percent of the total vote cast, it said.

Similar high rates of disqualification were seen in Kaipara's local council election.

However, it's important to note that local body elections are not run by the Electoral Commission, but by local councils, and can have different rules and procedures.

In a council post-mortem on the Auckland local elections, it was found that "in most cases the reason for the declaration not being in order was the required 'occupation' field left blank, leading to special votes being disallowed on what could be perceived as a technicality."

That occupation requirement is no longer needed in parliamentary elections.

"For the general election, the required fields on special voting declaration forms are your name, the grounds (reason) for casting a special vote, and your signature," the Electoral Commission spokesperson said.

"Some special voting declaration forms may still include an occupation field. This field is no longer required and can be left blank. We are gradually phasing out older versions of the form that include this field."

The Auckland Council's report said that in the future "a similar amendment should be made to remove the requirement to include occupation from the special voting declaration for local elections".

"Why should providing your occupation determine whether your vote is counted?" City Vision candidate Raphaela Rose asked The Spinoff in a report on the invalidated local body votes.

Only 29 percent of those eligible voted in Auckland in 2025, and Auckland has moved to remove postal voting at the next local body elections and require in-person voting.

Shaw said the changes to voter enrolment this year are a bit of an X-factor in trying to figure out how important special votes will be in November's election.

"One possibility, given the new policy settings, is that special votes are less, not more, important as far as the final outcome is concerned, in the sense that there may well be fewer of them that count this time round.

World.title: 'Tail wagging the dog': Developer wants political parties to butt out of carparking rules
World.content:
An Auckland property developer wants political parties to butt out of the city's housing density and car parking rules.

The National Party is proposing to remove Auckland's blanket ban on minimum car parking requirements in city and district plans if re-elected.

The requirements were abolished by Labour in an aim to encourage intensification and reduce car dependency.

But National's Transport spokesperson Chris Bishop said too many of Auckland's suburban streets were clogged and hard to get through.

Ockham Residential Developer Mark Todd said that was an exaggeration.

"This is just propaganda. We don't have streets clogged with cars.

"Developers are very sensitive to what they can and can't sell, and there are very few houses built in suburban areas with no car parking.

"We're very sick of both sides of the house interfering with Auckland's Unitary Plan."

He said bringing back minimum car parking requirements would increase house prices and car use.

"[Removing minimum car parking requirements] has been hugely successful for Auckland's housing affordability and supply."

"This is a step backwards. It'll make housing more scarce and unaffordable.

"Auckland's on a road to be the size of Sydney or Melbourne. If you legislate on one or two car parks for every suburban house you'll get tens of thousands more cars on the road every year."

He believed National was trying to appeal to "wealthy voters complaining about intensification in their suburbs".

World.title: Whanganui electorate contenders face off in Stratford
World.content:
Audio player for " Whanganui candidates face off in Stratford election debate " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/1914998%2Fwhanganui-electorate-contenders-face-off-in-stratford

Whanganui candidates face off in Stratford election debate Morning Report Download MP3 4m

It wasn't only party heavyweights going head-to-head on the campaign trail on Wednesday night.

In Stratford the leading contenders in the Whanganui electorate faced off at a debate hosted by Federated Farmers at the TET Multisports Complex.

Ahead of the debate RNZ hit Broadway to gauge interest in the upcoming election.

Nelly was busy at an ATM with her daughter in tow. She was across the issues.

"Probably the money, petrol, not being able to afford much. Yeah, I don't know, personally it's just a lot of like trying to pay the bills."

About 50 people attended the debate at the TET Multisports Complex. RNZ / Robin Martin

But Nelly wasn't clear who was standing in the sprawling Whanganui electorate.

"I haven't looked too much into them, really. I need to do some research it's getting closer and closer."

Graham was picking up supplies. He was up to speed.

"Oh I know the National one is ... I'm just thinking of his name ... Carl Bates and the girl [Angela] Roberts she's Labour and that's about it or all I know."

Graham was worried about the state of the economy.

"Mainly unemployment, I suppose, jobs and stuff, but businesses are closing down they can't afford to keep going and that's just the way the country has gone, I think."

Graham was not sure what the politicians could do to help.

Federated Farmers put on hot drinks and savouries for debate attendees. RNZ / Robin Martin

Kerry was at Colonel Malone's Restaurant & Bar. She wasn't heading along to the debate.

"It's my birthday so I'm not really into politics on my birthday didn't even know there was a debate on tonight so there you go."

Kerry had a favourite candidate.

"Carl Bates. He's the only one I know because he's the only one I'll vote for."

She had another issue on her mind.

"Probably too many immigrants and not enough employment."

At the TET Multisports Complex, incumbent National MP Bates was joined by Labour's Roberts and New Zealand First's Harete Hipango-Brownlie in an often fiery debate in a packed room of about 50 people.

National candidate Carl Bates. RNZ / Robin Martin

MC, Taranaki Federated Farmers president Nick Brown, turned the talk to tax.

Bates kept to the party line.

"From National it's pretty simple there are no new taxes under National. I think it's very interesting to hear from Angela taxing behaviour is a short term approach. Well, that's what the ute tax was and we got rid of it."

Brown asked Roberts whether she supported a land tax.

She said Labour was only interested in a targeted capital gain tax, but Hipango-Brownlie wasn't buying that.

New Zealand First's Harete Hipango-Brownlie. RNZ / Robin Martin

"Isn't that interesting because the reality is Labour is likely to go into a coalition government with the Greens and with Te Pāti Māori, so who's talking about tax there when you're in coalition.

"So, let's be very clear and here's a reality check Labour in coalition with the Greens you're going to be taxed baby taxed."

Roberts hit back.

"So, you think we've got nine new taxes, where's your $25 billion and how comfortable are you with freezing the minimum wage."

After the debate, Eddie said he was impressed by Roberts.

"I've actually seen the lady in our town. I haven't seen Carl in our town. I go to Hāwera and he's never there. She's in Stratford, I'm in Stratford."

Labour candidate Angela Roberts. RNZ / Robin Martin

He wasn't concerned Roberts had taken some flak from the floor and her rivals.

"Oh she's got broad shoulders, she's got broad shoulders."

Charlotte was backing a continuation of the coalition.

"The have inherited a giant mess from the last government and it's going to take one term to turn things around and we've just got to be a little more patient."

While Neils was fed up with the lot of them.

"I must admit just lately I've just become disillusioned. Now I just want whoever's in charge to look after our money."

World.title: Corrections admits failures over sexual harassment claims
World.content:
Corrections has acknowledged it failed a number of women who raised allegations of sexual harassment against a former staffer, RNZ can reveal.

The department has apologised to each of the women telling them they should have been able to expect Corrections to manage their concerns appropriately and effectively.

"This did not happen to the standard that it should have, and for that I am very, very sorry."

It comes after some of the complainants were recently informed of a review which found "significant shortcomings" in how the complaints were handled.

The Corrections staffer at the centre of the allegations earlier told RNZ he "refuted entirely" the complaints that were made.

RNZ first approached Corrections about the (now former) staffer in April in relation to another former staff member, who RNZ is calling Sarah*. She earlier made a formal complaint alleging he sexually harassed her.

Sarah recently received a letter from Corrections informing her that an independent review was carried out in 2024.

The review looked at the response to, and management of, the complaints received about the former staffer.

The first complaint resulted in allegations not being upheld. Sarah later lodged a formal complaint, while another staff member separately raised concerns during the investigation. A subsequent complaint did not result in an employment investigation. After the staffer resigned, further concerns were raised with Corrections.

The letter, from deputy chief executive Rebecca Powell, said the findings of the review identified "a number of significant shortcomings in how complaints were handled".

This included that employees felt "unable to speak up, for fear of retribution or adverse impacts", and that policies and procedures were not readily available and key staff were unaware of them, or where to access them.

Corrections deputy chief executive Rebecca Powell. Supplied / Corrections

There was also a "lack of designated responsibility" for tracking, monitoring and reporting cases of potential wrongdoing.

"The complaint process (investigation and decision making) for the investigated matters was not carried out in a timely manner.

"There was inadequate consultation on whether complainants wanted a matter fully investigated and whether more informal, and/or more culturally responsive, resolutions could have been utilised."

Powell's letter also said the review found that "potentially there was a degree of tolerance shown for harassment in one instance where findings of the independent investigator were not followed".

"The investigators and decision makers adopted a standard of proof approach which was not appropriate. Further, relevant evidence was not considered on one matter, which if considered on a reasonableness basis, may have resulted in a different outcome.

"There was a strong adoption of robust process, resulting in compartmentalisation. A pattern had emerged, which was not acted on by decision makers as they were not aware of it, although senior leaders within the organisation were."

Powell also provided a summary of the review's recommendations which included implementing compulsory sexual harassment training for all staff and the development of policies for staff consuming alcohol at work-related events and "clear parameters" for managers and senior staff socialising with colleagues.

The review also called for a system to be created to record all complaints of sexual harassment made in relation to a staff member.

Powell said all of the recommendations had been accepted.

She also passed on an apology from former chief executive Jeremy Lightfoot.

"Jeremy has asked me to convey his sincere regret ...

"He is deeply apologetic for the harm that these events may have caused to you."

Powell said the concerns that were raised by the complainants "have become a call to action for meaningful change across our organisation".

"However, we acknowledge that we did not hear you, or respond in the way we should have, at the time. For that, I am deeply sorry."

In response to questions from RNZ Powell said the review did not seek to relitigate any of the complaints, but did identify failings in how Corrections managed or responded to them.

Not all of the matters solely related to sexual harassment, Corrections confirmed.

The Corrections staffer at the centre of the allegations earlier told RNZ he "refuted entirely" the complaints that were made. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Powell confirmed she had written to each of the women regarding concerns they raised.

"I have apologised to them because they were entitled to expect that we would manage their concerns appropriately and effectively, and we did not. In different ways, we failed each of them.

"To respect the privacy of these women, I will not be commenting further on the contents of the letters as this relates to each of the women and their experiences. However, if the women wish to share the letters with others - they are able to do so."

Powell said Corrections also commissioned a review into how Corrections could strengthen its approach to preventing and responding to sexual harassment across the organisation.

The review found one in four staff members reported experiencing sexual harassment from another staffer.

"Women, young people, European, Māori, and prison-based staff were more likely to experience such incidents. The rate of staff being sexually harassed at Corrections is higher than a national survey of workers and is likely under-reported."

It also said Corrections' "male-dominant workplace culture is an enabler of sexual harassment".

"This culture lacks understanding of sexual harassment, is tolerant of inappropriate behaviour and is protective of staff with problematic behaviour. This permissive culture is particularly evident in prison settings, which are shaped by the environment, colonisation, gender, and other historical contexts.

"Staff experienced a continuum of experiences from the unwanted (e.g., sexist jokes and comments based on gender stereotypes and physical appearances) to the unlawful (e.g., non-consensual groping and non-consensual sex). Sexual harassment takes place in the workplace, training, social gatherings and online settings."

Corrections accepted all six of the recommendations of the review, which included developing and implementing an organisation-wide culture change programme, building Corrections-wide knowledge of what constitutes sexual harassment and how to respond and support people effectively.

Corrections has also started work to develop a new complaints response model and in March it launched a refreshed code of conduct.

"While eliminating sexual harassment at Corrections is a long-term programme of work and we have more work to do, I want our staff to have confidence that when they do raise concerns, regardless of the situation, their welfare and wellbeing is at the heart of our approach."

Former Corrections chief executive Jeremy Lightfoot. RNZ / Diego Opatowski

Lightfoot, who is now chief executive at the Ministry of Cities, Environment and Transport told RNZ in a statement that he had previously accepted all the findings of the review which looked at the response to, and management of, the complaints received about the former staffer.

"Including my part in failing the women who complained about [him]. I stand by that."

He confirmed his decisions did not follow appropriate practice and "sent the wrong message about positive and safe workplaces to leaders, all staff and especially to the complainants".

He said he was pleased the apology was sent to the women on behalf of Corrections.

"It is critically important to me, in the organisations I lead, that there is zero tolerance of workplace sexual harassment and bullying.

"This includes making sure staff understand what sexual harassment is, and that there are policies and systems in place that ensure people are confident to bring complaints and know there will be a safe and effective response when they do. A key part of this is putting the needs of the complainant first."

Sarah told RNZ Corrections treated her "appallingly" and is happy to see it has now said it failed her.

"Yes, you did. Finally you admit that you failed me. But does that make anything that happened better?"

She initially reached out to RNZ about her complaint after reading coverage about other workplace investigations at Corrections.

She wanted people to know about what happened in her situation.

"Like I have said time and time again from the report that Corrections brought out that they have treated me like I was a young, dumb mum who didn't understand the workplace, and that the things that had happened to me were normal things that happened in the workplace, that I complained about, that I shouldn't have."

In relation to the independent review of the complaints, Sarah said that for so long she was made to doubt herself "again and again".

"It was my support system that had to remind me, I wasn't crazy, it was wrong, and I was correct for reporting it," she says.

"Finally, this is recognition from them, that I wasn't silly and small and insignificant, I was a strong woman for speaking my truth.

World.title: Costco megastore step closer in Christchurch
World.content:
Audio player for " Costco could be heading to Christchurch " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/1916845%2Fcostco-megastore-step-closer-in-christchurch

Costco could be heading to Christchurch Morning Report Download MP3 4m

A Costco megastore in Christchurch is a step closer with the government giving the US-based company the go-ahead to lodge a fast-track application.

Minister Tama Potaka said Costco's referral application for the planned development has been approved.

"A referral application is a request for the Minister to consider whether a project should enter the Fast-track approvals process," he said in a statement.

The proposed Costco would be built between Avonhead Road and Memorial Avenue.

Costco would now need to submit a substantive application and provide additional information, Potaka said.

John Plato who is the co-founder of Christchurch marketing and advertising agency Plato told Morning Report that having a Costco in Christchurch would be "massive".

"It's really just another feather in the cap for Christchurch, you know being able to attract international investment of that scale, so I think it's hugely exciting for the city."

World.title: What we learnt from a rough and tumble finance debate
World.content:
Audio player for " Six parties clash over the economy at Queenstown debate " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/1905390%2Fwhat-we-learnt-from-a-rough-and-tumble-finance-debate

Six parties clash over the economy at Queenstown debate Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Analysis - National's Nicola Willis and Labour's Barbara Edmonds turned up to Queenstown ready for a bit of rough and tumble on Wednesday evening.

The ASB Great debate featuring cross-party finance spokespeople has a history of getting a bit rowdy, and while it's often the large audience responsible for a lot of that, this year it was the panelists leading the charge.

In addition to Willis and Edmonds the 800-strong southern crowd got served up Act's David Seymour, New Zealand First's Shane Jones, the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick, and newcomer Qiulae Wong of the Opportunity party.

Stood side-by-side in the middle of the panel of five, Willis and Edmonds scrapped it out about the government's Investment Boost and Labour's plan to scrap it and replace it with a policy that targets small businesses.

Debate moderator TVNZ's Jack Tame asked Edmonds what a business like Coronet Peak, which has benefitted from Investment Boost's tax support for businesses would do without it, Edmonds fired back "I don't have to copy Nicola, we are two very different people" to huge applause from the crowd.

In an unusual twist, Swarbrick and Jones paired up regularly throughout the debate, and were highly amused by the scrap playing out in the middle of the panel, leading Jones to pipe up and suggest the Green co-leader "offer some clarity".

Edmonds held her ground against Willis however, saying in her opening remarks she would be the next finance minister: "Not Chlöe Swarbrick and not Nicola Willis - Barbara Edmonds the MP for Kenepuru will be."

Seymour summarised the Willis and Edmonds showdown saying: "It's like two bald men fighting over a comb in the middle there."

Jones also received some big laughs in his opening remarks when he detailed how slow and clogged up the economy had become, shouting: "Look at my beloved fast-track, it's turned into a constipated beast."

Tax was also a big talking point with Wong, Edmonds, and Swarbrick given a shot at pitching their respective land, capital gains, and wealth tax proposals to the audience.

The debate descended into sledges and lots of shouting as Willis and Seymour took their turns picking holes in them all.

Swarbrick revved up at Willis, who said Labour would introduce a capital gains tax (CGT) and Swarbrick who wants a wealth tax would "kick the door wide open" and expand it.

Given an opportunity to respond, Swarbrick harked back "to a time even I can remember" when National criticised the international visitor levy, only to then increase it when in government.

Seymour was highly amused by that, quipping: "I love how Chlöe said she was old enough to remember something that happened in 2018."

A new coalition also came out of the tax debate when Wong, Edmonds, Jones and Swarbrick were all asked whether they would support a bed tax for Queenstown if in government, and it was a unanimous yes from them all, much to the delight of the crowd.

Another big laugh came when Willis and Seymour were in the thick of a debate on breaking up the supermarkets and Jones interrupted to say: "Now you know what our Cabinet meetings are like."

Seymour - not one to miss an opportunity - replied: "One person has to bring the basic economics to Cabinet, that's exactly what it's like!"

One of the final topics rounding out the debate was the issue of superannuation and how the country will afford it in years to come.

All of the politicians were asked if they supported being part of a cross-party review on the country's retirement future.

Seymour said he would entertain it with a yes, but noted he was disappointed it wasn't a big feature of the debate overall, given what a significant issue it is.

Wong was supportive, saying Opportunity needed to be in Parliament and in the room "to be the broker in a heated environment where people don't agree and have proven not to hold themselves accountable to long-term plans".

Edmonds acknowledged Willis who had agreed to the idea with her at the weekend. Willis returned that and said she too wanted to celebrate Edmonds on that front but added she was disappointed the conversation hadn't happened during this term, which she blamed on Labour.

Swarbrick was also in the 'yes' camp but said the "missing piece" in this election was also talking about investment in climate change adaptation and planning.

World.title: Here's where house prices have risen fastest over 10 years
World.content:
Audio player for " Do I know enough about my financial state to retire? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/1913511%2Fhere-s-where-house-prices-have-risen-fastest-over-10-years

Do I know enough about my financial state to retire? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 17m

Increased supply of housing into Auckland has meant its house price growth has stalled over the past 10 years compared to the rest of the country, Cotality says.

It has released new research that shows the 10-year growth rate of prices around the country, as well as how far they are from their post-Covid peaks.

Mackenzie District had the highest fastest growth, up 125 percent over 10 years and now back to its peak price.

But the Auckland districts were at the bottom of the table.

Waitakere was up just 9 percent over 10 years and was 26 percent below the peak.

Central Auckland prices were up 10 percent over 10 years and still 27 percent below the peak.

North Shore was up 10 percent over 10 years, too, and still 21 percent below the peak.

Audio player for " Susan Edmunds on Auckland's housing supply and prices " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/1913511%2Fhere-s-where-house-prices-have-risen-fastest-over-10-years

Susan Edmunds on Auckland's housing supply and prices Morning Report Download MP3 2m

Parts of Wellington were similarly off their 2022 highs but had experienced faster growth over 10 years.

Lower Hutt, for example, was up 50 percent over 10 years but down 29 percent from the peak.

"When you look at how supply has changed in Auckland relative to the population over the past seven, eight, nine years, it's been striking that housing supply has adjusted and lo and behold there's been some pretty subdued house price growth," Cotality chief property economist Kelvin Davidson said.

SUPPLIED

"Aside from the migration spike in 2023, housing stock growth has consistently outpaced Auckland's population since 2018 which was also when the unitary plan was enacted. In that light, it's no surprise to see that Auckland is at the bottom of the list in terms of value growth over the past 10 years."

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said that was probably part of it, but Auckland had also been through a deeper recession than many other parts of the country, and net migration had dropped. Auckland was usually more affected by population growth from migration than other parts of the country.

Davidson said it might be sensible for New Zealanders to reframe the discussion away from how far from the peak prices still were.

For the people responsible for roughly 80,000 transactions that happened at that peak time, the drop since then would be important. But for the owners of the remaining 95 percent of housing stock, prices might still be higher than when they purchased.

Davidson said the national median property measure by Cotality's figures was 19 percent below the peak but 37 percent higher than 10 years ago.

Within that, 12 areas had values double since 2016, an annual average of 7 percent growth, or more.

"Whanganui and Gisborne, as examples, have both seen large falls from the peak yet have still shown those significant longer - term gains. By contrast, markets such as Ashburton and Christchurch are within 1 percent of their previous peak, yet they haven't risen nearly as much over the past 10 years - 48 percent and 58 percent.

"That is to say, focusing mostly on the change from the peak means losing the longer - term context in many cases. Meanwhile, even for buyers at the peak, it's also worth noting that if they're still servicing the debt, there's also less to be concerned about. Indeed, low mortgage arrears and mortgagee sales volumes show that the vast majority of people are faring well on this front."

He said he thought house price growth would be slower in future.

"Both major parties have committed to reform around land planning and resource management … it feels as if supply might not be such a concern in future. Once people start to believe that housing supply will always be more responsive, they probably pare back their expectations for house price growth, too."

World.title: ParaMatildas hunt more Australian football history at World Cup
World.content:
The ParaMatildas begin the 2026 IFCPF World Cup in uncharted territory for an Australian football team.

At the 2024 tournament in Spain, the side broke through as the nation's first-ever winner of a round ball World Cup.

Now, the players are aiming to become the first Australian team to successfully defend a world title.

It has been a rapid ascent for the side, only officially launched in 2022, but coach Charlotte Ercil said her players were comfortable with added expectation.

"I think it adds a little bit of pressure, but it's exciting at the same time," Ercil told ABC Sport.

"But we always prepare like every game, including our first group game, is the World Cup final."

The ParaMatildas became Australia's first football World Cup winners in 2024. (Supplied)

The ParaMatildas, and their male counterparts, the Pararoos, play football designed for athletes with cerebral palsy, acquired brain injury and symptoms of stroke.

The sport features smaller fields and goals as well as shorter halves than in the mainstream game and does not include the offside rule.

This month's tournament in the US city of Atlanta will be just the third instalment of the Women's World Cup and the first edition to be held outside Spain, while the Pararoos are hopeful of a best-ever finish in the concurrently running men's competition.

In the brief international history of the women's game, Australia and the US have emerged as its two great powers, with the ParaMatildas going down to the stars and stripes in the final of the 2022 tournament before exacting revenge in the 2024 decider.

The ParaMatildas have enjoyed rapid growth since officially launching in 2022. (Getty Images: Con Chronis)

Getting one over the Americans in their own backyard looms as the ultimate test for the ParaMatildas, and Australia central defender Eloise Northam does not doubt the hosts' motivation to reclaim their crown.

"I feel like they definitely are plotting against us," Northam told ABC Sport.

"I think that's what we were doing back in like the second World Cup — we were ready to take on the US and take their championship away from them."

The ParaMatildas are also wary of the sport's expanding talent pool. The growth of the global game means that teams and tactics are evolving rapidly, while players with newly acquired brain injuries are constantly welcomed into the fold.

Australia will face Ireland, the Netherlands and newcomers Colombia during the group stage.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

"Every year or every time we interact with or play against any country, there are always changes and improvements, which is good for the game; it means it's growing," coach Ercil said.

Throw in lingering summer temperatures as well as the possibility of severe thunderstorms, and the ParaMatildas are taking nothing for granted in the American south.

The Pararoos, meanwhile, are bullish on progressing from a difficult group featuring Brazil, Spain and Chile.

The Australian squad for the tournament comes with bucketloads of experience, with 11 of the 14 players selected having previous World Cup experience.

Taj Lynch hopes the Pararoos can progress from a difficult group. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

One of those returning athletes is Taj Lynch, who believed his side was now well placed for a breakthrough top-10 finish.

"I feel confident in the players we're taking across; a lot of us have been there before," Lynch told ABC Sport.

"We've learned a lot, we've got a lot of things wrong, but we've grown, and we've improved.

"We're not a team of boys playing against men anymore. I think we're finally starting to be a team of men who can take on the best teams in the world."

Captaining the Pararoos in Atlanta is Australian football legend David Barber.

The veteran debuted for Australia in 1999, and will overtake Andorra's Ildefons Lima as the male player with the longest international football career when he steps out for the Pararoos' tournament opener against Brazil.

World.title: Walters explains choice of Walsh over Tedesco for World Cup opener
World.content:
Kevin Walters has declared the battle for Australia's fullback berth remains wide open despite Reece Walsh winning the nod over James Tedesco to start in the Kangaroos' World Cup opener.

Walters claimed ahead of Thursday night's clash with New Zealand that Tedesco, the captain as Australia lifted the trophy four years ago, would have a chance to prove his worth in the group-stage game against Fiji in Brisbane on October 25.

Walsh, the hero of last year's Ashes whitewash, will don the No.1 jersey at Sydney's Allianz Stadium, but as for whether the Brisbane Broncos star will be first choice later in the tournament, Walters is keeping an open mind.

Less can be more for Rugby League World Cup The Rugby League World Cup exists in a constant state of change but ahead of the tournament opener between Australia and New Zealand the much-maligned tournament can prove less can be more.

The Kangaroos coach indicated he had chosen to rest Tedesco and playmaker halfback Sam Walker following their exploits in the Sydney Roosters' NRL grand final win.

"I feel it's in the best interest of the team they get a spell this week and they'll play next week," Walters said on Wednesday.

"To be honest, I haven't decided that (fullback) position yet, that's why we're here, and they'll both get an opportunity.

"They're both Clive Churchill medallists, the last two, so I look at it that way. I'm very fortunate to have both of them in the team.

"They're different players, but I love what they both bring to the team. Teddy's the more experienced custodian and Reece is on the way up as such."

Walsh has retained his place after his heroics in last year's Ashes. (Getty Images: PA Images/Mike Egerton)

The one drawback to Walsh is his fitness, with Thursday's opener his first competitive match in close to two months after sustaining an ankle injury in clubland.

"He (Walsh) has had a good preparation and there's a few players in that position themselves, so it's good to get them around the group," Walters said.

Walsh will be part of a relatively settled Kangaroos spine, with Cameron Munster at five-eighth and Harry Grant at hooker.

Halfback Mitchell Moses is the only new addition to the key playmaking roles.

Moses was on last year's Ashes tour but didn't take the field, with the Parramatta skipper an understudy to Nathan Cleary, who has missed this World Cup following his compound ankle fracture.

Tedesco last played for Australia in 2023. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

"He's a very influential player, an experienced player, particularly his kicking game around the halves will be invaluable," Walters said.

"He gets his opportunity and I'm sure he's looking forward to taking it as well.

"They (Munster and Moses) are very calm and know what we need to do in different situations."

The Kangaroos have not lost to New Zealand on Australian soil since 2015, and while the Kiwis have a monster forward pack, Walters insists his side have the firepower to match them.

"It's a strong New Zealand side, certainly, but I feel like the guys that we have picked in the Australian squad, they're not mugs," the Kangaroos coach added.

"We've got Origin players, Test players, premiership winners, that's what the World Cup is all about: seeing the best players on the world stage."

AAP

World.title: Roos miss out as Dees, Dons and Eagles complete dramatic deadline day trades
World.content:
Adelaide defender Nick Murray has been left stranded as the AFL trade period drew to a close with a flurry of late deals.

Despite offering the Crows a raft of trade offers as the deadline approached, the Kangaroos were unable to pry Murray away from the South Australians.

Murray's failed move came as Essendon and Brisbane reached an agreement to send Keidean Coleman to the Bombers, while the Lions also sent Will McLachlan to Melbourne in a three-team deal that saw premiership duo Trent Rivers and Jack Viney head to West Coast.

Six players were moved inside the final half an hour of the trade period after the first four hours of the final day saw just three pick swaps, with one of those netting Richmond a second top five pick in this year's draft.

Follow the live blog below for a recap of all the trade deadline action as it happened.

World.title: Afghan batter recreates infamous hamstring injury used against Australia
World.content:
Sediqullah Atal's maiden Test century has led Afghanistan to an epic draw against Bangladesh in a one-off cricket Test.

Afghanistan batted for 142 overs, 92 on the fifth and final day, in its second innings to force a sensational draw on Tuesday. It began the day on a dodgy 132-3, lost five more wickets, but fought on to hold out to stumps at 346-8.

But it was the actions of number nine Qais Ahmad in the dying minutes that drew the most attention in the match's final act.

With the finish line in sight and just two wickets left, Ahmad played a forward defence to spinner Taijul Islam before collapsing to the ground clutching his hamstring.

The Bangladesh team was not impressed, and had commentator Ahmad Farhad Fidai in stitches as he likened it to the actions of Afghanistan's Gulbadin Naib, who suffered a suspicious cramp fielding at slip in their famous 2024 T20 World Cup win over Australia.

"Qais Ahmad does it again. This reminds me of Gulbadin Naib," an amused Fidai said, clearly believing Ahmad's fall to the turf was nothing more than time-wasting antics.

"Oh boy, not again.

"You really don't need to see the replay; we can understand from here what's going on."

Ahmad soldiered on and finished the match with a six over midwicket.

Bangladesh dominated the match after winning the toss and batting first. Bangladesh earned a first-innings lead of 106 runs, then declared its second innings at 7-372 after player-of-the-match Litton Das was out for 102. That gave Bangladesh an imposing lead of 478 and four and a half sessions to bowl out Afghanistan.

But Afghanistan defied the odds despite losing two wickets in the first seven overs on Monday.

First drop Atal, in his third Test, ate up most of the chase as he faced 332 balls over 8.5 hours to score 111. He was caught close to the wicket after tea, the seventh man out.

Afghanistan still had 23 overs with just tailenders left. But 34-year-old Yamin Ahmadzai faced 85 balls for a career-best 19, and Ahmad, who has played franchise cricket in eight countries, faced 80 to finish with an unbeaten career-best 49.

AP/ABC

World.title: Less can be more for Rugby League World Cup
World.content:
The only things that stay the same about the Rugby League World Cup are that it never stops changing and it continually has to justify its own existence.

For the third tournament in a row, there will be a different format and a different number of teams, dropping from 16 to 10, and for the umpteenth tournament in a row, the sceptics will question why it's worth playing a Rugby League World Cup at all and compare it unfavourably to the rugby and football versions.

Those world cups exist in different universes than the league equivalent, even as nation-swapping and diaspora-heavy squads, two hallmarks of the much-maligned international rugby league, become more prevalent in their larger cousins.

The Rugby League World Cup has to prove itself anew every four years. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Measure the Rugby League World Cup against those that dwarf it in scale and it will always be miles behind. It is playing a different game, one that is carving out a place all its own.

On the back of the rise of Tonga and Samoa over the past 10 years, Test football is at its strongest and most vibrant in years, with the two Pasifika nations emerging as legitimate draws and top-class teams.

Tonga's two matches against Australia in the 2024 Pacific Championships drew crowds of more than 33,000 and 28,000, and both Tonga and Samoa have made their first tours to England since the last World Cup.

When the ancient island rivals went head-to-head in Brisbane last year, more than 40,000 came through the gates, the second-largest non-World Cup final crowd for a Test in Australia in the last half-century.

Samoa creates rugby league magic The passion of the Pacific shines through in Samoa's rugby league team, and the pride the people have is evident on the island.

A similar attendance is expected for the tournament opener between Australia and New Zealand on Thursday night, and if the Sydney Football Stadium can sell out, it'll be the biggest Test crowd in Sydney since 1974.

It marks the beginning of a chance for the Rugby League World Cup to reshape itself a little more permanently and take advantage of the renewed interest by recasting itself as a pinnacle for the game rather than a starting point.

Rugby league had to make a choice whether its World Cup was a beginning or an end, a proving ground for developing nations or a battleground for the best, because it could not be both at the same time.

At the sharp end of recent tournaments, when it's the best teams in the world having it out, the product is reliably compelling, rich and powerful. The problem is it's just taken too long to get there.

In 2022, there was a crackerjack knockout phase, highlighted by Samoa's epic win over Tonga in Warrington, New Zealand sneaking home against Fiji in Hull, and two brilliant semifinals, including a golden point epic that doubles as one of the best games in the tournament's history.

The night a rag-tag group of rugby league Russians took on the world champions Russia might only make one trip to the Rugby League World Cup but the memories forged in the 2000 tournament, especially in their record loss to Australia, are wild enough to last a lifetime.

But the group stage was a forgone conclusion almost all the way. Only two of the 24 preliminary matches were decided by one score or less. There were 10 scores over 60 and two scores over 90.

Australia's 110-4 massacre of Russia in 2000 remained untouched as the most lopsided result in World Cup history, but matches from 2022 fill out the second, third and fourth spots on that list.

Developing nations have their place in the international rugby league and the emotional scenes upon qualification for Jamaica, or Greece's epic tale of playing qualifying matches on the edge of war zones and in undisclosed locations to stay one step ahead of the authorities, are proof of the value developing nations can bring.

But it is hard to see the benefits of England nearly putting 100 points on the Greeks, or a disinterested Australia beating Scotland 84-0.

The trickle-down effects of those games, such as they are, can take decades to rise to the surface, if they ever do at all.

The knockout phase of recent World Cups have been rugby league dynamite. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

The game's wholehearted embrace of the set restart rule and the increased speed of play makes it harder for the smaller nations to compete on a physical level, and the perfunctory nature of the group stages makes the tournament even longer.

In a world where fan interest and player fatigue are already being stretched to their limits, it adds even more to an already overstuffed season.

So while it may not please the true believers, the move to 10 teams is a good one. This tournament is leaner and has the potential to be meaner.

The lack of northern hemisphere teams — it's just England, France and Lebanon, with none from the Americas and no other home nations after Scotland and Ireland were demoted to affiliate status and Wales failed to qualify — is regrettable, but exclusivity cuts both ways because less can be more.

This is a tournament with barely any fat on it, and as a result, it's as open at the top as it's ever been.

Australia is still the favourite because such is the largesse of talent available that it's almost impossible to name a Kangaroos team that isn't oozing with class, but it's far from invulnerable.

Its talent pool has been diluted, and there are several squad members who are coming off indifferent or underdone seasons.

Some have made it due to coach Kevin Walters's loyalty to the side that retained the Ashes in a 3-0 whitewash last year, but others are in because there's a lack of other options as the eligibility rules slowly spread the talent around.

Nobody has benefited more from that spread than New Zealand, who welcome Kalyn Ponga to the squad for his belated Test debut as the herald of a new era.

On paper, it's a better side than the one that handed Australia its biggest-ever defeat just three years ago — it has all three middles from this season's Dally M Team of the Year — and a second World Cup title is a distinct possibility.

The bookies have Samoa and Tonga as equal-third favourites to make the final, well ahead of England, and their group-stage clash at Parramatta Stadium has been sold out for months.

Samoa and Tonga have already sold out their group stage match. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

The English have a little more to prove after last year's lacklustre Ashes showing, an embrace of heritage players that has divided their fan base and the controversial exclusion of Leeds halfback Jake Connor from the squad.

Outside the top five, there's still plenty to follow. Write off the perennially underrated Fijians, who beat New Zealand in 2017 and came within six points of doing the same in 2022, off at your peril.

France and Lebanon won't be as dangerous, but the French have 20 homegrown players in their squad and 10 of Lebanon's starting 13 for their first game have NRL experience.

Even the Cook Islands, which will play in front of crowds that dwarf its home's population, will have Cronulla's KL Iro and former Kangaroo Valentine Holmes to call upon.

Another Australian victory is far from a guarantee in this World Cup. (Jan Kruger: Getty Images for RLWC)

Injuries have robbed Papua New Guinea of some of their biggest names, but their group matches against Samoa and Lebanon will be the Kumuls' biggest on home soil since the PNG Chiefs were admitted to the NRL and shape as the first dress rehearsals for what awaits the game in the land where they love it most.

Through it all, this World Cup can have it all. There will still be stories of paupers taking on princes against all odds and of the unbridled passion and pride that has kept international football alive despite the many obstacles.

Those tales and teams will always have their place, but for the most part, this tournament will be collections of top-level rugby league talent crashing into each other in the fast until only the world champions are left to rise from the wreckage.

What the tournament gives up in diversity and novelty, it can win back in quality, because at some point, a World Cup has to be about the best of the best being at their best, and there are more nations who can dream of that than ever before.

Never in the World Cup's 72-year history has the sky seemed so open. Ten teams might not seem like many, but if five have designs on the crown, it can be plenty.

World.title: F1 returns to Africa with Rwanda signing 10-year deal
World.content:
Africa will return to the Formula 1 calendar for the first time since 1993 with Rwanda set to host a grand prix from the early 2030s in a 10-year deal.

Formula 1 last raced on the continent at South Africa's Kyalami Circuit to the north of Johannesburg and has long sought a way back.

The race will be called the African Grand Prix, and held at a circuit that is yet to be built alongside a new international airport under construction at Bugesera, about 40 kilometres south of the capital Kigali.

"Today is a landmark moment for Formula 1," F1 chief executive Stefano Domenicali said at a press conference with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and International Automobile Federation (FIA) head Mohammed Ben Sulayem on Tuesday.

"With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the world championship closer than ever to fans around the globe.

"Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact."

Kagame announced his landlocked East African country's bid two years ago.

The purpose-built grade one track, designed by Austrian former driver Alex Wurz with long-time F1 architect Tilke also involved, is expected to be completed early in the next decade and be fast and flowing with significant changes of elevation and putting spectators close to the action.

Rwanda Development Board chief executive Jean-Guy Afrika said the track would have a 100,000 capacity and also be a multi-purpose facility with year-round utilisation as a concert and exhibition venue.

"We want to make it bigger than just Rwanda. We want to make it the moment when the sport came back to Africa and then never left," he told a press conference, adding that the initiative would likely be "powered by the private sector and coordinated by the government".

Rwanda will be the third African country to host a round of the championship since the start in 1950, with Morocco putting on a race outside Casablanca in 1958.

Reuters

World.title: De Minaur sets up Shanghai quarterfinal with Zverev
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has taken a giant stride towards clinching another ATP Finals berth after roaring into the last eight of the Shanghai Masters.

Continuing to defy the hip flexor injury that threatened to end his season less than a week ago, de Minaur downed dual grand slam semifinalist Karen Khachanov 6-3, 6-4 to jump to seventh place in the Race to Turin's live standings.

Crucially, Australia's baseline warrior has leapfrogged Novak Djokovic and Frances Tiafoe, who have already been eliminated in China, as he chases more valuable rankings points in the quarter-finals — and potentially beyond.

De Minaur retires injured, handing China Open title to Djokovic Alex de Minaur says he did not want his Beijing campaign to end in the way it did, with injury forcing the Australian to retire early in the second set.

But Alexander Zvererv, who will be the year-end world number one, stands in his way after the German beat Alexander Bublik 7-6(6), 4-6, 7-6(1).

In his fifth encounter against Khachanov, de Minaur knew efficiency was key.

"It was really important for me to serve well and I think I definitely did that, especially down the stretch," he said.

"I got into a little bit of trouble, a couple of love-30 games, and I was able to find some good serves when I needed it."

De Minaur, who reached the semi-finals at the prestigious season-ending tournament last year, cut a forlorn figure after being forced to retire early in the second set of last week's China Open final against Djokovic, when a set down.

His comeback has been nothing short of remarkable.

"Ultimately I've been getting better and better every day," the 27-year-old said.

"Today was by far my best match and I think that I'm only going to get better.

"I know that once I'm fit physically and mentally, I'm the player that I [want to be] and I'm excited to be competing and going to the tail end of these tournaments and feeling great about myself."

Despite a 4-8 record against Zverev, de Minaur prevailed in their past two meetings, both at Laver Cup, including two weeks ago. Zverev has fitness problems of his own.

"My ankle was acting up, unfortunately," Zverev said, who saved three set points against Bublik in the first-set tiebreak.

"It was understandable because I have been playing a lot of tennis, which is kind of a good sign because I have been playing well. I am starting to feel my body more and more but I am happy to get through."

AAP

World.title: Regulator says he would quit over political influence in Man City scandal
World.content:
The chair of English football's regulatory body says he would resign if any political interference affected potential sanctions against Manchester City.

City has been found guilty of widespread breaches of the Premier League's financial rules, which could result in punishments including a massive fine, points deductions or even expulsion from England's top flight.

Separately, the Independent Football Regulator can force club owners to sell and can withhold a license to operate if it deems them unfit.

An independent panel found the United Arab Emirates-backed City had artificially inflated its revenue by more than $1 billion over nearly a decade, circumventing fair-play rules.

Loading...

Football regulator chair David Kogan said it was still awaiting the outcome of City's appeal against the verdict.

The UAE is a big investor in the UK. Asked about the regulator's ability to remain independent given wider relations between the governments, Kogan said: "Any form of political interference in the way we operate is going to result in my resigning from this role, and I stand by that completely.

"We've come under absolutely no political pressure whatsoever on this or any other topic. And I don't expect to in the future," he said.

Kogan's comments came after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would be "really concerned" to lose City's current ownership. Mr Burnham also said he would not get "directly involved in the process."

City is accused of providing misleading information about its finances over a nine-year period from 2009-18. During that time, it won three titles and signed some of the world's best players. It went on to enjoy a period of unprecedented dominance of English soccer.

The guilty verdict marks the biggest scandal in Premier League history and raises questions about the club's future, owned by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates and a member of Abu Dhabi's royal family.

Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan owns Manchester City. (Reuters: Ameer Al-Mohammedawi/Pool)

The British government established the Independent Football Regulatory Commission last year to set governance standards in English soccer.

Part of that includes the issuing of licenses for clubs to be able to operate, which will begin in November.

Kogan suggested the guilty verdict would not affect issuing a license to City because its appeal is ongoing.

"A verdict once it's gone through an appeal process will certainly be something that we would clearly be taking into account when looking at awarding a license or looking at the owners, directors and senior executives," he said.

Majority of English clubs are loss-making

Kogan was speaking in Manchester about the regulator's "State of the Game" report on English soccer.

The report states that despite the success of English soccer — including the Premier League, the world's richest and most popular league — 94 per cent of clubs across the pyramid are loss-making, and more than a quarter would be unable to survive more than 30 days if owners pulled funding.

It says a major problem is teams spending too much to keep up with rivals.

"At the heart of English football's success is a massive contradiction. While some of our clubs are among the richest and most competitive in the world, others are standing on the edge of financial disaster," Kogan said.

"This lack of resilience can no longer be ignored."

Seventeen clubs "would be loss-making even if their players played for free," the regulator's CEO Richard Monks said.

"Owners in many football clubs will inject the money two or three days before payday and not keep any cash in the club. This is not how most businesses are run, and it's a major issue which we will require football to address."

The regulator has been involved in negotiations between the Premier League and the English Football League regarding what are known as solidarity payments to help develop England's lower leagues. That includes parachute payments to teams relegated from the top flight.

The regulator is proposing to spread those payments more evenly among teams. It is part of a suite of proposals, including measures to help clubs improve financial risk management.
