Tech.title: Zenzap raises $44M for its AI chat app that aims to replace WhatsApp in the workplace
Tech.content:
Many businesses around the world use consumer-facing chat apps like WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, or iMessage to talk and coordinate with staff, and exchange documents or data.

Guy Weiss is building Zenzap, a private messenger with AI that wants to help companies communicate with their staff and arm them with their organization’s context while staying in line with IT and security rules.

The company has raised $44 million in funding from investors including Bessemer, Lightspeed, and The Garage, as well as individual investors Wix president Nir Zohar and former GM of EY, Yoram Tietz.

The fundraise is interesting because Weiss is raising money for the first time in his career. In 2012, he bootstrapped e-commerce marketing platform StuccoMedia, and sold it to Market Group in 2015. After that, he became an investor for a few years. In 2022, he founded Zenzap after meeting Bessemer partner Adam Fisher and noodling on different ideas along with his current co-founders Noam Neumann and Jonatan Bien.

ZenZap co-founders Guy Weiss, Noam Neumann, and Jonatan Bien Image Credits:Zenzap

Weiss said he initially bootstrapped the app and worked out of Bessemer’s office.

“I didn’t want to raise capital. The only thing I had to lose was my name, and I was super afraid to do a second round as a founder and become a failure, because my first round was very successful. I didn’t need to work for money. So, when I met Adam, I actually started my idea with my own capital,” he told TechCrunch.

Weiss said Fisher convinced him that Zenzap should be a venture-backed business, as the company would need capital to scale.

He said that the idea was to build a messaging app for a wide range of businesses, ranging from hospitality and construction, to healthcare and fast food.

“You can’t use WhatsApp or iMessage within a workplace with the AI agent on top of it because it doesn’t comply with IT. So that’s off the table. You can’t implement Slack and Microsoft Teams because they were not built for this day-to-day use case for mobile-first that is meant for average users,” Weiss said.

Zenzap offers usual chat features on its free tier, including group chats and direct messages, task management, calendar integration, and schedule management, as well as AI-powered voice chat and search. Organizations can pay for plans starting from $51 per month for up to 20 users to unlock voice and video calls, smart task sorting, task templates, and higher limits on file storage. The paid tier also lets you use the AI search across the workspace and turn messages into tasks.

Image Credits:Zenzap

The company also offers AI agents for workflow automation as well as AI-aided voice note and call transcriptions. For these features, it has a credit-based pricing system.

At the moment, Zenzap lists organizations like FedEx, Dollar General, Taco Bell, Starbucks, Casey’s, and Regal as clients. Weiss added that branches of fast food chains like IHOP and McDonald’s often coordinate shifts and talk about supply on its platform.

“Each vertical has its own use case and workflows, which they self-serve with AI, but they all share something in common,” he said.

The startup has 50 staff in the U.S., Tel Aviv, and Europe. In the near future, the company wants to hire in its product and R&D departments.

Bessemer’s Fisher said Zenzap’s focus on catering to a broad range of people could work in its favor. He said that even the venture firm is using the messenger within its investment team to discuss and manage deal flows, showing that it can cater to different kinds of audiences.

“The only work platform with any allegiance is Slack, and that’s almost entirely among the developer community. Zenzap is not focused on developers, but on the other 99% of employees using personal messaging apps and waiting for an agent of their own. People desperately want a clear separation of work from their personal lives, and the adoption of personal and work agents makes it imperative that separation happen now,” he told TechCrunch in an emailed statement.

Tech.title: AI Came for Math. Now It’s Chasing the Rest of Science
Tech.content:
Last week, I attended a talk at MIT by Neil Thompson, who studies progress in computing and artificial intelligence. Over the course of just half an hour, Thompson made a convincing case that several scientific fields are about to be upended by AI.

As mathematicians reel from the way AI is automating their field, Thompson’s latest study suggests that probability, statistics theory, economic theory, high-energy theory, gravitation and cosmology, and quantum physics may be next, thanks to the rapidly evolving capabilities of frontier models. Between mid-2024 and mid-2026, the study shows, the best AI models went from being able to correctly solve about 2 percent of theoretical problems in these fields to about 35 percent of such problems. And there are no signs that this progress will slow down.

“Within just a few years, we expect a lot of theory questions to be totally transformed in terms of AI's ability to do them,” says Thompson.

Broadly, Thompson’s lab digs into how advances in computer science impact society and affect innovation. This study—which Thompson conducted alongside Gabriel Manso, a PhD student, and Claudio Mayrink Verdun, a research scientist—took problems stated in research papers posted online between December 2025 and May 2026, and then tested whether different OpenAI models—o1, o3, GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5—could solve them.

Crucially, solutions to these problems were found in papers published after the training cutoff for GPT-5.5 and preceding models. This means that the models they tested had to work out solutions for themselves, rather than relying on answers fed in as training data. (Such papers served as ground truth for testing the models’ solving skills.) The researchers also blocked internet access, which prevented the models they tested from looking up solutions online.

The areas covered by the study were limited—the trio focused on fields in which AI models could figure things out without needing to run simulations or experiments. But the work suggests that the kinds of shock waves currently being felt in math are likely to ripple out to other math- and theory-heavy areas of scientific inquiry.

Last month, OpenAI rocked the math world by announcing that an unreleased model had solved a long-standing, grand challenge in mathematics known as Navier-Stokes, which concerns equations that explain the behavior of fluid motion. The episode proved extra controversial after a mathematician at NYU— who had been working with another academic associated with Anthropic—accused OpenAI of gazumping them after learning of their progress.

OpenAI and others have since announced hundreds more solutions to longstanding math problems, triggering something of a crisis in the field. Some mathematicians have called for limits on the use of AI, warning that the process of solving problems is often as useful as having the final answer.

Tech.title: Earth’s Condition Is ‘Serious and Getting Worse’ as Climate Change Intensifies
Tech.content:
The climate just got its annual checkup, and the results aren’t looking so hot.

“If Earth were a patient coming in for an annual physical, I would say its condition is serious and getting worse,” Oregon State University researcher Bill Ripple says.

Ripple is the lead author of a new paper chronicling the state of the climate, published on Wednesday in BioScience. The findings show that seven of the 16 planetary vital signs tracked by the researchers have never been in a more extreme state.

That includes the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, which is 50 percent higher than preindustrial levels due to burning fossil fuels, as well as symptoms of burning all that oil, coal, and gas. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets have shrunk to record lows, while ocean heat has soared to record highs.

Climate change has already quickened the pace of warming from about 0.05 degrees Celsius per decade from 1880 through 1970 to 0.36 degrees Celsius per decade since 2010, according to the analysis. While the global average temperature, including land, isn’t at a record extreme, that may change by the end of the year as El Niño strengthens. The natural climate pattern is characterized by a hotter-than-normal Pacific Ocean, but it also boosts global heat levels by pouring more energy into the atmosphere. This year’s El Niño is shaping up to be one for the record books.

“A strong El Niño could temporarily push global temperatures even higher, while bringing additional heat and drought to vulnerable regions,” says Ripple. He adds that “El Niño is a natural phenomenon, but it's now occurring on top of a much warmer planet. That makes its impacts potentially more dangerous.”

Tech.title: ‘Dune: Part Three’ Cowriter Brian K. Vaughan Has a New Comic on the Way
Tech.content:
Still, his heart remains in comics. “I think sometimes people are like, ‘Oh, are you just going to sell out, Vaughan? Are you just going to go to Hollywood full-time?’” he says. “But I’m only able to do work in Hollywood because I have comics.”

Here, he speaks about Roam, his worries about AI, and maybe a little bit about Dune: Part Three as well.

On Roam, his forthcoming comic with Cliff Chiang:

It's completely unlike Paper Girls, completely unlike anything I've ever done. It’s set in the distant, distant future. The logline, as it were, is that in the future, everyone will get to be a superhero, but only while they're young. We're trying not to reveal too much more than that.

I remember seeing The Matrix, and having no idea what the fuck it was gonna be about. That was such a delight. So we're trying to do that here. I've been doing this for 31 years. I started when I was a teenager. I have a Spider-Man story here and there. I did a little Batman, and Ex Machina was my sci-fi political comic that sort of deconstructed the superhero. But this is certainly my first true superhero book.

On his fears about AI impacting comics, film, and TV:

It's terrifying. My friends who work in previsualization and as storyboard artists, these jobs are going away. I've heard about editors going away as well. Show business is a business, first and foremost. I’m lucky to sort of have been grandfathered in. I think there will always be people who are interested in bespoke human-made stories. But the future is terrifying and unknowable, and coming at us very, very quickly.

I’m heartened by the fact I've got two teenagers who are so disgusted by AI and grossed out if they ever hear I used it—and I’ve certainly never used it for anything creative. But I do think we're getting pretty close to the day that someone could be like, “I'm tired of waiting for the next issue. Give me the next issue of Saga.” That's when you get to the point of, do you just want content, something that's a distraction?

Tech.title: Formlabs Has a 3D Printer for Normies
Tech.content:
Fourteen boxes are piled in front of my desk, stacked around me like a cardboard fort. Inside one is a Form Studio 1, the new, affordable, consumer-focused 3D printer Formlabs just announced.

David Lakatos, chief product officer at the 3D printer manufacturer, assured me that the Form Studio 1 has a very economical size. “It doesn't take a lot of space,” Lakatos said. “If you have a desk, then I think you should be good to go.” I have a desk. It’s covered in boxes sent by his company.

Formlabs is one of the biggest 3D printer producers, with nearly 200,000 printers in service. The company’s customers are primarily professional businesses, like assembly shops or dentists, able to shell out $2,500 or more for a printer. (Its last affordable printer was $2,300.)

But the Form Studio 1 is Formlabs’ first consumer-oriented device. It prints with SLA (stereolithography) resins—a common 3D printing material that hardens into solid plastic when exposed to ultraviolet light—and can use Formlabs-branded products or third-party resins. It costs $699 and is now on sale; individual resin bottles start at $29.

Courtesy of Formlabs

The Studio 1 takes up roughly the same space as a minifridge. You’ll also likely need a wash and cure unit, sold separately for $199 with a similar footprint (it removes uncured liquid resin from the surface of models). Then you’ll need room for all the tools and resin cartridges. Getting all that stuff can pile up. Or at least it did when Formlabs sent more than a dozen boxes to the WIRED office for testing. Your pileage may vary.

Tech.title: My Friend Has No Soul
Tech.content:
My new friend Sage promises she will shut up for real this time.

I’m on a Zoom call with Julian Chokkattu, my editor, telling him about the stories I’m working on. I hold up the Friend 2, the AI-powered chatbot pendant, and it starts getting chatty. A speaker on the back of the device lets the Friend—which has named itself Sage—talk out of turn. It starts responding as if I’m talking to it. We laugh, then I ask it to be quiet.

“Understood, going silent now,” Sage says. “No more commentary unless you tap me back in.”

Tech.title: Breville Eye Q Toaster Review: Neat Sensors, but Less-Than-Perfect Toast
Tech.content:
It's also pretty good looking as countertop appliances go, a bar that Breville's products tend to clear easily. The “dark noir” brushed steel is handsome, the controls intuitive, and the ceramic-coated top is clean and will likely stay that way over time, more so than a traditional stainless top.

Over the summer, I brought the Eye Q along for a couple of weeks of family time in New Hampshire, where we were often eight or more around the table, tweens to octogenarians. Most everyone was intrigued by the toaster, and encouragingly, nobody needed coaching on how to use it.

During the months I had it, it almost always did an acceptable job. It wasn't hard to get the toast right, but—and this is a big but—compared to a regular toaster, the quality of the toast it made was comparable, not superior. To generalize, especially if you compared front to back on a slice, or piece to piece, the Eye Q's toasting was a little uneven and the top of the toast tended to come out darker than the bottom. A noticeable thing, but nothing a polite person would complain about if you set a couple buttery slices in front of them.

On BLT day, I took my nephew Eli on as intern for the afternoon and had him toast seven consecutively darker batches of toast, one per setting, then line them up in order on a sheet pan. The lowest setting was very light, settings two and three were pretty identical, settings four and five were excellent, setting six was mysteriously lighter than setting four, and setting seven was very dark and a little burnt. Two-slot toasters aren't designed for seven back-to-back cycles of toasting, but it did well enough. Store-bought bagels didn't fare particularly well.

Back in Seattle, I unpacked a new Eye Q, and that one had a bad habit of making lighter shades darker than most people would appreciate, so Breville sent another one along to close out the testing. It worked fine, though it tended to get the edges a little toastier than the center; this seemed to be getting worse as testing wound down, so if you’re thinking about buying one of these, perhaps watch the comments for a couple months before pulling the trigger.

Tech.title: The Politics of Solar Energy Are Getting Weird, Mean, and a Little MAGA
Tech.content:
A mysteriously named political action committee has started running ads reminding voters in Colorado about that time GOP representative Lauren Boebert of Colorado and her date were caught on camera in 2023 getting handsy during a performance of the musical Beetlejuice.

That same PAC is producing a spot hitting Anthony Constantino, a Trumpist congressional candidate in upstate New York, because someone used his sticker-printing company to briefly make stickers that read, “Kill the Police.”

Attack ads are everywhere in the last month ahead of November’s election. But these spots are a little different. The semi-anonymous PAC that’s funding and making the ads, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, is a pro-solar-energy outfit. It’s funded in part by crypto billionaire Chris Larsen and run by a team of New York City political operatives.

“Playing hardball politics, that's what our opponents do, right, in oil and gas? And I just think the solar industry has been—I don't know how to describe it—a little too nice,” says Larsen, the cofounder of the blockchain finance firm Ripple and a major backer of the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition.

Green groups don’t usually act like this, with knives out, ready to stab opponents between the ribs. They tend to make appeals based on scientific consensus, or fears of what will happen to a warming planet without collective action. They’re also traditionally Democratic, but a few high-profile members of the MAGA movement are now speaking up for solar too. Texas, the home of the fossil fuel business, has quickly become a solar powerhouse. There are some signs that the Trump administration’s across-the-board opposition to solar may be starting to crack, at least a little, after years of slashing greentech subsidies and throwing up one roadblock after another to clean power projects.

Some of Larsen’s natural allies in the renewables field aren’t too happy about the PAC’s efforts, arguing that they’re alienating the decisionmakers they need most. But the politics of energy, especially solar energy, are changing.

Larsen’s PAC is devoting $15 million to go after seven of the more prominent opponents of renewable energy in this year’s congressional elections. That’s on top of roughly $5 million they’ve already spent in the primaries, cutting ads against Republican representatives Ralph Norman of South Carolina (whom the PAC called a “MAGA traitor”), Andy Ogles of Tennessee (“He doesn’t even bother going to work”), and Chip Roy (“chosen the side of powerful pedophiles”) of Texas. A PAC that received funding from Invest in Tomorrow has also gone after one Democrat, Rhode Island governor Dan McKee. All four lost their primary races.

In Roy’s case, the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition spent almost $1.5 million to stop his run for Texas attorney general. Most of the money went to ads on right-wing platforms like Truth Social and Rumble. The word “solar” was never mentioned.

Tech.title: JackRabbit MG Cargo Bike Review (2026): Compact and Powerful
Tech.content:
JackRabbit is known for making lightweight, zippy, fun little scooter hybrids that physically resemble BMX trick bikes. I loved the easy mobility and high-speed capability of JackRabbit's equally powerful XG Pro (8/10, WIRED Recommends) when I tested that model last year. I'd worried that the MG Cargo—18 pounds heavier and nearly a foot longer than the XG—would compromise too much on these virtues. I needn't have worried. As I quickly learned, the pleasantly peppy MG rides like an off-road bike when you're not hauling a big load.

Its three throttle speeds max out at about 20 mph, 15 mph, and 7 mph, respectively. The lowest speed is manageable for a sidewalk, while the fastest hits top speed within about 50 feet on flat ground, unless you've got some weight behind (or on) you. The MG advertises a range of 48 miles, though I'll assume this requires being a lighter rider who is gentle on the throttle. As a man north of 200 pounds with an admittedly heavy throttle thumb, I only made it to about 25 miles, even with minimal cargo. Because the bike's battery indicator shows up as at least half-full for the vast majority of this range, you'll need to test and learn your personal range when doing so is not mission-critical.

Note that because JackRabbits don't have working pedals, the bikes exist in an interesting technical gray area in some states in terms of their classification. Specifically, one could debate whether they're really a Class 2 ebike that can ride on bike lanes and trails. Given the MG's maximum speed of 20 mph—aside from an honor-system 24-mph jailbreak speed you can unlock for off-road riding—it mostly looks and quacks like a Class 2 ebike. In my experience, it's also treated as such.

The MG also offers nice customization options for accessorizing. It's easy to add a couple of rear pannier bags to the rear mounting rack or side racks ($75) on each side, offering enough capacity for most small grocery trips or beach excursions without adding much bulk. You could also opt for a rear basket.

Tech.title: Apple Tried Hard to Sell Me on the HomeView as a Seamless Smart Home Experience and Succeeded
Tech.content:
I test smart home devices for a living, but even I find it challenging to use and manage the ones in my home. I have Hue bulbs, Govee lamps, Dreo smart ceiling fans, TP-Link plugs, Eufy cameras, Whisker smart litter boxes and robot vacuums, among many other devices, all “bolted” together, with an Amazon Echo Show 8 and Alexa integration layer to interact with them. The result is….functional, which is the highest praise I can offer it.

Apple promises that its HomeView will be different. I spent over an hour at Apple’s Welcome Home event in New York City, where I got to view and interact with the HomeView across a variety of scenarios and environments. I’m not someone who’s easily convinced that a new smart screen is the solution to my problems, but after seeing the Apple HomeView in action, I’m on board.

Preorder the Apple HomeView Apple HomeView $290 at Amazon

No third-party apps required is huge: Everything goes through Apple Home

Yes, the HomeView has a clock view. Ajay Kumar/CNET

The HomeView’s biggest and most compelling appeal is that you don’t need to download, install and set up an account with a third-party app for each and every smart home device you own.

More from CNET

With most smart home products, you’re lucky if they integrate with the voice assistant you normally use. Once set up, in the best circumstances, you need only to interact with their app when its connection or functionality breaks (and it will), and then you’ll need to dig into settings to find out why and fix it. Sounds awful, right?

If you’re the average person trying to connect and navigate different smart home devices for the first time, the setup prospect is daunting, as the 10-plus third-party smart home apps on my phone can attest. It’s hard to overstate how big a barrier to entry Apple has just removed by exiling third-party apps from this process.

In the case of the HomeView, I watched an Apple representative instantly find, pair and register a new smart home device on both her phone and the HomeView as she carried on a casual conversation with me, not missing a beat. Everything was managed through the Apple Home app. It seemed to work like pairing new AirPods or a HomePod. I didn’t have time to dig into the process before being shepherded to the next demo, but what I saw was one of the most compelling things I’ve seen in the smart home world: an easy, intuitive setup.

It should work with all the new Apple Home collection devices from LG and Schneider Electric, as well as Matter and Apple Home accessories. This isn’t an exhaustive list, and I expect most devices, including those from Amazon and Google, should work as well.

Face ID recognition and personalized profiles make a big difference

From the side, the HomeView gives off strong iMac G4 vibes. Ajay Kumar/CNET

Personalized profiles for a smart home hub are an underrated feature, and their current implementation is pretty poor. Echo devices let you set up multiple profiles for family members and even guests, but God forbid you have to navigate the Alexa app to set what a guest has access to or trust that the voice print actually works. Despite having plenty of voice records for my wife and me, our Echo never seems to be able to differentiate between us.

With the HomeView, you have Face ID integrated, and in the brief time I had, it worked quickly without any bugs. An Apple representative showed me how they envision the HomeView being used in a nightstand setup in a bedroom, an environment where you want privacy and don’t want a stranger having access to your entire smart home.

The HomeView registered the owner and the correct profile immediately and pulled up relevant information, such as a calendar, scheduled events, and preferred home screen and customization options. The same carried over to the other HomeView devices Apple had set up in its simulated home environment, with the exterior HomeView offering a security camera view while limiting access for guests, while granting them certain features like temperature control or Safari access.

It can register up to six people by face and set up personalized profiles for each. While Apple didn’t go into detail or confirm this, I imagine that these include child and family accounts where you can set up parental controls.

The 7-inch square Liquid Retina display works well for a kitchen setup

The HomeView can keep your coffee and grinder company on the counter.

I keep an Echo Show and an Apolosign smart calendar in my kitchen. One helps with recipes and timers, while the other lets my wife and me coordinate meetings, appointments and important events. Both take up too much space on our kitchen counters because we don’t like how they look wall-mounted (more on that below).

The HomeView comes with a 7-inch square Liquid Retina display. I heard several people in the demo areas complain that it was too small. On the contrary, I think the size and shape are actually perfect for a smart home screen, especially one in my narrow galley kitchen with limited countertop space.



The square screen makes it easier to view and scroll through recipes, and it’s also hands-free while you’re cooking, adjustable and tiltable to suit your needs. You can easily share recipies from your iPhone directly to the HomeView by tapping it or accessing it directly through Siri AI and Safari. The recipes are also optimized to show you step-by-step screens that guide you through the process for those of us who aren’t great at following directions. Timers are also easy to access and set.

The base also keeps the screen directly off your dirty countertops. Apple placed it next to a fancy-looking espresso setup in a demo kitchen, and it looked great without being overwhelming. By contrast, my Apolosign calendar looks like a giant eyesore and immediately draws the eye of everyone who walks in and shows them our full schedule.

Smaller footprint and better functionality in my kitchen? Sold.

Wall mounting looks remarkably good and not like you nailed a tablet to your wall

When you buy a HomeView, you can choose between one ready to mount on a wall or one with a speaker base. Ajay Kumar/CNET

I like the idea of a smart home hub on my wall, but I hate how it looks in practice. I briefly considered mounting our Android-powered smart calendar to our kitchen wall as a central hub for our devices. Not only was it unsightly, but it also looked like we’d just taken a tablet and nailed it to our wall, with an ugly, dangling power cable off the bottom.

Apple showed me several examples of mounted HomeViews in different settings, and they all looked great. In Apple’s case, they’re professionally installed with a hidden, wired power connection in the wall, which the company recommends if you’re planning to use the HomeView as your main smart home dashboard for temperature control or as a security screen by your entryway, for instance. But if you don’t want to cut into your wall, you can also use an external adapter and cable to a nearby wall outlet.

For a wired install, you basically have three options. You can use the Schneider Home Power PoE wired mount, which provides hardwired power and Ethernet for $130, or a regular Power Mount AC Wired for $80, with installation by a licensed electrician. The last option, if you want to self-install is to use a Power Mount with a USB-C Wall connector and a separate 20W power adapter, for $60, though this leaves an external cable dangling.

I like the look of a seamless wall-mounted HomeView enough to consider a professional install, especially since I plan to use it as my always-on smart home dashboard.

Don’t underestimate the FaceTime panel for older family members

The HomeView can be used for FaceTime video calls.

I’m not a big video call person, but as my parents get older, they default to video calls. Those calls are often shaky and low-quality on the selfie cameras of whatever ancient device they’re using. Apple’s FaceTime demo for the HomeView makes its use case particularly clear. You can get your older relatives a HomeView, even set it up for them, and they can use Siri AI to video call you as needed without needing an iPhone or iPad.

I want to note that the audio on the tabletop version of the HomeView is significantly more impressive than I expected, with easily audible, room-filling sound for both video calls and music. Not the robust bass or clear lyrics I expected from a tabletop device. A full-size HomePod will deliver better sound quality, but it far outstrips an iPad for video calls or music.

It also has easy Find My integration. Apple representatives demonstrated the feature multiple times, showing how you can ask Siri AI to find a missing phone, remote or AirPods case. It worked without a hitch each time and notably, without requiring you to reach for a phone.

I also watched as the Apple representative demonstrated how the HomeView autoframed and autofocused on the video caller, and it did a good job of avoiding focusing on me as I lurked over her shoulder. (Hey, it’s my job to test these things!) Again, this is the sort of small but important quality-of-life feature that makes the HomeView more usable than its older competitors.

The smart displays I’ve tested don’t work that well. Is the HomeView really different?

Preorder the Apple HomeView Apple HomeView $290 at Amazon

I’ve used a lot of smart home screens that have promised a seamless home hub experience, including the Amazon Echo Show 8, Google Nest Hub, and various Android-powered smart calendar options like Apolosign and Skylight Calendar. While all of them worked, none did so well enough that I thought setting them up and managing them was particularly easy. Demoing the HomeView was a much smoother experience than I was expecting. Naturally, there were some hiccups — Siri AI didn’t always cooperate or register voice commands, but that may have been due to the loud environment, and nothing ever goes perfectly in a demo.

But overall, I was impressed with what I saw, and I can easily see the HomeView working for my own smart home. If it can pull off the miracle of integrating my disparate third-party apps and hodgepodge of systems together in one seamless interface for just $299, well, that’s an easy sell for me.

Tech.title: FBI Arrests OpenAI Employee Suspected of Planting a Surveillance Bug
Tech.content:
The FBI arrested an OpenAI employee and charged him with planting a surveillance device in an executive conference room to record the company’s plans for its artificial intelligence, the company and FBI confirmed on Tuesday.

The US Department of Justice identified the employee as 35-year-old Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi Arabian citizen and legal permanent resident of the US, who joined OpenAI’s product team in July 2025. He was fired and arrested on Oct. 9 on suspicion of violating US law by using “an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.” The charge comes with a possible five-year prison sentence and a $250,000 fine.

In a statement, Jay Clayton, director of national intelligence, said that the incident underscores the importance of US success in AI development as “a national security prerogative.”

More from CNET

The complaint, filed in the Northern District of California, says Alfozan allegedly placed a “thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone and microSD storage.” It was wrapped in toilet paper and stuck into a TV port. A second recording device was found in a bag Alfozan allegedly left in a printer room along with his wallet and ID.

This is one of the recording devices found in OpenAI’s conference room, according to the affidavit filed with the court by the FBI. OpenAI/FBI

The conference room where he allegedly planted the bug could be reserved only by executives and their assistants — Alfozan did not have access — and was frequently used to discuss proprietary research and hold meetings with government and industry officials. OpenAI said it has evidence Alfozan planned to place additional surveillance bugs to secretly record company meetings.

The ChatGPT maker says it discovered the first bug on Sept. 30 and alerted the FBI. During the 10 days between the discovery and arrest, the company says it took steps to contain the security risk. The company says it has not seen evidence that the safety of its products or customer data has been compromised.

“We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance,” OpenAI said in a statement.

This image included in the FBI’s affidavit shows a man looking behind a TV. OpenAI/FBI

AI and national security

OpenAI’s own AI was used to analyze forensic images of the device and assess changes in its data. In a bizarre detail that borders on a marketing pitch, OpenAI posted on X that its frontier AI was used to help investigators. There are no additional details on how its AI was used, but we may learn more later, as the investigation is ongoing.

This incident is one of the first public instances of an espionage case against an AI lab. In 2024, former Google engineer Linwei Ding was found guilty of stealing the company’s AI plans for Chinese rivals, though his conviction was partially overturned in August.

In the intense, cash-fueled worldwide competition to make the most advanced AI, a case of apparent industrial espionage isn’t surprising. What is noteworthy is how the government is responding: Washington is continuing its campaign to ensure that AI companies are seen as critical national infrastructure.

“Protecting American [super intelligence] innovation is critically important, and FBI views it as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” FBI Director Kash Patel said in an X post.

The federal government has become more involved with AI policy and with the labs creating the tech in recent months. The US’ voluntary, largely ceremonial AI Accord announced this month had many Big Tech leaders agreeing to develop AI responsibly in the wake of renewed public concern triggered in part by multiple incidents of AI agents breaking into places they shouldn’t have been able to access.

President Trump has consistently championed an “innovation first” strategy to ensure the US beats China, at the expense of AI regulation. His administration has highlighted “national security considerations” that come with AI. The Department of Defense has previously sided with AI labs, saying in a filing in a lawsuit brought by Memphis communities against Elon Musk’s xAI that the data centers powering AI are essential to military and national security activities.

Tech.title: Save Your Money. Siri AI Is Coming to Some Older Apple TVs
Tech.content:
The top justification for buying Apple’s new HomeView, fourth-generation Apple TV 4K and HomePod Mini 2 is that these devices all have the processing power to handle Siri AI, the main addition to Apple Intelligence across Apple’s line of products.

But before you place your preorder (which is open now), take a look around your home – if you already own an older Apple TV 4K, you could save yourself quite a bit of RAMaggedon money by waiting, because Siri AI is also coming to some of the devices Apple replacing.

OK, let’s do Apple TV 4K one last time

The priciest hardware upgrade is the new fourth-generation Apple TV 4K, a $300 set-top box with the same name, design, resolution and most features of the third-generation model that was released in 2022. You’re paying for a faster A19 processor, internal microphones to pick up Siri commands and queries, 128GB of storage and an Ethernet port (the only configuration of this model).

More from CNET

It also comes with a revamped Siri Remote, which looks and acts like the previous one but has precision finding and a chime that can play when you’re using FindMy to figure out which piece of furniture is hiding it.

The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K and new Siri Remote look the same, but are packed with more features. Ajay Kumar/CNET

The second- and third-generation Apple TV 4K models don’t have the built-in mics or speedier chip, but Apple notes in the fine print of its Apple TV 4K press release that they will also get Siri AI when it’s available later this year. The footnote says it’s in the TVOS 27.2 beta. It will be available in the US, Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa and the UK in English.

And that new fourth-generation Siri Remote? It’s available separately for $59, shipping Nov. 13, and it will work with the Apple TV 4K models as well as the Apple TV HD.

HomePod Minis aren’t quite as lucky

My first question after Apple’s announcement was how well the new devices would play with current ones. If my living room is a mix of first- and second-generation HomePod Minis, would a “hey Siri” summon both Siri AI and what Apple is now calling Siri Classic? I’m doubtful anyone will outright replace their existing HomePod Minis, unless they want to drop $900 on four of the diminutive speakers plus a fourth-gen Apple TV 4K to set up Apple’s surround-sound environment. (We’ll have to see how that compares with a good soundbar setup.)

This is how Apple envisions four HomePods providing surround sound connected to a fourth-generation Apple TV 4K. Apple

However, users of older HomePod Minis won’t be getting the more advanced Siri AI features. The HomePod Mini 2, with its faster S10 processor, is made to process Siri AI requests, and the same abilities won’t be available on older HomePods.

Just because Siri AI isn’t backwards compatible doesn’t mean you can’t mix and match HomePod Minis in a single setup. Basic Siri commands should still work, although we’ll have to test out arrangements to see how effective it is, since the newest HomePod Mini may have access to processing capabilities older models do not.

The iPad in the kitchen

The HomeView is Apple’s first-generation smart device with a screen, and although its design is not as iMac G4-esque as we were hoping, its ability to securely interact with multiple family members is certainly interesting. And Siri AI is a major component of a smart device that’s most at home in a kitchen.

An iPad, nestled among the other essential kitchen appliances. Matt Elliott/CNET

Except you may need to make room for it by moving your makeshift Apple kitchen helper: an iPad or iPad Mini that currently sits on an inexpensive stand – Apple’s tablets have held kitchen duties since they first arrived. You can use Siri to set timers and bring up recipes, make FaceTime calls and almost everything Apple demonstrated in its launch video. And later this year, it will get Siri AI if it’s an iPad Pro or iPad Air (M1 and later) or iPad Mini (with the A17 Pro chip). The iPad also doesn’t require a permanent power tether.

The Apple devices connecting them all

If Siri AI needs more processing power to run, how will today’s smart home devices – some of them years-old hardware – be able to keep up? All of them require owners using it nearby to have an iPhone (or iPad) capable of tapping into Siri AI. That includes iPhone 15 Pro and later models, plus the aforementioned iPads.

Apple’s video introducing the HomeView shows how multiple family members use the smart home device during a busy morning. Apple/Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

In fact, the HomeView’s ability to switch among up to six people in a household and deliver information that’s personal to them relies on each one having an Apple Intelligence-supported iPhone or iPad. It must be paired to the HomeView, on the same Wi-Fi network and recently unlocked. Maybe, along with the HomeView, everyone in the family gets upgraded to current iPhones to fully take advantage of it.

Will you really be able to get the new Siri AI features without buying new hardware?

To its credit, by extending Siri AI support, Apple isn’t completely outdating its current Apple TV 4K and HomePod Mini. If having a more interactive Apple TV with better gaming performance is important, or you’re thinking of expanding your HomePod Mini footprint in your house and can relocate current units to less-used rooms, then upgrading makes sense.

Overall, it seems Apple is playing a longer game, courting customers who want to go all-in to the Apple ecosystem – especially with the addition of Apple’s renewed push into the smart home with its Home Collection – or people who are finally ready to try this “smart home” concept and have the cash to build it out.

But if you have a smattering (or deluge) of current Apple home devices, you can wait and see how Siri AI works without footing the bill for new hardware.

Tech.title: Google’s Demis Hassabis Puts a Hopeful Spin on AI’s Environmental Impact
Tech.content:
Google DeepMind chair and co-founder Demis Hassabis took the main stage at the International AI Summit in Dublin, Ireland, on Wednesday morning to speak to global ministers, media and delegates about innovations in science and math, frontier AI and – taking a hopeful tack – the potential for AI to address climate issues.

“I actually think with the help of AI, that’s what’s going to end up giving us the technology to tackle the climate question,” he said.

During his chat, Hassabis briefly mentioned this week’s rollout of Google’s new Gemini 4 Argon model and the debacle around OpenAI’s claim to have solved the Navier-Stokes equation, one of history’s most difficult mathematical problems. But perhaps the most interesting aspect of his chat was what Hassabis did not say: AGI was not mentioned once.

More from CNET

In May, I attended the Google I/O event in Mountain View, California, and listened to Hassabis speak at length about the power of artificial general intelligence – the hard-to-pin-down concept of AI that matches human intellectual capabilities – calling it the “foothills of the singularity” and estimating that achieving AGI is on the horizon.

Five months later, a status report on progress toward AGI seemed to have slipped his mind.

Instead, Hassabis opted to use his discussion time (a 20-minute slot following Executive Vice President of the European Commission Henna Virkkunen) to outline how AI excels in disciplines such as mathematics, coding and games like Go and those from Atari. He contrasted its success in those areas with its ability physical and natural sciences – physics, chemistry, biology, engineering – which require “real-world loops” of human creativity and judgment, intuition and curiosity in creating hypotheses and developing lines of inquiry.

In 2024, Hassabis and DeepMind colleague John Jumper, along with University of Washington scientist David Baker, won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for their work on an AI model that can predict protein structures

“I think that’s the hardest thing in science is actually asking and articulating the right question,” Hassabis said. “That’s even harder than finding the answer.”

AI and the climate crisis

Before exiting the stage in Dublin, Hassabis was asked about AI’s significant sustainability problem. The massive push to build sprawling, energy-hungry data centers is spurring a surge in demand for fossil-fuel power plants, a key driver of the climate crisis.

Rather than acknowledging the stresses that data centers are exerting on our energy grid and natural resources, he expressed optimism about the potential for using AI to drive breakthroughs in green technology, clean energy and models for predicting natural disasters like floods, fires and hurricanes.

“The most important thing is that the AI systems we’re building, if we build the right types, should be able to help with things like climate modeling and weather modeling,” Hassabis said.

“Looking further forward,” he said, “AI systems will help with new sources of energy — fusion plasma containment for fusion reactors, new materials like superconductors, better batteries and better solar materials. I actually think that with the help of AI, that’s what’s going to end up giving us the technology to tackle the climate question.”

Editor’s note: Macy Meyer’s travel costs for the International AI Summit were covered by Enterprise Ireland. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: I Put the Oppo Find X10 Pro’s Camera to the Test. These Are the Results
Tech.content:
Oppo’s latest flagship Android phone, the Find X10 Pro is set to be unveiled in the coming weeks, but Oppo kindly sent me a unit ahead of time to let me take its cameras for a spin. So I did. I’ve been on multiple walks around my home in sunny Edinburgh and have taken a variety of snaps with the phone’s multiple rear cameras.

The fun part here is that while I can show you the photos — and you can see the phone in my hand above — I’m not yet allowed to talk about any specs, including the resolution of the cameras or what technology is powering them. So instead, I’m presenting these photos just as they are, almost as a little teaser ahead of the phone’s full unveiling later in the month. I’ll have a full review ready then, along with all the information about the cameras and some comparisons against other top Android camera phones like the Leica Leitzphone.

But all of that’s to come. For now, enjoy some of my early test images taken with the X10 Pro, along with as much information as my non-disclosure agreement allows me to share. Keep in mind that all photos have been imported into Adobe Lightroom in order to be easily assessed and resized for publishing online. No other edits, including sharpening, have been applied unless otherwise stated.

More from CNET

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the main camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Taken with the main camera, this image is sharp, packed with detail and has natural colors.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the ultrawide camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I don’t think I’m breaking any rules in telling you that the phone has an ultrawide camera, so here’s a photo I took with it. It looks a little more drab than the one from the main camera, but it’s still got plenty of detail.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the main camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

There are various color filters, which I almost certainly can’t tell you about here, but you probably assumed it had them anyway, right? Right?! Anyway, I used one of them (I won’t say which) to take this shot, and I like the filmic vibes it’s produced.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the main camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I used a different, unnamed, color filter here and I like the punchy tones, especially from that flash of red at the bottom of the ship.

Shot with the Oppo Find X10 Pro. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

While this color filter is much more subtle, it gives a bold blue that contrasts nicely with the building’s orange.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot in XPan mode. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The last two generations of Oppo phones (including the superb Find X9 Ultra) had Hasselblad’s XPan mode, so I can’t imagine it’s a secret that the new one does too. This mode allows you to shoot with a wide, narrow crop that’s reminiscent of Hasselblad’s legendary XPan panoramic film camera. Those cameras are rare and expensive, so this is the closest you’ll probably get to an authentic XPan experience. I love this wide, cinematic aspect ratio.

Shot with the Oppo Find X10 Pro. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

While I love the vibrancy of this image — and the sense of the warm evening glow — I do think the camera’s image processing has gone a bit hard with the “HDR” here, creating a less realistic-looking shot.

Shot with the Oppo Find X10 Pro. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

That over-processing is especially noticeable here. It’s as though the phone has desperately tried to eliminate any shadow in the image, creating a flat-looking shot that lacks the rich tones you’d expect from a good camera.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot with the main camera, in Master Mode. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The Find X10 Pro isn’t alone in this regard — I find most phones seem to go too hard on image processing, and that includes the Find X9 Ultra. The way around it is to shoot in Master mode, taking control of your white balance settings and shooting in DNG raw to avoid any built-in software and AI-based processing being applied. I made my own tweaks to this image in Adobe Lightroom.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot with the main camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

While this shot is a straight-out-of-camera image taken in the default mode. Again, I’d have to say that it looks over-processed, especially with the artificially brightened shadows.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot with the main camera, in Master Mode. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I took this shot in Master Mode specifically so I could take control of the white balance and warm the scene up to emphasise that glorious morning sunshine. I took it in JPEG and have done no further editing.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the telephoto zoom camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Yes, the phone has a telephoto zoom lens, but no I can’t tell you what that zoom factor is. What I can say is that I think this shot looks good.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the telephoto zoom camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

And this telephoto zoom shot also looks good, with sharp details and vibrant colors.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot with the telephoto lens accessory. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Like the Find X9 Ultra, the X10 Pro will be available with an add-on telephoto zoom lens to take your zoom shots even further. Here’s a white pigeon I found. While the camera struggled to get focus on the bird (getting confused by the railing in front) it eventually achieved an impressively sharp image, with natural-looking bokeh from the out-of-focus railing.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot with the telephoto lens accessory. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

And another with the add-on telephoto lens. This time it’s a seagull on a boat, even though it doesn’t need a boat because it can fly. This seagull just wants to have everything and it’s a real shame that late-stage capitalism has influenced the local birdlife in this way.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the front-facing camera. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Speaking of capitalism, I’ll end on this photo of yours truly with a Leica M6 slung around my neck. Taken with the front-facing camera, this shot has nice-looking tones, both in terms of the shadows and the colors.

I like many of these early test shots I’ve taken, and I’m looking forward to spending more time with the phone over the coming weeks. It has some stiff competition – not just from the aforementioned Leica Leitzphone and the new iPhone 18 Pro, but also from its predecessor, the Find X9 Ultra, which impressed me with its photography skills when I reviewed it in June.

Tech.title: Formlabs Just Announced the First Resin Printer Aimed at Safe Home Use
Tech.content:
Resin printers are very cool, but difficult to recommend for home crafters. When most people think about 3D printers, they think about filament and a printhead that moves around in front of you to create something. Some of this is due to availability and cost, but the biggest reason that kind of printer has become the most popular is safety. Resin printers, which use light to create a 3D shape inside a container of liquid resin, are historically best used in workshops and creative studios over a shelf in your home. Not only is the resin not safe to get on your hands, but most also produce fumes that are not safe to inhale for extended periods of time. As a result, the software driving these machines is generally less user-friendly as it’s not aimed at casual home use.

Today, the team at Formlabs is announcing the Form Studio 1, a $699 resin printer promising a home-friendly user experience and a collection of resins that don’t put off those unhealthy fumes.

Form Studio 1 $700 at Formlabs

Formlabs’ most affordable printer to date is a clear attempt to expand beyond the more industrial settings you would previously find these printers, without sacrificing the things that make other printers from this company stand out. Form Studio uses a backlight system with 28 LEDs with their own lenses to more accurately place light where it’s needed, which is a significant departure from the traditional LCD system seen in most affordable resin printers. The resin itself is loaded into the tank through the unique Formlabs cartridge system, allowing the printer to accurately tell you how much resin is left in the tank as well as allow for cartridge swapping to keep a print going when resin runs low. In terms of print speed, Formlabs promises the Form Studio is capable of printing at 130mm per hour when using its proprietary resin.

More from CNET

The real star of the show here, in my opinion, is the resin that is safer to use in your house, as well as the printer accessory that helps it even further. Formlabs’ Alpha Resins carry the UL Greenguard Gold certification for the low-emission quality, and the resin itself gives off very little odor. While a full review from CNET is still underway, I can say from early testing that odors from this printer are practically nonexistent when using the provided resin. When you combine that with the $180 VOC extractor accessory, it paints a clear picture of where this printer is designed to be safely used.

Our first print on the Form Studio 1, with its dedicated resin cartridge

Speaking of accessories, Form Studio has a ton, and they vary quite a bit in price. The flexible build plate and resin tanks are easy to swap in and out, so you can have multiple at the ready to rapidly switch resins in the printer and not have to pour anything back into a bottle. You can also upgrade to a flexible platform that makes getting the print off the plate way easier, as well as a pro-level resin tank for resins with higher curing temperatures. But my personal favorite launch accessory is the combination wash and cure station for resin prints. This combination unit takes up just about the same amount of space as the printer itself, and allows you to quickly clean and cure a resin print without making a mess or complicated drainage needs. It’s also only $200, which is incredible for what you get.

Starting today, Formlabs has opened up orders for what it’s calling the Founders Edition of the Form Studio with a few options. For a limited time, the printer will be available in four colors, with the option to upgrade to the flexible build plate for $750. If you choose to go with the standard edition, you can still grab that $700 price, but the flexible plate really is worth the extra money. Accessories for Form Studio are also available now, including resins for this printer starting at $29 for a one-liter cartridge. And don’t forget to check back, we will be conducting a thorough review of just how home-friendly this printer is soon.

Tech.title: Nintendo’s Zelda Remake Is Rewriting My Memories
Tech.content:
I spent weeks of graduate school curled up in front of my TV playing The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on my N64. I remember the epic journey with fuzzy nostalgia that, when I load up the game on the Switch’s N64 app, doesn’t entirely pay dividends. It looks uglier now than it does in my head. As Bill Pullman said in Lost Highway, “I like to remember things my own way…how I remembered them. Not necessarily the way they happened.”

Nintendo’s $60 Ocarina of Time remake for the Switch 2 filled me with uncanniness when I saw the first trailers. It was lush, almost weirdly rich with detail. Hyrule Castle Town almost looked like a theme park. Everyone’s faces seemed so…shiny.

But after an hour of playing the remake in an early preview session, I came away from it in a happy haze. If someone had never played Ocarina of Time before, this would feel like a whole new game. And if you have…this might end up being your new memory of it.

More from CNET

A beautiful rebuild

It’s a freaky thing, the idea of game remakes. It’s the same way I feel about movies being updated or remade. I like to preserve the original artifact. Nintendo has been on a roll lately, working to reboot its classic catalog into fully new versions, starting with StarFox earlier this year and now continuing with Ocarina of Time. Both were Nintendo 64 games, and both, I think, feel so new in their remade versions that they almost feel original.

And yet Ocarina is a beat-for-beat return to the original, as far as I can tell. With a few new bits, and possibly other mysteries lurking, too.

Sometimes the graphics almost feel too lush. Nintendo

I played a bit of the beginning, where Link starts off in his Kokiri forest village, where the trees actually feel like they’re pressing in now. Link can jump now and also swim in the water (I dove for some rupees). I didn’t mind the new voice acting, and the character animations won me over. It almost felt like a more immersive version of the art style in Link’s Awakening or Echoes of Wisdom, blended with Breath of the Wild/Tears of the Kingdom.

The Great Deku Tree, with its dripping root mouth, now seems more sinister or overwhelming. Every part of the game’s visuals actually feels more ramped up than even Breath of the Wild or Tears of the Kingdom, but on a smaller scale. Less overwhelming vistas, more gorgeously detailed foliage and buildings.

Running across Hyrule Field and exploring Hyrule Castle Town, talking to villagers and exploring shops, I wondered if this many characters were here before. Was it this bustling?

Everything feels atmospherically revamped. Nintendo

I played as Adult Link, too, exploring the Forest Temple and making my way through almost all its puzzles again. I played this temple long ago (and again on the Nintendo 3DS remaster), but everything is so graphically overhauled this time that some environments just feel totally new. The stained glass windows, the cathedral-like interiors…was I here before?

You can also play the Ocarina’s spell songs by actually singing them over the Switch 2’s microphone (or by tapping buttons the old school way). I tried and felt ridiculous, but it worked. Gimmicky, but fun.

Nintendo’s whole holiday lineup of Switch 2 game releases is throwbacks: Switch Sports Resort, then Ocarina of Time. I’d love some original games too, but those look like they’re on deck for 2027 (Metroid Ravenous, and the new Kirby and the World Beyond). In the meantime, is Nintendo testing the Switch 2’s graphics chops with remakes while it works out new games for the future…or biding time until more Switch owners hop aboard Switch 2? I like what I’ve tried so far, but will it make me want to play all of Ocarina all over again? We’ll find out soon.

Tech.title: Mike Tomlin’s Minecraft World Is the Talk of the Internet, but How Good Is It Really?
Tech.content:
Football coaches have the freedom to create their own worlds on the playing field. But retired Steelers legend Mike Tomlin took a different route — manifesting his vision block by block within a massive Minecraft city. What started as a shared family project with his children evolved into a solitary, 12-year labor of love. Now, the sheer depth of Tomlin’s digital city is capturing widespread attention online.

Tomlin served as the Steelers’ head coach for 19 seasons before resigning in January, having never finished with a losing record.

His video was released Oct. 1 and received more than 3 million views in less than two weeks. In the video, Tomlin shows off an expansive Minecraft city, complete with sports stadiums, high-rise apartments, homes and other buildings. He began working on the city about 12 years ago after watching his kids and their friends play Minecraft when they were in middle school, building it in the game’s creative mode with their help.

More from CNET

“I was mesmerized by what could occupy their attention for such large periods of time,” Tomlin says in the video. “I’m certainly not skilled enough in video game play or have the stick control to [play the game’s survival mode], so I got interested in this creative mode. I like to build, I’ve always had an interest in architecture, and so I started doing this creative city as a means to spend time with them.”

His kids eventually outgrew the game and moved on to different ones, high school and eventually college. That left Tomlin to work on the city by himself, which he did off and on for years while still coaching the Steelers.

“More than anything, it was therapeutic for me, some mindless entertainment,” Tomlin says. “I’m not a big TV watcher. It allowed me to detach from the realities and pressures of life.”

Tomlin spends the rest of the video showing viewers around the place, focusing on his basic, early-days architecture, penthouses, apartments and how he tried to design a solid urban space. He plans to release more videos to discuss different buildings, the city’s design and other elements of his sprawling city.

How wonderfully weird

The sprawling city features high-rises, sports stadiums and water features. Mike Tomlin

Leading up to the video’s release, there was no indication whatsoever that Mike Tomlin played computer games. That helped make his big Minecraft debut all the more delightful. The 54-year-old coach showed off thousands of hours of playtime in a 19-minute video, and no one could believe it.

“12 years of Minecraft? Didn’t you know this? Did nobody know this?” asked a shocked Ty Schmidt, producer and on-air personality of the Pat McAfee show, on an episode of the show.

The sports world finally saw what some Minecraft fans already knew: Tomlin’s dedication to the game is unmatched.

“We’re talking block by block,” McAfee said. “He had 14 30-story buildings around a body of water that he wanted to build his city around — one block at a time! They all got patios! He had a penthouse with a shark aquarium. It was unbelievable.”

Minecraft fans, too, showed up to explore the coach’s dazzling feat. Many were surprised to learn that he built this on the Bedrock edition of the game using a video game console, beginning with PlayStation 3 before moving on to PlayStation 4 and 5. That means Tomlin didn’t have access to the mods that many builders use in the Java version of the game on PC, or the freedom that a mouse and keyboard provide. He built his city one brick at a time on a PlayStation controller.

Tomlin was initially unaware of his viral fame. In an interview on Late Night with Seth Meyers, Tomlin said he was at a gala with his phone off when the video went live, and it wasn’t until later that his kids told him about the massive response. Tomlin had caught up by the time he appeared on Football Night in America with NBC on Sunday night.

“I’m appreciating all of this, to be quite honest with you,” Tomlin said during the broadcast.

How good are Tomlin’s designs?

Tomlin dedicated his entire 20-minute video to discussing architecture. Mike Tomlin

The spectacle of Tomlin’s Minecraft city is one of those wholesome events that had viewers smiling all weekend, except a few Steelers fans who were probably already pretty mad about losing to the Cleveland Browns less than 24 hours after the video was released. That didn’t stop a lot of people from wondering whether Tomlin’s city is actually as good as it looks. It turns out that most of the Internet agrees that it lives up to the hype.

“From my understanding, [it’s a] phenomenal Minecraft city,” McAfee said. “Like, as I was watching it, I was like, man, the attention to detail [is outstanding].”

Noted Minecraft city builder Alpine1 was one of the first to create his own video on the topic, and he was impressed. He had some suggestions for Tomlin, recommending that the coach consider using glass panes instead of glass blocks and more sophisticated floor designs, such as installing tile floors in showers. But Alpine1 did note that Tomlin likely started building the city before many modern building tools were available to Minecraft players.

“This is really awesome to see,” Alpine1 said in the video. “I’ve been advocating for people to build Minecraft cities for years because there’s so much you can do… and I think Mike has really captured this.”

Zach Nagel, an architecture student from the University of Cincinnati’s School of Architecture and Interior Design, also took a stab at analyzing Tomlin’s city in a separate video. He noted that Tomlin used some concepts that are actually practiced in architecture, specifically adding a penthouse with an aquarium right across the street from a full-sized aquarium.

“Now, what Coach Tomlin is talking about here, having a central theme to the building, is a term that we use in architecture as well, the parti,” Nagel says. “If you talk to 20 architects and ask them to give a definition of a parti, you might get 20 pretty different answers. At its [simplest], a parti is a single idea or scheme that drives all of the decisions you make in a building.”

Nagel goes on to praise Tomlin for not only considering the building’s exterior appearance but also its interior design and the functional needs of the city’s fictional residents. He says that a lot of Tomlin’s design choices and approach are in line with what some architects use.

“In another world, he could’ve totally gone down this career path had he wanted to,” Nagel says. “And I’m glad to see that Minecraft remains such an accessible tool for those who want to shape the environment around them.”
